facts.fact: Sound travels through air at about 340 meters per second, so counting the seconds between a lightning flash and its thunder and dividing by three gives the storm's distance in kilometers.
facts.hook: a camper counting thunder realizes the storm is closing in

facts.fact: Light bends when it passes from water into air, so a fish under the surface appears shallower and closer than it really is. To spear or net it, you have to aim below where it seems to be.
facts.hook: a first-time spear-fisher keeps missing until someone explains refraction

facts.fact: Sound moves about four times faster through water than through air, and about fifteen times faster through steel. That is why an ear pressed to a rail hears a distant train before the sound arrives through the air.
facts.hook: kids on a bridge hear the train through the rail first

facts.fact: At the same room temperature, a metal spoon feels colder than a wooden one only because metal pulls heat out of your hand much faster; a thermometer shows both are equally warm.
facts.hook: an argument about which object is colder, settled by a thermometer

facts.fact: Water expands by about nine percent when it freezes, which is why ice floats and why a completely full, sealed bottle of water can crack in a freezer.
facts.hook: a glass bottle left in a freezer shatters overnight

facts.fact: Warm air is less dense than cool air, so it rises. The air near a room's ceiling is usually noticeably warmer than the air near the floor.
facts.hook: a top bunk that is always too hot, and a thermometer proves it

facts.fact: The pitch of a siren sounds higher while it moves toward you and drops as it moves away, because the sound waves are squeezed together and then stretched out. This is called the Doppler effect.
facts.hook: a blindfolded listener can tell which way a car is going

facts.fact: A magnifying glass can focus sunlight into a spot hot enough to char paper or start tinder burning, because it gathers light from its whole surface into a single point.
facts.hook: starting a fire with a pair of reading glasses when the matches are wet

facts.fact: A rainbow always appears on the side of the sky opposite the sun, with the sun behind the viewer. You cannot see one while looking toward the sun.
facts.hook: a photographer waits in the wrong direction for a rainbow

facts.fact: Evaporating water carries heat away with it, which is why sweat cools you and why a bottle wrapped in a wet cloth stays cooler than the surrounding air when there is a breeze.
facts.hook: keeping medicine cool on a hot trip with no ice

facts.fact: A flat mirror only needs to be half your height to show your entire body, and stepping farther back does not let you see any more of yourself.
facts.hook: a family buys a mirror twice as tall as they needed

facts.fact: Pressure is force spread over an area, so lying flat on thin ice spreads your weight and makes the ice less likely to break than if you stood on it.
facts.hook: a rescue on a frozen pond done by crawling instead of walking

facts.fact: With a lever, a small push far from the pivot can lift a heavy load close to the pivot; a long plank resting on a rock can move a boulder that no one could lift directly.
facts.hook: two kids move the boulder that blocked the trail

facts.fact: Tapping glass bottles holding different amounts of water gives a lower note for more water, but blowing across their tops gives a higher note for more water, because tapping vibrates the glass while blowing vibrates the air column.
facts.hook: a homemade bottle instrument that sounds backwards when played a new way

facts.fact: Light from the sun takes about eight minutes to reach Earth, so you always see the sun as it was eight minutes ago.
facts.hook: a character realizes the sunrise they are watching already happened

facts.fact: Sea otters eat sea urchins, and sea urchins eat kelp. Where otters disappear, urchins multiply and can chew a kelp forest down to bare rock.
facts.hook: divers find bare seafloor where a kelp forest used to be

facts.fact: A honeybee returning to the hive performs a waggle dance in which the angle of the dance from straight up equals the angle of the flowers from the sun, and the length of the waggle tells the distance.
facts.hook: a young beekeeper decodes a dance to find a hidden flower patch

facts.fact: The roots of about nine out of ten plant species partner with soil fungi, trading sugar for water and minerals. Seedlings planted in sterilized soil often grow poorly without them.
facts.hook: a school garden that thrives only in soil brought from the forest

facts.fact: A lichen is a fungus and an alga living together as one organism. Many lichens die in polluted air, so tree trunks covered in lichens are a sign of clean air.
facts.hook: students map lichens to find the cleanest part of town

facts.fact: Only about ten percent of the energy at one level of a food chain reaches the next level, so it takes a huge area of plants to feed the few large predators at the top.
facts.hook: a nature reserve too small to keep even one tiger alive

facts.fact: Adult salmon find their way back from the ocean to the exact stream where they hatched by remembering its smell.
facts.hook: a stream loses its salmon after a new road culvert changes the water

facts.fact: Frogs absorb water and some oxygen directly through their thin skin, so they take in pollutants easily and are often the first animals to vanish from a contaminated pond.
facts.hook: a pond that looks fine but has gone silent at night

facts.fact: Many songbirds migrate at night, and bright lights on tall buildings and towers can confuse them, so some cities dim their lights during migration season.
facts.hook: dead birds found each morning under a brightly lit tower

facts.fact: Beaver dams slow streams into ponds and wetlands that store water and support fish, frogs, birds, and insects. Removing the beavers often lets the wetland drain away.
facts.hook: a meadow dries up the year the beavers are trapped out

facts.fact: The yellow and orange pigments of autumn leaves are present all summer but hidden by green chlorophyll. When trees stop making chlorophyll in fall, the other colors show through.
facts.hook: a kid predicts which tree will turn which color

facts.fact: Some pines, such as lodgepole and jack pine, have cones sealed with resin that open only in the heat of a fire, so those forests reseed themselves after burning.
facts.hook: seedlings covering a hillside the spring after a wildfire

facts.fact: Owls swallow small prey whole and cough up the bones and fur as a pellet. Pulling a pellet apart shows exactly which animals the owl has been eating.
facts.hook: solving what is eating the barn's mice by dissecting pellets

facts.fact: Ants lay a chemical trail from food back to the nest that other ants follow. Wiping a finger across the trail erases it, and the ants behind that point lose their way until it is rebuilt.
facts.hook: a kid redirects an entire ant column with one finger

facts.fact: At rest, the human heart pumps about five liters of blood each minute, roughly the body's whole supply, so a drop of blood makes a full circuit in about a minute.
facts.hook: a medicine's effect spreads through the body in about a minute

facts.fact: Goosebumps happen when tiny muscles at the base of each hair pull it upright. In furry animals this traps a layer of warm air; in humans it does almost nothing.
facts.hook: a shivering character notices their arms doing something useless

facts.fact: A newborn baby has around 300 bones, but many fuse together during childhood, leaving an adult with 206.
facts.hook: a bone count that comes out wrong for a baby

facts.fact: The knee-jerk reflex travels only to the spinal cord and back, never up to the brain, which is why your leg kicks before you could decide to move it.
facts.hook: a character tries and fails to stop their own reflex

facts.fact: Muscles can only pull, never push. Every joint that moves both ways needs a pair of muscles, like the biceps that bends the elbow and the triceps that straightens it.
facts.hook: a robot arm design that fails until it uses paired cables

facts.fact: Skin sheds its outer layer constantly and replaces it about every month, and some of the dust in any home is made of these dead skin cells.
facts.hook: a detective explains where the dust in a sealed room came from

facts.fact: Stomach acid is strong enough to corrode some metals, and the stomach protects itself with a mucus lining that it rebuilds every few days.
facts.hook: a swallowed coin turns up looking corroded

facts.fact: Breathing is done mainly by the diaphragm, a muscle under the lungs. A hiccup is a sudden spasm of this muscle, followed by the vocal cords snapping shut.
facts.hook: a hiccup cure that works by controlling breathing

facts.fact: Fluid in three curved canals in the inner ear tells the brain how the head is moving. After spinning, the fluid keeps swirling for a moment, which is why you feel dizzy after you stop.
facts.hook: a spinning contest explains why the loser fell down

facts.fact: Each eye has a blind spot where the optic nerve leaves the retina, but the brain fills in the gap so you never notice it. A dot on paper vanishes when its image lands on this spot.
facts.hook: a magic trick that makes a mark disappear is really a blind spot

facts.fact: A fever is not caused directly by germs; the body raises its own temperature setting on purpose, because many germs multiply more slowly when it is warmer.
facts.hook: a character learns why the doctor is not alarmed by a mild fever

facts.fact: During the teenage years, the sleep hormone melatonin is released later at night, so most teenagers naturally get sleepy and wake up later than younger children.
facts.hook: a school debate over moving the first bell later

facts.fact: Up to 80 percent of the sun's ultraviolet rays pass through clouds, so you can get sunburned on an overcast day.
facts.hook: a sunburn on the cloudy day everyone skipped sunscreen

facts.fact: Carbon monoxide, a gas with no smell, binds to red blood cells about 200 times more strongly than oxygen does, so it starves the body of oxygen even in small amounts.
facts.hook: a headache in a cabin that is really a faulty heater

facts.fact: The area of a circle grows with the square of its width, so a 16-inch pizza has almost twice as much pizza as a 12-inch one, not just a third more.
facts.hook: deciding which pizza deal is really cheaper

facts.fact: A 20 percent price drop followed by a 20 percent rise does not get back to where it started: 100 becomes 80, then 96.
facts.hook: a store's sale and markup leave a customer short-changed

facts.fact: In a group of just 23 people, there is a better than 50 percent chance that two of them share a birthday, because there are 253 different pairs to compare.
facts.hook: a classroom bet about shared birthdays

facts.fact: A fair coin that has landed heads five times in a row still has exactly a 50 percent chance of heads on the next flip; the coin has no memory.
facts.hook: a friend who is sure tails is now 'due'

facts.fact: If a model is built at one-tenth scale in every direction, it has one-hundredth the surface area and one-thousandth the volume and weight of the original.
facts.hook: a model boat that floats very differently from the real one

facts.fact: On a map with a scale of 1:50,000, one centimeter on the paper is 500 meters on the ground, so a route that looks like six centimeters is a three-kilometer walk.
facts.hook: a hike planned from a misread map scale runs far too long

facts.fact: One very large value can drag the average (mean) far above what most people have, while the median, the middle value, is not affected.
facts.hook: a 'typical salary' claim that looks wrong to the workers

facts.fact: A cylinder's volume depends on the square of its radius, so a short wide glass can hold more than a tall narrow one that looks bigger.
facts.hook: picking the wrong cup at a lemonade stand

facts.fact: A single penny doubled every day is worth over five million dollars on the thirtieth day, because repeated doubling grows explosively.
facts.hook: a bet a parent accepts and instantly regrets

facts.fact: With two six-sided dice, a total of 7 comes up more often than any other number, one time in six, while 2 and 12 each come up only one time in 36.
facts.hook: a board-game strategy built around where 7 lands

facts.fact: When a discount and a tax both apply, the order does not matter: 0.8 times 1.1 is exactly the same as 1.1 times 0.8.
facts.hook: an argument at a checkout over which to apply first

facts.fact: A triangle with sides of 3, 4, and 5 units always has a right angle, and builders still use a 3-4-5 rope or tape to check that corners are square.
facts.hook: a shed built crooked until someone brings a tape measure

facts.fact: A wheel travels its circumference, about 3.14 times its diameter, with every turn, so a bike wheel 70 centimeters across moves about 2.2 meters per rotation.
facts.hook: measuring a long path by counting wheel turns

facts.fact: On a sunny day, the ratio of your height to your shadow equals the ratio of a tree's height to its shadow, so you can find a tree's height by measuring both shadows.
facts.hook: settling how tall the old oak is without climbing it

facts.fact: Crushed ice melts faster than a solid block of the same weight because the small pieces have far more surface touching the warm air.
facts.hook: a cooler packed with the wrong kind of ice

facts.fact: Water heats and cools much more slowly than land, so coastal cities usually have milder winters and cooler summers than inland cities at the same latitude.
facts.hook: a move inland brings a shocking first winter

facts.fact: When moist air is pushed up a mountain range it cools and drops its rain on the windward side; the far side gets very little, which is why deserts often sit just behind mountains.
facts.hook: a green valley and a desert only one ridge apart

facts.fact: Seasons are caused by the tilt of Earth's axis, not by distance from the sun; Earth is actually closest to the sun in early January.
facts.hook: a character's confident explanation of winter turns out wrong

facts.fact: The Southern Hemisphere has its seasons reversed, so December is midsummer in Australia, South Africa, and Argentina.
facts.hook: a December visit that needs a swimsuit instead of a coat

facts.fact: China keeps a single time zone across its whole width, so in its far west the sun can rise at ten in the morning by the clock.
facts.hook: a video call scheduled from a wrong guess about sunrise

facts.fact: Dry desert air holds little heat overnight, so deserts like the Sahara can be scorching by day and drop below freezing on winter nights.
facts.hook: a desert trip packed only for heat

facts.fact: Air cools by about 6.5 degrees Celsius for every 1,000 meters of height, which is why Mount Kilimanjaro, close to the equator, has snow on top.
facts.hook: snow on a mountain right beside a tropical forest

facts.fact: Water boils at a lower temperature at high altitude, about 90 degrees Celsius at 3,000 meters, so food takes noticeably longer to cook in mountain camps.
facts.hook: pasta that stays crunchy at a mountain campsite

facts.fact: The Nile flows from south to north, from the highlands of East Africa to the Mediterranean Sea; 'up' on a map has nothing to do with which way a river runs.
facts.hook: a treasure map read the wrong way because of a river

facts.fact: Most Icelanders have no family surname; a child's last name is a parent's first name plus 'son' or 'dottir', so parents and children have different last names.
facts.hook: a family with three last names confuses a hotel clerk

facts.fact: The common Mercator map stretches land near the poles, making Greenland look as big as Africa, when Africa is actually about 14 times larger.
facts.hook: a geography bet lost to a globe

facts.fact: Antarctica is the driest continent on Earth; its interior gets so little snow each year that it counts as a desert.
facts.hook: an explorer's water supply matters more than the cold

facts.fact: In much of Europe and South America, a comma marks the decimal and a period groups thousands, so 1.500,50 means one thousand five hundred and a half.
facts.hook: a price misread by a factor of a thousand on a trip

facts.fact: In about a third of the world's countries, including the United Kingdom, Japan, India, and Australia, cars drive on the left side of the road.
facts.hook: a visitor steps into the street looking the wrong way

facts.fact: The Islamic calendar follows the moon and is about 11 days shorter than the solar year, so Ramadan, the month of daytime fasting, begins about 11 days earlier each year.
facts.hook: a friend's fast falls during exams one year and summer holidays another

facts.fact: The Black Death of 1347 to 1351 killed roughly a third of Europe's people. It spread along trade routes carried by fleas, and the shortage of workers afterward pushed wages up.
facts.hook: a village where the surviving workers suddenly demand more pay

facts.fact: The Great Fire of London in 1666 spread so fast because houses were built of wood and packed tightly together; afterward the city was rebuilt largely in brick and stone.
facts.hook: a town council argues over a rule to build in brick

facts.fact: In the 1840s, Ireland's poor depended almost entirely on one variety of potato. When a plant disease called blight destroyed the crop several years running, about a million people died and a million more emigrated.
facts.hook: a farm that grows only one crop faces one bad season

facts.fact: Gutenberg's printing press, developed around 1450, made books far cheaper to produce, so ideas and news spread across Europe faster than ever before.
facts.hook: a printed pamphlet reaches more people than a year of speeches

facts.fact: The Titanic in 1912 carried lifeboats for only about half the people aboard, because the rules of the time based lifeboat numbers on a ship's size, not on its passengers.
facts.hook: a safety rule that was followed exactly and still failed

facts.fact: A French attempt to dig the Panama Canal in the 1880s collapsed largely because of yellow fever and malaria. The later American effort succeeded after first draining swamps and controlling mosquitoes.
facts.hook: a project that fails until someone fights the mosquitoes instead of the jungle

facts.fact: In 1747 the ship's doctor James Lind showed that citrus fruit cured scurvy in sailors, but the British navy did not issue lemon juice to its crews until 1795, almost fifty years later.
facts.hook: a proven cure that no one in charge will adopt

facts.fact: In the 1930s, farmers on the American plains plowed up the deep-rooted prairie grass, and when drought came the loose topsoil blew away in enormous dust storms.
facts.hook: a windstorm carries a farm's soil to the next state

facts.fact: The Rosetta Stone, found in 1799, carried the same decree in Greek and in two Egyptian scripts, which let scholars finally decode hieroglyphs in the 1820s.
facts.hook: a code broken because one message was written three ways

facts.fact: In 79 CE, ash from Mount Vesuvius buried the Roman town of Pompeii so quickly that streets, shops, and even loaves of bread were preserved for nearly 1,700 years.
facts.hook: an ordinary day frozen exactly as it was

facts.fact: During an 1854 cholera outbreak in London, John Snow mapped the deaths and found they clustered around one water pump on Broad Street; removing its handle helped end the outbreak.
facts.hook: a map of sick houses points to a single well

facts.fact: The Berlin Wall was built in 1961 to stop East Germans from leaving for the West, and its sudden opening in 1989 led to Germany reuniting the next year.
facts.hook: a family split by a wall that appears overnight

facts.fact: The 1815 eruption of Mount Tambora in Indonesia threw so much ash into the sky that 1816 became the 'year without a summer', with June frosts and failed harvests in Europe and North America.
facts.hook: snow in summer blamed on a volcano across the world

facts.fact: For centuries, sailors could find their latitude from the sun and stars but not their longitude, until John Harrison built clocks in the 1700s that kept exact time at sea.
facts.hook: a ship lost because it cannot tell how far east it has sailed

facts.fact: Until 1883, each North American town set its clocks by its own local noon; the railroads created standard time zones so that their timetables would make sense.
facts.hook: two towns whose clocks disagree cause a missed train

facts.fact: A gasoline engine draws in fuel and air, squeezes the mixture, ignites it with a spark plug to push the piston, then pushes out the exhaust. A diesel engine has no spark plug; squeezing the air alone makes it hot enough to ignite the fuel.
facts.hook: the wrong fuel in a tank, and a mechanic who explains why it matters

facts.fact: Data on the internet is chopped into small packets that can each take a different route and are reassembled at the destination, so a message still arrives if one link fails.
facts.hook: a message that gets through while half the network is down

facts.fact: Electric current only flows around a complete loop. A bird on a power line is safe because both feet are on the same wire at nearly the same voltage, so no current passes through its body.
facts.hook: a rescue on a power line that hinges on touching only one wire

facts.fact: A circuit breaker or fuse cuts the power when too much current flows, so the wires do not overheat. A breaker that keeps tripping is a warning, not just a nuisance.
facts.hook: a breaker that trips every time two appliances run together

facts.fact: A lemon with a copper coin and a zinc nail stuck in it makes a small battery of about 0.9 volts. Wiring three or four in a row gives enough to light an LED.
facts.hook: a science-fair light powered by a bowl of lemons

facts.fact: Microwave ovens heat food by making the water molecules inside it vibrate, which is why a dry ceramic plate stays cool while the food on it gets hot, and why metal in the oven sparks.
facts.hook: a cold plate under piping-hot food

facts.fact: A GPS receiver works out its position by comparing timing signals from at least four satellites. It only listens, so a phone's GPS works with no cell signal as long as it can see the sky.
facts.hook: lost with no signal, but the map still knows where you are

facts.fact: A refrigerator does not make cold; it pumps heat from inside the box to the coils on its back. Leaving the door open makes the kitchen warmer overall, not cooler.
facts.hook: cooling a room with an open fridge backfires

facts.fact: Most phone touchscreens sense the electrical properties of a fingertip rather than pressure, which is why they ignore a plastic pen or an ordinary glove.
facts.hook: a phone that will not answer in winter gloves

facts.fact: Bicycle gears are a ratio: a big front gear with a small rear gear moves the bike far for each pedal turn but takes more force, while a small front and big rear makes hills easy but slow.
facts.hook: a race won by choosing gears instead of pedaling harder

facts.fact: An electric motor and a generator are the same machine run in opposite directions: feed a motor electricity and it spins, or spin it by hand and it produces electricity.
facts.hook: a hand-cranked toy motor recharges a dead flashlight

facts.fact: Almost all internet traffic between continents travels as pulses of light through fiber-optic cables laid on the ocean floor, not through satellites.
facts.hook: a ship's anchor snaps a cable and a whole region goes offline

facts.fact: Computers store everything as bits, which are zeros and ones, and eight bits make one byte with 256 possible values. That is why colors and characters are often counted in steps of 256.
facts.hook: a locked file whose code has exactly 256 possibilities

facts.fact: Water towers are tall because the height of the water creates pressure: every 10 meters of height adds roughly one atmosphere, enough to push water through the pipes even when the pumps are off.
facts.hook: a town's taps keep running the night the pump fails

facts.fact: Psychologist Thomas Gordon coined the term 'I-message' in the 1960s: a sentence like 'I felt left out' describes the speaker's feelings instead of blaming the listener with 'you'.
facts.hook: Drafting what to say to a best friend, a student crosses out 'You ditched me' and tries starting with 'I felt'.
facts.activity: falling out with a best friend and making up

facts.fact: The 'fundamental attribution error', named by psychologist Lee Ross in 1977, is the habit of blaming someone's behavior on their character while overlooking the situation they were in.
facts.hook: A kid decides their friend is just selfish for skipping the sleepover, then learns the friend's grandmother was in the hospital.
facts.activity: falling out with a best friend and making up

facts.fact: The term 'active listening' was introduced by psychologists Carl Rogers and Richard Farson in 1957; it means trying to understand the speaker's point of view, often by repeating their meaning back in your own words.
facts.hook: Midway through making up, one friend says 'So you felt I picked her over you?' and the other finally relaxes.
facts.activity: falling out with a best friend and making up

facts.fact: Saying 'I'm sorry if you were upset' is often called a non-apology, because it expresses regret about the other person's feelings rather than about what the speaker did.
facts.hook: A friend reads 'sorry if you got upset' aloud and says it sounds like it is her fault for being upset.
facts.activity: falling out with a best friend and making up

facts.fact: Hostile attribution bias is the tendency to assume someone meant to hurt you when what they did was unclear or could easily have been an accident.
facts.hook: A student is sure a friend bumped their tray on purpose, until the friend shows the slippery spot on the floor.
facts.activity: falling out with a best friend and making up

facts.fact: Relationship researcher John Gottman distinguishes a complaint, which is about one specific action, from criticism, which attacks a person's character with words like 'you always' or 'you never'.
facts.hook: A student rewrites 'You never keep secrets' into 'You told Sam what I said on Friday' before talking to a friend.
facts.activity: falling out with a best friend and making up

facts.fact: A 2015 study that followed 573 friendships formed in seventh grade found that friends who were less alike were more likely to see the friendship end.
facts.hook: Two friends who drifted apart after joining different teams find something new they both care about.
facts.activity: falling out with a best friend and making up

facts.fact: Psychologists distinguish forgiving, which means letting go of resentment, from reconciling, which means rebuilding the relationship; a person can forgive someone without the friendship returning to exactly how it was.
facts.hook: A kid tells a parent they have forgiven a friend but are not ready to be best friends again yet, and wonders if that is allowed.
facts.activity: falling out with a best friend and making up

facts.fact: Babies under one year should be put to sleep on their backs, on a firm, flat surface with no pillows, blankets or toys, which lowers the risk of sudden infant death.
facts.hook: A new babysitter reaches for a fluffy blanket for the crib, then remembers the parents' note about safe sleep.
facts.activity: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time

facts.fact: Honey should not be given to babies under 12 months old, because it can contain bacteria spores that grow in an infant's gut and cause a serious illness called infant botulism.
facts.hook: A babysitter almost sweetens a baby's food with honey until an older sibling points to the parents' written instructions.
facts.activity: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time

facts.fact: In the United States, the national Poison Help line is 1-800-222-1222, and it connects callers to a local poison control center at any hour.
facts.hook: A babysitter finds a toddler holding an open bottle of cleaner and finds the poison helpline number taped to the fridge.
facts.activity: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time

facts.fact: Shaking a baby can cause serious brain injury, because an infant's neck muscles are too weak to support its heavy head.
facts.hook: Frustrated by a baby who will not stop crying, a babysitter puts the baby safely in the crib and steps away for a moment to calm down.
facts.activity: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time

facts.fact: A young child can drown in just a few inches of water and without splashing or crying out, so children should never be left alone in or near a bath.
facts.hook: The phone rings during a toddler's bath and the babysitter wraps the child in a towel and brings them along instead of leaving.
facts.activity: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time

facts.fact: An emergency dispatcher usually first asks for the address of the emergency, so a babysitter should know the exact address of the house they are in.
facts.hook: Before the parents leave, a babysitter asks for the street address and writes it next to the phone, just in case.
facts.activity: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time

facts.fact: Crying when a parent leaves is called separation anxiety; it is a normal stage of development that commonly begins in the second half of a baby's first year.
facts.hook: A baby screams as the parents walk out, and the babysitter learns the crying usually fades once a fun distraction begins.
facts.activity: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time

facts.fact: Health agencies recommend scrubbing hands with soap for at least 20 seconds, including after changing a diaper and before preparing food.
facts.hook: After a messy diaper change, a babysitter hums a song twice at the sink before starting the child's lunch.
facts.activity: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time

facts.fact: Medicines and cleaning products should be kept up high and out of reach, because young children explore by putting things in their mouths.
facts.hook: A babysitter notices vitamins left on a low coffee table and moves them to a high shelf before the toddler toddles over.
facts.activity: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time

facts.fact: More than 200 different viruses can cause the common cold, and rhinoviruses are the most frequent cause.
facts.hook: Home sick, a student wonders why there is no single cold vaccine and looks up how many viruses cause colds.
facts.activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home

facts.fact: According to the U.S. CDC, adults catch an average of two to three colds a year, and children often catch more.
facts.hook: A kid complaining about their third cold since fall learns that is pretty normal for their age.
facts.activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home

facts.fact: Antibiotics kill bacteria but have no effect on viruses, so they do not help cure a cold or the flu.
facts.hook: A kid asks the doctor for antibiotics to get back to school faster and learns why they would not work.
facts.activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home

facts.fact: People with the flu can spread it starting about one day before they feel any symptoms.
facts.hook: A student realizes they may have caught the flu from a friend who seemed perfectly healthy at the sleepover.
facts.activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home

facts.fact: According to the U.S. CDC, people with the flu are most contagious during the first three days of their illness.
facts.hook: Feeling a little better on day two, a student wants to go to a party, and a parent explains why staying home still matters.
facts.activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home

facts.fact: Prescription flu antiviral medicines work best when started within two days after symptoms begin, which is one reason to see a doctor early.
facts.hook: A family debates waiting out a sudden high fever until the weekend, then decides to call the doctor that day.
facts.activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home

facts.fact: Green or yellow mucus comes from immune cells and an enzyme they release, so its color alone does not show whether an infection is caused by bacteria or a virus.
facts.hook: A kid panics at green tissues, sure they need medicine, and the pharmacist explains what the color really means.
facts.activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home

facts.fact: Children and teenagers should not take aspirin during flu or chickenpox, because it is linked to Reye's syndrome, a rare but serious illness affecting the liver and brain.
facts.hook: Looking for a pain reliever in the cabinet, a teen checks the label and asks an adult why the aspirin is off-limits.
facts.activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home

facts.fact: Soap breaks apart the fatty outer layer that surrounds flu viruses, which is one reason washing with soap removes them better than rinsing with water alone.
facts.hook: A younger sibling asks why they cannot just rinse with water, and the recovering older kid explains what soap does to the virus.
facts.activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home

facts.fact: A stuffy nose during a cold is caused mainly by swollen blood vessels and inflamed tissue in the lining of the nose, not only by a buildup of mucus.
facts.hook: Blowing their nose again and again with no relief, a student learns why their nose still feels blocked.
facts.activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home

facts.fact: In their 1999 dual process model, researchers Margaret Stroebe and Henk Schut described grieving people as moving back and forth between focusing on the loss and getting on with daily life.

facts.fact: In Judaism, shiva, from the Hebrew word for 'seven', is a seven-day period of mourning after a burial, when visitors come to comfort the family.

facts.fact: During Mexico's Dia de los Muertos on November 1 and 2, families build altars called ofrendas with photos and marigolds, whose color and scent are said to guide spirits home.

facts.activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died

facts.fact: During China's Qingming Festival, usually on April 4 or 5, families visit their ancestors' graves to clean them and leave offerings.

facts.activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died

facts.fact: Japan's Obon festival, held in mid-August in most regions and in July in some, honors the spirits of ancestors, who are believed to return home for a visit.

facts.fact: A eulogy is a speech praising a person who has died; the word comes from Greek roots meaning to 'speak well of'.

facts.fact: Grief can affect the body as well as feelings, often causing tiredness, trouble sleeping or changes in appetite.

facts.fact: An obituary is a published notice of someone's death that usually includes a short account of their life, such as their family, work and interests.

facts.fact: Fractures of the radius near the wrist are the most common fractures seen in children, and they usually happen from falling onto an outstretched hand.
facts.hook: A skater tries to catch a fall with their hand and ends up at the emergency room with a sore, swollen wrist.

facts.fact: The forearm has two bones: the radius, on the thumb side, and the ulna, on the little-finger side.

facts.activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast

facts.fact: A greenstick fracture is a break where the bone cracks on one side and bends on the other, like a young green branch; it happens mostly in children because their bones are more flexible.

facts.activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast

facts.fact: As a broken bone heals, the body forms a callus, a mass of cartilage and new bone that bridges the gap between the broken ends.
facts.hook: At a follow-up visit, the doctor points to a fuzzy lump on the new X-ray and explains it means the bone is healing.
facts.activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast

facts.fact: Young bones generally heal faster than adult bones, so children usually spend less time in a cast than adults with a similar break.
facts.hook: A kid and their grandfather compare casts and wonder why the grandfather's will stay on much longer.
facts.activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast

facts.fact: Bones show up white on an X-ray because the calcium in them absorbs more X-rays than the softer tissue around them.
facts.hook: A student staring at their X-ray asks why the bones glow white while their skin is barely visible.
facts.activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast

facts.fact: Near the ends of long bones are growth plates made of cartilage, where bones lengthen during childhood; a break through a growth plate can affect how the bone grows.
facts.hook: A doctor tells a family that the break missed the growth plate, and the kid asks why that is good news.
facts.activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast

facts.fact: Dutch army surgeon Antonius Mathijsen developed the plaster-of-Paris bandage for setting broken bones and published his method in 1852.
facts.hook: Choosing a cast color, a student asks how people kept broken bones still before modern casts.
facts.activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast

facts.fact: A cast saw's blade vibrates rapidly back and forth instead of spinning, which lets it cut hard plaster or fiberglass without cutting the skin underneath.
facts.hook: A kid panics as the loud cast saw approaches, and the nurse explains why it will not cut their arm.
facts.activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast

facts.fact: Doctors warn against sliding objects like pencils or sticks into a cast to scratch an itch, because they can scrape the skin and damage the cast's lining.
facts.hook: Driven crazy by an itch under the cast, a student reaches for a ruler, then remembers the doctor's warning.
facts.activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast

facts.fact: Muscles in a limb kept still in a cast weaken and shrink, which is why an arm often looks thinner when the cast comes off.
facts.hook: When the cast is removed, a kid is shocked at how skinny and weak their arm looks compared to the other one.
facts.activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast

facts.fact: An anecdote is a story about one person's experience; it cannot show that one thing caused another, because other explanations for what happened have not been ruled out.
facts.hook: An uncle at a family gathering insists a bracelet cured his back pain, and a teen asks what else might explain it.
facts.activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience

facts.fact: A control group in an experiment gets everything the test group gets except the thing being tested, so any difference between the groups can be linked to that one thing.
facts.hook: Testing whether a plant fertilizer works, a student realizes they need an identical pot with no fertilizer.
facts.activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience

facts.fact: The placebo effect is when people feel better after a treatment with no active ingredient, such as a sugar pill, simply because they expect it to help.
facts.hook: A friend swears a new energy drink made them run faster, and a student wonders if believing it did the work.
facts.activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience

facts.fact: In a double-blind trial, neither the participants nor the researchers know who is receiving the real treatment, so their expectations cannot sway the results.
facts.hook: Planning a taste test for a science fair, a student makes sure even the person serving the samples doesn't know which is which.
facts.activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience

facts.fact: Scientists assign people to groups at random so that differences like age or health are likely to be spread evenly, rather than letting people choose their group.
facts.hook: A student wonders why a study didn't just let volunteers pick whether to try the new medicine.
facts.activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience

facts.fact: Correlation does not prove causation: two things rising together, like ice cream sales and sunburns, may both be caused by something else, such as hot weather.
facts.hook: Reading a headline that links a food to good grades, a student asks what else those students might have in common.
facts.activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience

facts.fact: Results from a large sample are generally more reliable than results from a few people, because chance differences between individuals tend to even out in larger groups.
facts.hook: A kid's survey of three friends says everyone loves a snack; the class survey of 200 says something different.
facts.activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience

facts.fact: Before most scientific papers are published in a journal, other experts in the field review them for errors, a process called peer review.
facts.hook: Comparing a blog post and a journal article at the library, a student learns only one was checked by other scientists.
facts.activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience

facts.fact: Regression to the mean means unusually bad days tend to be followed by more ordinary ones, so people who try a remedy when symptoms are worst may improve even if it does nothing.
facts.hook: A grandparent credits a new tea for ending a terrible headache, and a teen wonders if it would have eased anyway.
facts.activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience

facts.fact: Psychologists Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman described the availability heuristic in 1973: people judge how common something is by how easily examples come to mind.
facts.hook: After hearing one vivid story about a shark attack, a kid refuses to swim, then checks how rare attacks really are.
facts.activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience

facts.fact: At the Scripps National Spelling Bee, spellers may ask for a word's definition, part of speech, language of origin, or a sentence using it.

facts.fact: In the Scripps National Spelling Bee, a speller may start over, but changing any letters already said counts as a misspelling.

facts.fact: Between about 1400 and 1700, English vowel sounds changed in the Great Vowel Shift after spellings had started to become fixed, which is a major reason English spelling often doesn't match pronunciation.

facts.fact: Samuel Johnson's 'A Dictionary of the English Language', published in 1755, helped settle how many English words were spelled.

facts.fact: Noah Webster's 1828 'American Dictionary of the English Language' promoted simpler spellings such as 'color' instead of 'colour', which became standard in the United States.

facts.fact: In 2021, Zaila Avant-garde became the first African-American contestant to win the Scripps National Spelling Bee.

facts.fact: Knowing a word's language of origin can help with spelling: the 'k' sound in 'chorus' is spelled 'ch' because it comes from Greek, while the 'sh' in 'chef' comes from French.

facts.fact: U.S. food safety guidelines say poultry is safely cooked when its thickest part reaches 165 degrees Fahrenheit, or about 74 degrees Celsius, measured with a food thermometer.

facts.fact: Using separate cutting boards for raw meat and for ready-to-eat foods like salad prevents cross-contamination, the spread of bacteria from one food to another.

facts.fact: Water should never be poured on a grease fire, because it turns to steam instantly and spreads the burning oil; turning off the heat and covering the pan with a lid smothers it.

facts.fact: Scooping flour straight from the bag packs it down, so a cup can hold much more flour than a recipe expects; weighing flour is more accurate.

facts.hook: a friend insists a false statement is 'just my opinion'
facts.activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked

facts.fact: Judgment words such as best, worst, beautiful, boring and should are often signs that a sentence expresses an opinion.
facts.hook: a student highlights every 'best' in a product review
facts.activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked

facts.fact: A single sentence can mix both: in 'The new park, which cost two million dollars, is a waste,' the cost can be checked but 'a waste' is an opinion.
facts.hook: a letter to the local paper about a new skate park gets pulled apart at the dinner table
facts.activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked

facts.fact: A claim can be checkable even if nobody has checked it yet; 'most students at our school walk to school' could be tested with a survey.
facts.hook: a class decides to count how students really get to school
facts.activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked

facts.fact: An opinion supported with evidence is still an opinion, but it is a more convincing one than an opinion given with no reasons.
facts.hook: a student backs up her argument for a crosswalk with a count of near-misses
facts.activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked

facts.fact: A primary source is a firsthand record from the time, such as a letter, photograph or official data, and it is often the best place to check a claim.
facts.hook: a student checks a claim about the town's founding in the old newspaper archive
facts.activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked

facts.fact: Professional fact-checkers use lateral reading: instead of judging a website by its own pages, they open new tabs to see what other sources say about it.
facts.hook: a slick website about a miracle drink turns out to be run by the company selling it
facts.activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked

facts.fact: A reverse image search can show where a photo appeared online before, which can reveal that an old picture is being passed off as new.
facts.hook: a 'breaking news' flood photo turns out to be from years earlier
facts.activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked

facts.fact: Confirmation bias is the tendency to accept claims that fit what we already believe and to doubt claims that do not, without checking either.
facts.hook: a student shares a story about a rival team without checking it because it sounds right
facts.activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked

facts.fact: PolitiFact, a US fact-checking website founded in 2007, rates claims on a scale it calls the Truth-O-Meter, from True to Pants on Fire.
facts.hook: a family looks up a claim from a TV ad and finds it rated
facts.activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked

facts.fact: A claim that cannot be checked even in principle, such as a vague promise that something 'changes lives,' gives readers nothing to test.
facts.hook: a student notices an ad makes no claim that could ever be proven wrong
facts.activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked

facts.fact: In a 1974 study by Elizabeth Loftus and John Palmer, people who were asked how fast cars 'smashed' into each other gave higher speed estimates than people asked about cars that 'hit.'
facts.hook: the way a parent asks about a hallway collision changes how a student remembers it
facts.activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently

facts.fact: Akira Kurosawa's 1950 film Rashomon tells one crime through four witnesses whose accounts contradict each other.
facts.hook: four family members describe the same broken vase in four different ways
facts.activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently

facts.fact: The parable of the blind men and the elephant, from ancient India, describes people who each touch a different part of an elephant and describe it completely differently.
facts.hook: a club argues about a project because each member has seen only one part of it
facts.activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently

facts.fact: In February 2015 a photo of a dress went viral because some people saw it as blue and black and others as white and gold; the real dress was blue and black.
facts.hook: a family splits in half over the color of the same photo
facts.activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently

facts.fact: The Rubin vase, introduced by Danish psychologist Edgar Rubin in 1915, can be seen as either a vase or two faces, but not both at the same moment.
facts.hook: two friends at a community centre see different pictures in the same poster
facts.activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently

facts.fact: In the Sally-Anne test, first used in 1985, children from about age four usually say a character will look where she left her marble, not where it was moved while she was away.
facts.hook: an older sibling realizes a little cousin does not yet know others can believe something false
facts.activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently

facts.fact: Psychologist Lee Ross named the fundamental attribution error in 1977: the tendency to blame others' actions on their personality while underestimating their situation.
facts.hook: a student assumes a classmate is rude, then learns he had just gotten bad news
facts.activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently

facts.fact: Historians still do not know who fired the first shot at Lexington in April 1775; British and colonial witnesses each said the other side fired first.
facts.hook: a history club reads two eyewitness accounts of the same morning that disagree
facts.activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently

facts.fact: In traditional Chinese culture white is worn for mourning at funerals, while in many Western weddings the bride wears white.
facts.hook: a family gathering has an awkward moment over what color to wear
facts.activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently

facts.fact: Naive realism is the belief that we see the world as it really is, so people who disagree with us must be uninformed or biased.
facts.hook: two cousins each think the other is being unreasonable about the same family story
facts.activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently

facts.fact: Two people can agree on every fact about an event and still interpret it differently because they value different things, such as fairness versus loyalty.
facts.hook: an after-school club splits over whether a teammate who covered for a friend did right
facts.activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently

facts.fact: Most vegetable seeds need water, oxygen and warmth to germinate, but not light; a few, such as lettuce, sprout better with light and are sown very shallowly.
facts.hook: lettuce seeds buried too deep in a community garden never come up
facts.activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow

facts.fact: A common gardening rule of thumb is to plant a seed about two to three times as deep as the seed is wide.
facts.hook: a student compares a tiny carrot seed to a big bean seed before planting
facts.activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow

facts.fact: Frost-tender crops such as tomatoes, peppers and squash are planted outdoors only after the last spring frost, because freezing temperatures kill them.
facts.hook: a surprise cold night threatens seedlings planted too early
facts.activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow

facts.fact: Seedlings grown indoors are usually hardened off, set outside for a little longer each day, so they can adjust to sun and wind before planting.
facts.hook: seedlings moved straight from a windowsill to the garden wilt in the sun
facts.activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow

facts.fact: Beans and peas host bacteria in small lumps on their roots, called nodules, that take nitrogen from the air and turn it into a form plants can use.
facts.hook: a gardener pulls up a bean plant and finds little bumps on its roots
facts.activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow

facts.fact: Squash plants grow separate male and female flowers, and only a female flower, which has a tiny fruit at its base, can grow into a squash after being pollinated.
facts.hook: a squash plant covered in flowers produces no squash at all
facts.activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow

facts.fact: In the Three Sisters method used by many Indigenous peoples of the Americas, corn supports climbing beans, and squash leaves shade the soil against weeds.
facts.hook: a community garden plot copies a planting plan that is centuries old
facts.activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow

facts.fact: A tomato is botanically a fruit, but in 1893 the US Supreme Court ruled in Nix v. Hedden that it counted as a vegetable for import taxes.
facts.hook: an argument at a farmers' market stand over whether tomatoes are fruit
facts.activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow

facts.fact: A layer of mulch, such as straw or wood chips, keeps soil moist, blocks weeds from sprouting and evens out soil temperature.
facts.hook: one garden bed with straw stays damp while the bare bed beside it cracks
facts.activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow

facts.fact: Rotating crops, so the same plant family is not grown in the same spot year after year, helps keep soil pests and diseases from building up.
facts.hook: tomatoes planted in the same corner every year start getting sick
facts.activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow

facts.fact: Watering deeply and less often encourages roots to grow downward, while frequent light sprinkling keeps roots near the surface where soil dries fastest.
facts.hook: two plots watered differently react very differently to a hot week
facts.activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow

facts.fact: A note's pitch depends on how fast the sound source vibrates: faster vibration makes a higher pitch, and slower vibration makes a lower one.
facts.hook: a beginner hears a string's note drop as she loosens the tuning peg
facts.activity: learning to play a musical instrument

facts.fact: Pressing a string at its exact midpoint halves the length that vibrates, and the note rises by one octave.
facts.hook: a guitar student finds the note at the twelfth fret matches the open string, only higher
facts.activity: learning to play a musical instrument

facts.fact: A standard modern piano has 88 keys: 52 white and 36 black.
facts.hook: a student counts the keys on her grandparent's piano to check
facts.activity: learning to play a musical instrument

facts.fact: The treble clef is also called the G clef because its curl circles the staff line for the note G.
facts.hook: a beginner finally remembers where G is by tracing the clef's swirl
facts.activity: learning to play a musical instrument

facts.fact: Pressing a trumpet valve sends air through an extra loop of tubing, making the air column longer and the note lower.
facts.hook: a student in a community center band wonders how three valves make so many notes
facts.activity: learning to play a musical instrument

facts.fact: Practicing in several shorter sessions spread over days usually builds a skill better than the same total time crammed into one long session.
facts.hook: a student who practices only the night before each lesson keeps making the same mistakes
facts.activity: learning to play a musical instrument

facts.fact: Studies have found that a night of sleep after practicing a finger-movement sequence can improve performance the next day without any extra practice.
facts.hook: a tricky piano passage suddenly goes better the morning after a frustrating session
facts.activity: learning to play a musical instrument

facts.fact: Research on expert performers has found that how someone practices, focusing on specific weak spots, matters more than simply playing a piece many times.
facts.hook: a student stops playing the whole song and works only on the four measures she keeps missing
facts.activity: learning to play a musical instrument

facts.fact: Pressing guitar strings repeatedly makes the fingertips sore at first; with regular practice, the skin toughens into calluses and playing hurts less.
facts.hook: a new guitar student wants to quit after a week of sore fingertips
facts.activity: learning to play a musical instrument

facts.fact: Muscle soreness after new or hard exercise usually peaks 24 to 72 hours later, not right away; this is called delayed onset muscle soreness.
facts.hook: a player feels fine after the first practice and can barely climb stairs two days later
facts.activity: playing on a sports team for the season

facts.fact: Delayed muscle soreness is not caused by lactic acid, which returns to normal levels within about an hour after exercise.
facts.hook: a teammate blames 'lactic acid' for soreness that started a day later
facts.activity: playing on a sports team for the season

facts.fact: Psychologist Bruce Tuckman proposed in 1965 that groups go through stages called forming, storming, norming and performing.
facts.hook: a new team argues a lot in the first weeks of the season before it starts to click
facts.activity: playing on a sports team for the season

facts.fact: In 1977 Tuckman and Mary Ann Jensen added a fifth stage, adjourning, for when a group finishes its work and breaks up.
facts.hook: players feel strange at the end-of-season party knowing the team will not be the same next year
facts.activity: playing on a sports team for the season

facts.fact: In 1913 Max Ringelmann reported that as more people pulled on a rope together, each person's average pull became smaller.
facts.hook: in tug-of-war at practice, a coach notices some players easing off
facts.activity: playing on a sports team for the season

facts.fact: Sweat cools the body as it evaporates, so in humid weather, when sweat evaporates slowly, athletes cool down less well and overheat more easily.
facts.hook: a sticky summer game leaves players more drained than a hotter but drier one
facts.activity: playing on a sports team for the season

facts.fact: Growth plates, areas of growing cartilage near the ends of children's bones, are weaker than the bone around them, which is why young athletes have limits on repetitive stress.
facts.hook: a young pitcher is told he has reached his pitch limit for the day
facts.activity: playing on a sports team for the season

facts.fact: Muscles grow stronger during recovery after training, not during the workout itself, so rest days are part of getting better.
facts.hook: a player who trains hard every single day starts getting slower
facts.activity: playing on a sports team for the season

facts.fact: Across many sports, home teams win more than half their games on average, an effect known as home advantage.
facts.hook: a team that keeps losing on the road wins three straight at home
facts.activity: playing on a sports team for the season

facts.fact: According to the USDA, a refrigerator keeps food safely cold for about four hours during a power cut, as long as its door stays closed.
facts.hook: A kid keeps opening the fridge in the dark to look for a snack until an older sibling suggests everyone decide first and open it only once.
facts.activity: getting through an evening power cut at home

facts.fact: A full freezer holds a safe temperature for about 48 hours without power, and a half-full one for about 24 hours, if the door stays closed.
facts.hook: During a long outage, a family works out whether the frozen food will last, since the freezer was only half full that week.
facts.activity: getting through an evening power cut at home

facts.fact: USDA guidance says thawed freezer food can be safely refrozen if it still contains ice crystals or is at 40 degrees Fahrenheit (4 degrees Celsius) or below.
facts.hook: When the lights come back, a boy checks a bag of frozen peas for ice crystals before the family decides whether to throw it out.
facts.activity: getting through an evening power cut at home

facts.fact: Safety agencies recommend flashlights rather than candles during a power cut, because a candle can easily start a fire in a dark house.
facts.hook: A grandparent reaches for candles, and the grandchild offers the flashlights from the kitchen drawer instead, remembering a fire-safety lesson.
facts.activity: getting through an evening power cut at home

facts.fact: Portable generators and charcoal grills give off carbon monoxide, so safety agencies say to run them only outdoors, far from doors and windows, never in a house or garage.
facts.hook: At a farmhouse, a teen notices an adult about to start the generator in the garage and speaks up about running it outside.
facts.activity: getting through an evening power cut at home

facts.fact: Emergency agencies advise unplugging computers and other electronics during a power cut, because a surge of electricity when the power returns can damage them.
facts.hook: Before bed, a girl goes around unplugging the gaming console and the desktop computer so they are not hit by a surge.
facts.activity: getting through an evening power cut at home

facts.fact: A fallen power line can still carry deadly electricity even when it is not sparking, so it should be treated as live, kept well away from, and reported.
facts.hook: Walking home after the storm, two friends spot a wire across the sidewalk and turn back to tell an adult to report it.
facts.activity: getting through an evening power cut at home

facts.fact: A traditional corded phone on a copper landline usually keeps working in a power cut, because the phone company powers the line, but cordless phones need household electricity.
facts.hook: At a grandparent's house, the cordless phone is dead, and a kid finds the old wall phone in the kitchen still has a dial tone.
facts.activity: getting through an evening power cut at home

facts.fact: In the dark, the eyes slowly grow more sensitive as rod cells in the retina rebuild a light-sensitive pigment called rhodopsin, which takes half an hour or more.
facts.hook: After the lights go out, a boy can barely see his hand, but half an hour later he can make out the furniture in the living room.
facts.activity: getting through an evening power cut at home

facts.fact: A 2016 world atlas of light pollution estimated that about 80 percent of North Americans cannot see the Milky Way from where they live, because of artificial light.
facts.hook: With the whole street dark, a family steps outside and sees far more stars than usual, and a kid wonders why.
facts.activity: getting through an evening power cut at home

facts.fact: The Northeast blackout that began on August 14, 2003, cut power to about 55 million people in parts of the northeastern United States and Ontario, Canada.
facts.hook: Sitting in the dark, a grandparent tells the kids about walking home from work during a huge blackout years ago.
facts.activity: getting through an evening power cut at home

facts.fact: The bandwagon technique urges people to do or buy something because "everyone else is," appealing to the wish to belong rather than giving a reason.
facts.hook: A student notices an ad saying "join the millions who already switched" and asks what the product actually does better.
facts.activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda

facts.fact: The Institute for Propaganda Analysis was founded in the United States in 1937 to teach the public how to recognize propaganda.
facts.hook: A library research project about wartime posters leads a student to a 1930s group that tried to teach ordinary people to spot propaganda.
facts.activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda

facts.fact: A testimonial uses a famous or admired person to endorse something, even though that person may have no special knowledge about it and may be paid.
facts.hook: A boy wants a pair of sneakers because a basketball star wears them, then wonders whether the star even chose them.
facts.activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda

facts.fact: In the United States, the Federal Trade Commission requires influencers and celebrities to clearly disclose when they were paid or given free products to promote something.
facts.hook: Scrolling a video review, a girl spots "#ad" in the caption and rethinks how much to trust the glowing review.
facts.activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda

facts.fact: Loaded words carry strong feelings beyond their plain meaning, so calling the same crowd "protesters" or "rioters" can push readers toward opposite opinions.
facts.hook: During a class news project, two students compare two headlines about the same event and notice how the word choice changes their reaction.
facts.activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda

facts.fact: Glittering generalities are vague, positive words like "freedom" or "natural" that make people feel good about something without saying anything specific or checkable.
facts.hook: A kid reads "all-natural goodness" on a cereal box and flips it over to see what the ingredient list actually says.
facts.activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda

facts.fact: Card stacking is showing only the facts that support one side while leaving out the facts against it, so the message seems stronger than it is.
facts.hook: A student sees a tablet ad listing five great features and goes looking for what the ad left out, like battery life.
facts.activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda

facts.fact: The plain-folks technique presents a politician or company as ordinary, everyday people, so the audience trusts them as "one of us."
facts.hook: During a school election, a candidate's poster shows him eating lunch in the cafeteria, and a classmate asks what his actual plan is.
facts.activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda

facts.fact: In a 1977 study, Lynn Hasher and colleagues found that people rated statements as more likely to be true after seeing them repeated, whether or not they were true.
facts.hook: A girl realizes she believes a rumor mostly because she has heard it five times, not because anyone showed proof.
facts.activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda

facts.fact: The word "propaganda" comes from a Catholic Church committee for spreading the faith, the Congregatio de Propaganda Fide, set up by Pope Gregory XV in 1622.
facts.hook: Looking up word histories for a vocabulary assignment, a student is surprised by where "propaganda" comes from.
facts.activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda

facts.fact: In March 1933, Joseph Goebbels became head of Nazi Germany's new Reich Ministry of Public Enlightenment and Propaganda.
facts.hook: At a museum exhibit on World War II, a class stops at a display of posters made by a government propaganda ministry.
facts.activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda

facts.fact: During the pubertal growth spurt, hands and feet usually grow first, before the arms, legs and body catch up.
facts.hook: A boy's shoes stop fitting twice in one school year, even though his jeans still fit fine.
facts.activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty

facts.fact: A voice deepens during puberty because the larynx grows and the vocal folds inside it get longer and thicker, and the voice may crack while this happens.
facts.hook: During choir practice, a boy's voice cracks on a high note, and the music teacher explains why it is happening.
facts.activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty

facts.fact: Hormones in puberty make oil glands in the skin produce more oil, called sebum, which can clog pores and lead to acne.
facts.hook: At a pharmacy, a girl compares face washes and reads the labels to understand why pimples started showing up this year.
facts.activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty

facts.fact: Fresh sweat has almost no smell; body odor comes when bacteria on the skin break down sweat from armpit glands that become active at puberty.
facts.hook: After gym class, a boy wonders why he never used to need deodorant, and an older cousin explains what changed.
facts.activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty

facts.fact: Antiperspirants reduce sweating by temporarily plugging sweat ducts, while deodorants do not stop sweat but reduce or cover the smell.
facts.hook: Standing in the store aisle, a kid has to choose between two products and reads the labels to see which one does what.
facts.activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty

facts.fact: In the United States, a large CDC survey found the median age of a girl's first period is about 12 years old, with a wide normal range around it.
facts.hook: At a friend's house, two girls talk about how their older sisters got their first periods at quite different ages.
facts.activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty

facts.fact: Bones grow longer at growth plates near their ends, and once these plates close after puberty, a person stops getting taller.
facts.hook: At the doctor's office, a boy asks whether he will keep growing, and the doctor points out his growth plates on an X-ray.
facts.activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty

facts.fact: The prefrontal cortex, the part of the brain involved in planning and controlling impulses, keeps developing through the teenage years and into a person's twenties.
facts.hook: After an impulsive choice, a teen reads that the brain's planning region is still developing and thinks about what that means.
facts.activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty

facts.fact: Fast growth during puberty often causes stretch marks, thin lines on the skin that are common and usually fade over time.
facts.hook: A girl notices faint lines on her hips and worries, until her mom mentions they are common during growth spurts.
facts.activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty

facts.fact: Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights, is marked by lighting small oil lamps called diyas and is usually celebrated over five days.
facts.hook: At a grandparent's house, a kid helps line up the diyas along the window ledge before dark, with an adult lighting them.
facts.activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family

facts.fact: Eid al-Fitr is the Muslim celebration marking the end of Ramadan, the month in which many Muslims fast from dawn until sunset.
facts.hook: A boy's family visits relatives on Eid morning after a month of fasting, and his friend from school comes along for the first time.
facts.activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family

facts.fact: Lunar New Year, celebrated in China, Korea, Vietnam and elsewhere, falls on a new moon between January 21 and February 20.
facts.hook: A kid tries to plan a school project around the family's Lunar New Year dinner and discovers the date moves every year.
facts.activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family

facts.fact: At a Passover Seder, the Jewish meal retelling the Exodus from Egypt, the youngest able child traditionally asks the Four Questions.
facts.hook: The youngest cousin at the table practices the Four Questions all week and is nervous about reading them aloud.
facts.activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family

facts.fact: A Hanukkah menorah, or hanukkiah, has nine branches: eight for the eight nights of the holiday and one for the shamash, the helper candle used to light the others.
facts.hook: A visiting friend asks why the menorah has nine candles when Hanukkah lasts eight nights.
facts.activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family

facts.fact: Sikh gurdwaras serve langar, a free communal meal offered to every visitor regardless of religion, often with everyone seated together on the floor.
facts.hook: At a gurdwara, a boy's friend is surprised he can eat a meal without paying and helps serve roti afterward.
facts.activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family

facts.fact: Sikhs celebrate Vaisakhi as the day in 1699 when Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Sikh Guru, founded the Khalsa at Anandpur.
facts.hook: During a Vaisakhi procession, a kid asks her uncle why this day matters and hears the story of the Khalsa.
facts.activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family

facts.fact: Many places of worship, including mosques, Hindu temples and Sikh gurdwaras, ask visitors to remove their shoes, and gurdwaras also ask everyone to cover their head.
facts.hook: A girl brings her friend to a gurdwara and makes sure to lend her a scarf before they go in.
facts.activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family

facts.fact: Día de los Muertos, celebrated in Mexico mainly on November 1 and 2, honors family members who have died with home altars called ofrendas.
facts.hook: At a cultural center, a class helps set up an ofrenda, and a student adds a photo of her great-grandfather.
facts.activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family

facts.fact: Nervousness triggers the release of adrenaline, which speeds up the heart and pulls blood away from the stomach, causing the "butterflies" feeling.
facts.hook: In the car on the way to the dance, a boy's stomach flips and his heart races before he even walks in.
facts.activity: going to a first school dance

facts.fact: Glow sticks light up when bending breaks a glass vial of hydrogen peroxide inside, letting it mix with other chemicals and a dye in a reaction called chemiluminescence.
facts.hook: At the dance, a friend cracks a glow stick bracelet, and another kid wonders where the light is coming from.
facts.activity: going to a first school dance

facts.fact: A glow stick shines brighter but runs out faster when it is warm, and glows dimmer but lasts longer when it is cold.
facts.hook: After the dance, a girl puts her glow stick in the freezer to see if it will still be glowing in the morning.
facts.activity: going to a first school dance

facts.fact: The U.S. agency NIOSH recommends limiting exposure to 85 decibels to eight hours a day, and each 3-decibel increase halves the safe listening time.
facts.hook: Standing next to the giant speakers, two friends move farther away when their ears start to feel strange.
facts.activity: going to a first school dance

facts.fact: Ringing in the ears after loud music, called tinnitus, is a warning sign that the ears were exposed to noise loud enough to damage hearing.
facts.hook: The morning after the dance, a boy's ears are still ringing, and he decides to stand farther from the DJ next time.
facts.activity: going to a first school dance

facts.fact: In 2009, scientists led by Aniruddh Patel showed that Snowball, a sulphur-crested cockatoo, could move in time to music and adjust when the tempo changed.
facts.hook: A shy dancer watches a video of a dancing cockatoo and decides that if a bird can keep the beat, she can too.
facts.activity: going to a first school dance

facts.fact: Line dances, in which a group repeats the same set of steps facing the same direction, let people dance together without needing a partner.
facts.hook: A boy with no one to dance with joins a line dance and finds he only needs to learn a few steps.
facts.activity: going to a first school dance

facts.fact: A mirror ball turns one spotlight into hundreds of moving spots of light because each small mirror tile reflects the beam in a slightly different direction.
facts.hook: Standing by the wall, a girl watches the spots of light sweep across the gym and figures out where they come from.
facts.activity: going to a first school dance

facts.fact: Light slowly fades the dyes and pigments in textiles, paper and some paintings, which is why many museums keep delicate items in dim rooms.
facts.hook: In a dark gallery, a student complains she can barely see an old quilt until a guide explains why the lights are low.
facts.activity: going on a school field trip with the class

facts.fact: Museums control temperature and humidity because changes make wood, paper and canvas swell and shrink, which can crack or warp old objects.
facts.hook: A student notices a humidity gauge in a display case and asks the guide what it is for.
facts.activity: going on a school field trip with the class

facts.fact: Many museums ask visitors not to touch objects, because oils and salts from skin build up over time and can stain or damage the surfaces.
facts.hook: On a historic site tour, a boy almost runs his hand along an old wooden desk, and a classmate stops him and explains why.
facts.activity: going on a school field trip with the class

facts.fact: Chicago's Engine Company 21 is widely credited with the first fire pole, installed in 1878 after a firefighter slid down a pole faster than others could take the stairs.
facts.hook: At a fire station visit, a firefighter asks the class to guess why stations once had poles instead of stairs.
facts.activity: going on a school field trip with the class

facts.fact: Dalmatians became firehouse dogs because they got along well with horses and ran ahead of horse-drawn fire carriages, helping clear the way.
facts.hook: At the fire station, a student asks why a painting of a spotted dog hangs by the old engine.
facts.activity: going on a school field trip with the class

facts.fact: In a fire, smoke and heat rise, so the cleaner, cooler air is near the floor, which is why firefighters teach people to crawl low under smoke.
facts.hook: During a fire station demonstration, the class practices crawling low under a haze from a harmless smoke machine.
facts.activity: going on a school field trip with the class

facts.fact: If clothes catch fire, the safety rule is stop, drop and roll, because running feeds the flames more oxygen.
facts.hook: A firefighter picks a volunteer from the class to show stop, drop and roll on a mat.
facts.activity: going on a school field trip with the class
