facts.fact: A cow's stomach has four compartments, and the first, the rumen, holds microbes that help break down tough grass the cow later brings back up and chews again as cud.
facts.hook: On a farm trip, the class watches a cow chewing slowly without eating anything new and asks what it is doing.
facts.activity: going on a school field trip with the class

facts.fact: A dairy cow only produces milk after she has given birth to a calf.
facts.hook: At a dairy farm, a student is surprised to learn that every cow in the milking barn has had a calf.
facts.activity: going on a school field trip with the class

facts.fact: Hens lay eggs whether or not a rooster is present; without a rooster the eggs are unfertilized and cannot hatch into chicks.
facts.hook: A kid collecting eggs on a farm trip asks if the eggs will hatch, since he doesn't see a rooster anywhere.
facts.activity: going on a school field trip with the class

facts.fact: Pigs have very few working sweat glands, so they wallow in mud or water to cool off on hot days.
facts.hook: On a hot farm visit, a student thinks the pigs are just dirty until the farmer explains the mud.
facts.activity: going on a school field trip with the class

facts.fact: The independent variable is the one thing a scientist changes on purpose, and the dependent variable is what gets measured to see the effect.
facts.hook: A student testing paper airplanes must decide whether she is changing the wing shape or measuring the distance.
facts.activity: building a project for the school science fair

facts.fact: In a fair test, every other condition is kept the same, so any difference in results can be traced to the one variable that was changed.
facts.hook: A kid's plant experiment falls apart when he realizes one pot sat by the window and the other did not.
facts.activity: building a project for the school science fair

facts.fact: A control group gets no change at all, giving a baseline to compare the tested groups against.
facts.hook: Testing fertilizer on bean plants, a student adds one plant that gets only plain water.
facts.activity: building a project for the school science fair

facts.fact: Repeating an experiment several times and averaging the results reduces the effect of random errors in any single trial.
facts.hook: A girl's first launch of her model catapult goes wildly far, so she runs it ten times before trusting the number.
facts.activity: building a project for the school science fair

facts.fact: A useful hypothesis must be testable, meaning an experiment could show it is wrong; it is often written as "If... then..."
facts.hook: A student's first idea, "music is good for plants," gets rewritten into a prediction she can actually test.
facts.activity: building a project for the school science fair

facts.fact: By convention, a graph puts the independent variable on the horizontal x-axis and the dependent variable on the vertical y-axis.
facts.hook: At the kitchen table the night before the fair, a boy redraws his graph after realizing his axes are swapped.
facts.activity: building a project for the school science fair

facts.fact: In a blind test, participants do not know which sample is which, so their expectations cannot sway their answers.
facts.hook: For a taste test of name-brand versus store-brand cereal, a girl hides the boxes and labels the bowls A and B.
facts.activity: building a project for the school science fair

facts.fact: A result that shows the hypothesis was wrong is still a real scientific result and is worth reporting.
facts.hook: A boy panics when his results prove his prediction wrong, and his teacher tells him to present them anyway.
facts.activity: building a project for the school science fair

facts.fact: Two things happening together, called correlation, does not prove that one causes the other; another factor may cause both.
facts.hook: A student finds that kids who eat breakfast get better grades and has to figure out whether breakfast is the cause.
facts.activity: building a project for the school science fair

facts.fact: A baking soda volcano erupts because baking soda (sodium bicarbonate) reacts with vinegar (acetic acid) to produce carbon dioxide gas.
facts.hook: A boy wants more than a plain volcano, so he measures how different amounts of vinegar change the eruption.
facts.activity: building a project for the school science fair

facts.fact: The American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommends 9 to 12 hours of sleep a night for children aged 6 to 12.
facts.hook: At a sleepover, the friends plan to stay up all night, then one of them remembers the soccer game the next morning.
facts.activity: going to a first sleepover at a friend's house

facts.fact: Feeling homesick while away from home is very common; nearly everyone misses something about home when they are away.
facts.hook: Lying awake in a friend's house, a girl feels homesick and is relieved when her friend admits she felt the same at camp.
facts.activity: going to a first sleepover at a friend's house

facts.fact: Sleepwalking is more common in children than in adults, and most children who sleepwalk outgrow it.
facts.hook: A kid wakes to find his friend walking toward the door with his eyes open and gently guides him back to bed.
facts.activity: going to a first sleepover at a friend's house

facts.fact: A sleeping pad keeps someone warm in a tent because the cold ground pulls heat away from the body faster than the air does.
facts.hook: In a backyard tent, a boy shivers on the bare floor until his friend's dad hands out foam pads.
facts.activity: going to a first sleepover at a friend's house

facts.fact: Since January 1, 2023, U.S. law has listed nine major food allergens, including peanuts, milk, eggs and sesame, which must be declared on packaged food labels.
facts.hook: Before ordering pizza, a host parent asks whether anyone has food allergies, and a guest checks the label on the snacks.
facts.activity: going to a first sleepover at a friend's house

facts.fact: Popcorn pops because water inside each kernel turns to steam when heated, building pressure until the hard hull bursts.
facts.hook: Making popcorn with a parent late at night, the friends notice a handful of kernels that never popped and wonder why.
facts.activity: going to a first sleepover at a friend's house

facts.fact: Snoring happens when relaxed tissues in the throat vibrate as air passes through them during sleep.
facts.hook: One friend snores so loudly that the others move their sleeping bags to the far side of the room.
facts.activity: going to a first sleepover at a friend's house

facts.fact: Yawning is contagious: seeing someone else yawn often makes people yawn too.
facts.hook: Late at night, one friend yawns and within a minute everyone in the room is yawning.
facts.activity: going to a first sleepover at a friend's house

facts.fact: Sleep talking is common in children and usually harmless, and sleep talkers normally have no memory of it the next morning.
facts.hook: The next morning, a girl insists she didn't talk in her sleep, but her friends quote what she mumbled.
facts.activity: going to a first sleepover at a friend's house

facts.fact: Bright screens late at night can delay sleep, because light, especially blue light, signals the brain to hold back the sleep hormone melatonin.
facts.hook: After hours of videos on a tablet, the friends can't fall asleep even after the lights go out.
facts.activity: going to a first sleepover at a friend's house

facts.fact: A scary story can set off a real fear response, with a racing heart and faster breathing, even when the listener knows it is made up.
facts.hook: After a ghost story in the dark, a boy jumps at a creak on the stairs and laughs when it is just the family cat.
facts.activity: going to a first sleepover at a friend's house

facts.fact: Snowflakes almost always have six sides or six arms, because water molecules link together in a six-sided pattern when they freeze.
facts.hook: Catching flakes on a dark mitten, a girl counts the arms on each one and finds they all have six.
facts.activity: spending a surprise snow day at home

facts.fact: Fresh snow is mostly trapped air, which makes it a good insulator; some small animals survive winter in tunnels under the snow.
facts.hook: Building a snow fort, two friends notice it feels less cold inside, out of the wind.
facts.activity: spending a surprise snow day at home

facts.fact: Snow looks white because its many clear ice crystals scatter and reflect all colors of light in every direction.
facts.hook: Staring out the window, a kid wonders how clear ice can make a white yard.
facts.activity: spending a surprise snow day at home

facts.fact: Salt melts ice by lowering the temperature at which water freezes, but ordinary rock salt stops working well below about minus 10 degrees Celsius (14 degrees Fahrenheit).
facts.hook: Helping shovel the front steps, a girl notices yesterday's salt isn't melting anything on a bitterly cold morning.
facts.activity: spending a surprise snow day at home

facts.fact: Fingers, toes, ears and the nose are the parts of the body most likely to get frostbite.
facts.hook: After an hour on the sledding hill, a boy's ears are numb, and his friend insists they go inside to warm up.
facts.activity: spending a surprise snow day at home

facts.fact: Wind makes cold air feel colder because it carries heat away from the skin faster, which is what the wind chill number describes.
facts.hook: A kid checks the weather app and sees the wind chill is far colder than the actual temperature.
facts.activity: spending a surprise snow day at home

facts.fact: Wet snow near the freezing point packs into snowballs well because it holds a thin layer of liquid water, while very cold, dry snow crumbles.
facts.hook: Two friends try to build a snowman, but the powder won't stick together, so they wait for the afternoon sun.
facts.activity: spending a surprise snow day at home

facts.fact: Snow squeaks underfoot when it is very cold, because the hard ice crystals rub and break instead of melting slightly under pressure.
facts.hook: Walking to a neighbor's house on a frigid morning, a kid notices every step makes a crunching squeak.
facts.activity: spending a surprise snow day at home

facts.fact: Shoveling heavy snow is hard work for the heart, so doctors advise taking breaks and lifting small loads rather than big shovelfuls.
facts.hook: A girl helps an older neighbor clear the driveway and suggests they take turns and rest between rows.
facts.activity: spending a surprise snow day at home

facts.fact: A batting average is hits divided by official at-bats, and walks do not count as at-bats, so the number gives a batter no credit for walks.
facts.hook: A kid argues his favorite player is underrated because the batting average ignores all the times he got on base by a walk.
facts.activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number

facts.fact: In both 1995 and 1996 David Justice had a higher batting average than Derek Jeter, yet Jeter's average for the two years combined was higher.
facts.hook: Comparing players on a computer, a kid is baffled that one player wins each season but loses when the seasons are added together.
facts.activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number

facts.fact: A percentage based on very few attempts can be misleading: a player who makes one shot out of one attempt shoots 100 percent.
facts.hook: A girl's teammate brags about a perfect shooting percentage after taking a single shot all season.
facts.activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number

facts.fact: Going from 40 percent to 50 percent is a rise of 10 percentage points but a 25 percent increase, so the two phrases describe the same change.
facts.hook: A kid reads two news stories about the same poll and can't understand why one says 10 and the other says 25.
facts.activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number

facts.fact: A ranking shows order but not distance: first and second place might differ by a hundredth of a second or by a whole minute.
facts.hook: Watching a race on TV, the family sees the silver medalist lose by less than a blink.
facts.activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number

facts.fact: The 2003 book "Moneyball" by Michael Lewis described how the 2002 Oakland Athletics used statistics like on-base percentage to find undervalued players.
facts.hook: At a sports bar with family, an uncle explains how a low-budget team used numbers to compete with rich teams.
facts.activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number

facts.fact: The NFL's passer rating combines several passing statistics into one number on a scale from 0 to a maximum of 158.3.
facts.hook: A kid on the couch asks why a "perfect" passer rating is such a strange number instead of 100.
facts.activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number

facts.fact: Two players can have the same average while one is steady and the other swings between great and terrible games, since an average hides how spread out the results are.
facts.hook: Picking a teammate for a tournament, two friends compare players with the same average but very different game-by-game records.
facts.activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number

facts.fact: The Gunnery camp, begun in 1861 by Connecticut schoolmaster Frederick W. Gunn, who led his students on a hike to a camp by the sea, is usually considered the first organized American summer camp.
facts.hook: a first-time camper reads the camp's history plaque and learns camps are older than she thought
facts.activity: going away to summer camp for the first time

facts.fact: The American Camp Association was founded in 1910, under the name Camp Directors Association of America, to set common standards for organized camps.
facts.hook: a camper notices an accreditation sign at the camp gate and asks a counselor what it means
facts.activity: going away to summer camp for the first time

facts.fact: Research on children at overnight camps has found that most campers feel at least some homesickness during their stay, and for most of them it stays mild.
facts.hook: a camper who thinks he is the only one missing home finds out his bunkmates feel it too
facts.activity: going away to summer camp for the first time

facts.fact: Smokey Bear's campfire rule is drown, stir, drown again, then feel for heat, because if a campfire is too hot to touch, it is too hot to leave.
facts.hook: a cabin group thinks their fire is out until a counselor has them check for heat
facts.activity: going away to summer camp for the first time

facts.fact: In parts of North America, blacklegged ticks, also called deer ticks, can spread Lyme disease, so campers there check their skin and hair for ticks after hiking through woods or tall grass.
facts.hook: a nightly tick check in the cabin that one camper wants to skip
facts.activity: going away to summer camp for the first time

facts.fact: Dermatologists advise reapplying sunscreen about every two hours outdoors, and right after swimming or heavy sweating, because it wears and washes off.
facts.hook: a camper sunburned after a long afternoon at the lake despite putting sunscreen on that morning
facts.activity: going away to summer camp for the first time

facts.fact: A canoe is most stable when paddlers keep their weight low and centered, which is why people step into the middle of a canoe rather than onto its side.
facts.hook: a first-timer in a life jacket learns why the canoe wobbled when he stepped on its edge
facts.activity: going away to summer camp for the first time

facts.fact: In the Northern Hemisphere, the two stars at the outer edge of the Big Dipper's bowl, called the pointer stars, point toward Polaris, the North Star.
facts.hook: campers lying on the dock at night try to find north without a phone
facts.activity: going away to summer camp for the first time

facts.fact: Many camps use a buddy system at the waterfront: each swimmer is paired with a partner, and at a 'buddy check' the pairs must find each other quickly so staff can count everyone.
facts.hook: a camper who wandered off at swim time realizes why her buddy looked so worried
facts.activity: going away to summer camp for the first time

facts.fact: The law of demand says that when the price of a good rises, people usually buy less of it, and when the price falls they buy more, as long as nothing else changes.
facts.hook: a kid notices fewer people buying lemonade after his sister doubles the price
facts.activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful

facts.fact: The law of supply says that when the price of a good rises, sellers usually offer more of it, because making and selling it becomes more profitable.
facts.hook: more neighbors start selling homemade bracelets after one friend's sell out at a high price
facts.activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful

facts.fact: The price at which the amount buyers want equals the amount sellers offer is called the equilibrium price, or market-clearing price.
facts.hook: a garage sale where the seller keeps adjusting a price until the last item sells
facts.activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful

facts.fact: When a price is kept below the equilibrium price, more people want the item than there are items for sale, and economists call that gap a shortage.
facts.hook: cheap concert tickets vanish in minutes and hundreds of fans get nothing
facts.activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful

facts.fact: Fresh fruits and vegetables are often cheapest at the peak of their local harvest season, when farmers have the most to sell.
facts.hook: strawberries at the farmers' market cost half what they did a month earlier
facts.activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful

facts.fact: When the price of one good rises, many buyers switch to a substitute, a similar good that does the same job, so demand for the substitute goes up.
facts.hook: a family switches snacks at the store when their usual brand's price jumps
facts.activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful

facts.fact: Demand for necessities, such as essential medicines, changes little when their price changes; economists call this inelastic demand.
facts.hook: a kid wonders why people keep buying something no matter how much its price goes up
facts.activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful

facts.fact: In 'The Wealth of Nations', published in 1776, Adam Smith pointed out that nothing is more useful than water, yet it will buy scarcely anything, while a diamond can buy a great deal.
facts.hook: a student asks why a bottle of water costs so little compared to a tiny gem
facts.activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful

facts.fact: In his 1890 book 'Principles of Economics', economist Alfred Marshall compared supply and demand to the two blades of a pair of scissors: it takes both to set a price.
facts.hook: two friends arguing whether buyers or sellers decide a price are both right
facts.activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful

facts.fact: In the United States, the cost of crude oil is usually the largest single part of the price of a gallon of gasoline, so pump prices tend to rise when crude oil prices rise.
facts.hook: a kid at the gas station asks why the price changed since last week
facts.activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful

facts.fact: In the Dutch Republic, prices for rare tulip bulbs soared in the winter of 1636 to 1637 and then collapsed in February 1637, when buyers stopped showing up.
facts.hook: a trading-card craze at school ends as suddenly as it started
facts.activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful

facts.fact: Studies of youth sports have found that players born early in the selection year are picked for teams more often than those born late, which researchers call the relative age effect.
facts.hook: a player born in December realizes most of the kids who made the team are months older
facts.activity: trying out for a school sports team

facts.fact: In the beep test, or multistage fitness test, runners go back and forth between markers usually 20 meters apart, and the beeps come faster at each new level.
facts.hook: a runner at tryouts has to decide whether to sprint early or pace herself
facts.activity: trying out for a school sports team

facts.fact: Muscle soreness after an unfamiliar workout is usually worst 24 to 72 hours afterward, which is called delayed onset muscle soreness.
facts.hook: a player who felt fine after day one of tryouts can barely climb stairs on day two
facts.activity: trying out for a school sports team

facts.fact: Title IX, a U.S. law signed in 1972, bans discrimination based on sex in schools that receive federal money, and it has been applied to their sports programs.
facts.hook: a girl trying out for a team learns why her school must offer girls' sports
facts.activity: trying out for a school sports team

facts.fact: Washington's Zackery Lystedt Law, passed in 2009, was the first U.S. state law requiring that a young athlete with a suspected concussion be removed from play until a health professional clears them.
facts.hook: a player hits his head during tryouts and wants to keep going so he doesn't miss his chance
facts.activity: trying out for a school sports team

facts.fact: All 50 U.S. states, and Washington, D.C., have passed laws on handling concussions in youth sports.
facts.hook: a coach pulls a player from the tryout after a hard fall, and the player learns it is the law
facts.activity: trying out for a school sports team

facts.fact: U.S. sleep experts recommend 9 to 12 hours of sleep a night for children aged 6 to 12, and 8 to 10 hours for teenagers.
facts.hook: a player stays up late gaming the night before tryouts and feels slow the next day
facts.activity: trying out for a school sports team

facts.fact: Losing about 2 percent of body weight in sweat without drinking enough can noticeably reduce athletic performance, especially in endurance events.
facts.hook: a swimmer forgets her water bottle and fades in the last heat of tryouts
facts.activity: trying out for a school sports team

facts.fact: A warm-up of light jogging and moving stretches raises heart rate and muscle temperature, which helps muscles work better before a hard effort.
facts.hook: a nervous player skips the warm-up to watch the others and regrets it
facts.activity: trying out for a school sports team

facts.fact: Many U.S. schools require a sports physical, a checkup by a doctor or other clinician, before a student is allowed to try out or practice with a team.
facts.hook: a player shows up to tryouts without the signed physical form
facts.activity: trying out for a school sports team

facts.fact: Many school pools are 25 yards or 25 meters long, called short course, while Olympic swimming races are held in 50-meter pools, called long course.
facts.hook: a swimmer's time from a bigger pool can't be compared directly with her tryout time
facts.activity: trying out for a school sports team

facts.fact: The first food bank, St. Mary's Food Bank in Phoenix, Arizona, was started in 1967 by John van Hengel.
facts.hook: a new volunteer reads the food bank's history on the break-room wall
facts.activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time

facts.fact: Canada's first food bank opened in 1981 in Edmonton, Alberta.
facts.hook: a volunteer asks how long food banks have existed in her country
facts.activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time

facts.fact: A food bank is usually a warehouse that collects and stores large amounts of food, while a food pantry is the local place where people pick up food directly.
facts.hook: a first-time volunteer is surprised there are no customers at the warehouse
facts.activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time

facts.fact: In the United States, Feeding America is a nationwide network of more than 200 food banks.
facts.hook: a volunteer notices the same logo on trucks from different cities
facts.activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time

facts.fact: In the United States, the USDA says a 'best if used by' date shows when a food will be at its best quality; it is not a food-safety date.
facts.hook: a sorter is about to throw out cereal one day past its date
facts.activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time

facts.fact: The U.S. Department of Agriculture estimates that between 30 and 40 percent of the U.S. food supply is wasted.
facts.hook: a volunteer sees a grocery store's donated produce and wonders how much food never gets eaten
facts.activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time

facts.fact: Gleaning means gathering crops left in fields after harvest, and some groups send volunteers to glean farms so the produce can go to food banks.
facts.hook: a Saturday picking leftover potatoes from a farmer's field
facts.activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time

facts.fact: Gleaning is an ancient practice: the Book of Leviticus in the Hebrew Bible tells farmers to leave the edges of their fields unharvested for the poor and for strangers.
facts.hook: a volunteer's grandparent recognizes the idea from an old story
facts.activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time

facts.fact: Food banks usually rotate stock by 'first in, first out', sending older items out before newer ones so less food expires on the shelves.
facts.hook: a volunteer stacks new cans in front and gets asked to redo the shelf
facts.activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time

facts.fact: The King Holiday and Service Act, signed in 1994, made Martin Luther King Jr. Day a national day of volunteer service in the United States.
facts.hook: a class signs up to volunteer on a school holiday in January
facts.activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time

facts.fact: The first Super Bowl was played on January 15, 1967, and the Green Bay Packers beat the Kansas City Chiefs 35 to 10.
facts.hook: a grandparent at the watch party claims to remember the very first one
facts.activity: watching a big game with family and friends

facts.fact: The first Super Bowl's official name was the AFL-NFL World Championship Game; the Roman numeral 'Super Bowl I' was added later.
facts.hook: a kid asks why the big game uses Roman numerals
facts.activity: watching a big game with family and friends

facts.fact: The first FIFA World Cup was held in Uruguay in 1930, and Uruguay won it, beating Argentina 4 to 2 in the final.
facts.hook: a family argues over which country won the first World Cup
facts.activity: watching a big game with family and friends

facts.fact: The Stanley Cup was donated by Lord Stanley, Canada's governor general, in 1892 and first awarded in 1893, making it the oldest trophy in North American professional sports.
facts.hook: fans at a playoff watch party wonder why the trophy looks so old
facts.activity: watching a big game with family and friends

facts.fact: Instant replay was first used in a live sports broadcast by CBS director Tony Verna during the Army-Navy football game on December 7, 1963.
facts.hook: a disputed call gets replayed and a relative says TV once couldn't do that
facts.activity: watching a big game with family and friends

facts.fact: The crowd 'wave' became known worldwide at the 1986 FIFA World Cup in Mexico, so many English speakers outside North America call it the Mexican wave.
facts.hook: a cousin from another country calls the wave by a different name
facts.activity: watching a big game with family and friends

facts.fact: In most major sports, home teams win more than half their games, an effect called home advantage.
facts.hook: friends argue whether their team only won because it played at home
facts.activity: watching a big game with family and friends

facts.fact: In the 2020 NFL season, when most games had few or no fans because of COVID-19, home teams finished 127-128-1, showing no significant home advantage.
facts.hook: a fan wonders whether cheering at the stadium really helps the team
facts.activity: watching a big game with family and friends

facts.fact: In 1997, Major League Baseball retired Jackie Robinson's number 42 for every team, the first time any professional athlete was honored that way.
facts.hook: a kid asks why no player on TV wears number 42
facts.activity: watching a big game with family and friends

facts.fact: James Naismith invented basketball in December 1891 at a YMCA training school in Springfield, Massachusetts, using peach baskets as the goals.
facts.hook: during a timeout, a kid wonders why it's called a basket
facts.activity: watching a big game with family and friends

facts.fact: The word diaspora comes from a Greek word meaning scattering, and it describes a people living spread out far from the homeland of their ancestors.
facts.hook: At a cultural festival, a friend's banner says 'diaspora' and nobody at the table can say what the word actually means.
facts.activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging

facts.fact: A name a group uses for itself is called an endonym, and a name outsiders use for it is an exonym; Germans call their country Deutschland, while English speakers say Germany.
facts.hook: A cousin visiting from abroad laughs when the family keeps using the English name for her home country instead of the one she uses.
facts.activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging

facts.fact: The word Inuit means 'the people' in the Inuktitut language, and one person is called an Inuk.
facts.hook: Writing a project caption at a community centre, a student has to decide between 'an Inuit' and the correct singular word.
facts.activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging

facts.fact: The United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, adopted on 13 September 2007, says Indigenous peoples have the right to determine their own identity and membership.
facts.hook: Two friends argue over who gets to decide which group a person belongs to, and one looks up what the UN declaration says.
facts.activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging

facts.fact: Canada's census has let people report more than one ethnic or cultural origin since 1981, so the origin totals add up to more than the country's population.
facts.hook: A student making a graph of a Canadian town's origins is puzzled that the percentages add up to well over one hundred.
facts.activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging

facts.fact: American sociologist Ruth Hill Useem coined the term 'third culture kid' in the 1950s for children raised in a culture different from their parents' home culture.
facts.hook: A new classmate who has lived in four countries can't answer 'Where are you from?' until someone mentions the phrase 'third culture kid'.
facts.activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging

facts.fact: In 1972 James Woodward proposed writing 'Deaf' with a capital D for the community and culture of sign-language users, and lowercase 'deaf' for the hearing condition itself.
facts.hook: Making a poster for a friend's sign-language club, a student has to decide whether to capitalize the word Deaf.
facts.activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging

facts.fact: A heritage language is one spoken at home or in the family that differs from the main language of the wider community, and heritage speakers may speak it without reading it.
facts.hook: At a family gathering, a kid who chats easily with her grandmother is embarrassed that she can't read the birthday card grandma wrote.
facts.activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging

facts.fact: In Hungarian, a person's family name is written before the given name, the same order used in Chinese, Japanese and Korean names.
facts.hook: A friend's Hungarian grandfather signs a card with his family name first, and the kid thinks he made a mistake.
facts.activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging

facts.fact: In experiments by psychologist Henri Tajfel, people favoured members of their own group even when the groups had been assigned completely at random.
facts.hook: At camp, cabins picked by drawing names from a hat start acting like rivals within a day, and a camper wonders why.
facts.activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging

facts.fact: In two-point perspective, both vanishing points sit on the horizon line, and the horizon line is always at the viewer's own eye level.
facts.hook: Drawing a room at a community art studio, a student puts one vanishing point near the ceiling and the other on the floor, and the room looks broken.
facts.activity: to draw a room in two-point perspective with two vanishing points

facts.fact: In two-point perspective, vertical lines such as wall corners and door edges stay straight up and down and parallel to each other; only the horizontal edges slant toward vanishing points.
facts.hook: A kid's drawing of a bedroom looks like it is tipping over because the door frame lines were angled toward a vanishing point.
facts.activity: to draw a room in two-point perspective with two vanishing points

facts.fact: Two-point perspective is used when you look at a corner, so each of the two walls meeting at that corner recedes toward its own vanishing point.
facts.hook: Sitting in a grandparent's living room, a student realizes she is facing the corner of the room and needs two vanishing points, not one.
facts.activity: to draw a room in two-point perspective with two vanishing points

facts.fact: If the two vanishing points are placed too close together, objects look stretched and distorted, so artists often put them far apart, sometimes even off the edge of the paper.
facts.hook: A drawing of a bookshelf comes out warped, and an older camper tapes extra paper to both sides of the page to move the vanishing points out.
facts.activity: to draw a room in two-point perspective with two vanishing points

facts.fact: Every horizontal line parallel to one wall, such as floorboards or a shelf edge along it, goes to that wall's vanishing point.
facts.hook: The floorboards in a student's room drawing point in random directions until she checks which wall each set runs along.
facts.activity: to draw a room in two-point perspective with two vanishing points

facts.fact: Horizontal edges above your eye level slope down toward the vanishing points, while edges below your eye level slope up toward them.
facts.hook: Drawing a room, a kid slopes the ceiling edges upward and can't figure out why the ceiling looks like it is floating away.
facts.activity: to draw a room in two-point perspective with two vanishing points

facts.fact: An object below eye level, like a table, shows its top surface in a perspective drawing, while an object above eye level, like a high shelf, shows its underside.
facts.hook: A student draws the top of a wall-mounted cupboard above her head and her friend points out you could never see it from there.
facts.activity: to draw a room in two-point perspective with two vanishing points

facts.fact: A piece of furniture turned at a different angle from the walls gets its own pair of vanishing points, but they still sit on the same horizon line.
facts.hook: The armchair in a room drawing is angled toward the TV, and the student wonders whether it can use the walls' vanishing points.
facts.activity: to draw a room in two-point perspective with two vanishing points

facts.fact: In perspective, a circle seen at an angle, such as a round rug on the floor, is drawn as an ellipse, a flattened oval.
facts.hook: A round rug in a perspective drawing still looks like a flat circle stuck on the page, and the student has to fix its shape.
facts.activity: to draw a room in two-point perspective with two vanishing points

facts.fact: Perspective construction lines are drawn lightly, often with a hard pencil, so they can be erased once the room's real edges are darkened in.
facts.hook: A student presses so hard on her guide lines that they won't erase, and her finished room drawing is covered in stray lines.
facts.activity: to draw a room in two-point perspective with two vanishing points

facts.fact: Watercolour paint is pigment bound with gum arabic, which lets it dissolve again in water even after it has dried.
facts.hook: A kid discovers that a dried paint mistake in her portrait smears when she brushes water over it, and asks why.
facts.activity: to paint a portrait in watercolour by layering washes from light to dark

facts.fact: Watercolour is transparent, so each wash lets the layers beneath show through; that is why painters work from light to dark, because a dark wash cannot be covered by a lighter one.
facts.hook: A student paints the dark hair of a portrait first and then can't add the light highlight she planned on top of it.
facts.activity: to paint a portrait in watercolour by layering washes from light to dark

facts.fact: In traditional transparent watercolour, the brightest highlights, like the shine in an eye, are usually made by leaving the white paper unpainted rather than adding white paint.
facts.hook: Halfway through a portrait at a summer camp, a kid realizes she painted over the spot she needed for the gleam in the eye.
facts.activity: to paint a portrait in watercolour by layering washes from light to dark

facts.fact: Glazing means brushing a thin transparent wash over a layer that is completely dry, so the colours mix optically instead of blending together on the paper.
facts.hook: Impatient to add shadows to a cheek, a student paints over a still-damp layer and the colours bleed into a muddy patch.
facts.activity: to paint a portrait in watercolour by layering washes from light to dark

facts.fact: Painting wet-on-wet, putting paint onto paper that is still wet, makes the colour spread with soft, blurry edges instead of crisp ones.
facts.hook: A student wants a soft background behind a portrait and asks why her crisp brushstrokes suddenly spread out like clouds.
facts.activity: to paint a portrait in watercolour by layering washes from light to dark

facts.fact: Watercolour usually looks noticeably lighter once it dries than it did while wet, so painters judge a colour only after it has dried.
facts.hook: A shadow under the chin that looked dark and strong while wet dries pale, and the student has to decide whether to add another layer.
facts.activity: to paint a portrait in watercolour by layering washes from light to dark

facts.fact: In watercolour, a wash is made lighter by adding more water to the paint rather than by mixing in white.
facts.hook: At a grandparent's house, a kid reaches for white paint to lighten a skin tone and her grandmother, a painter, hands her the water jar instead.
facts.activity: to paint a portrait in watercolour by layering washes from light to dark

facts.fact: Thin paper buckles, or cockles, when soaked with washes, so watercolour artists often use heavy paper of about 300 grams per square metre, also sold as 140-pound paper.
facts.hook: A portrait painted on printer paper wrinkles into waves, and a studio volunteer shows a student the thick watercolour pad.
facts.activity: to paint a portrait in watercolour by layering washes from light to dark

facts.fact: Masking fluid is a liquid rubber painted onto areas to keep them white; once it dries you paint over it, then rub it off to reveal the paper.
facts.hook: A student wants to keep tiny white highlights in a necklace while painting the dark shirt around it.
facts.activity: to paint a portrait in watercolour by layering washes from light to dark

facts.fact: Paint can often be partly lifted from watercolour paper by dabbing the area with a damp brush or clean tissue, which softens an edge or lightens a spot.
facts.hook: A too-dark blush on a portrait's cheek seems ruined until a friend shows how to dab some of it back up.
facts.activity: to paint a portrait in watercolour by layering washes from light to dark

facts.fact: On a shaded sphere, the highlight is the brightest spot, on the side facing the light, and its position shows where the light is coming from.
facts.hook: A student's sphere looks flat until a friend asks her which side the lamp is on.
facts.activity: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow

facts.fact: The terminator is the line on a sphere where the lit side turns into the shadow side, the edge where direct light stops reaching.
facts.hook: At a community art studio, the teacher's word 'terminator' makes a kid think of robots until she learns what it means on a sphere.
facts.activity: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow

facts.fact: The core shadow is the darkest band of shadow on the sphere itself, lying just past the terminator on the side away from the light.
facts.hook: A student shades the whole dark side of her sphere the same grey, and it looks like a flat disc instead of a ball.
facts.activity: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow

facts.fact: Reflected light is light bouncing back from the table onto a sphere's shadow side; it is lighter than the core shadow but always darker than the lit side.
facts.hook: A kid makes the bottom edge of the sphere's shadow side almost white, and suddenly the ball looks lit from two lamps.
facts.activity: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow

facts.fact: The cast shadow is the shadow the sphere throws onto the surface it rests on, and it always falls on the side opposite the light source.
facts.hook: Drawing by a window, a student puts the cast shadow on the same side as the window and her friend spots the mistake.
facts.activity: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow

facts.fact: The darkest part of a cast shadow is right where the sphere touches the surface, because almost no light can reach into that narrow gap.
facts.hook: A sphere drawing looks like it is hovering above the table until the student darkens the spot where ball and table meet.
facts.activity: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow

facts.fact: The lower a light source is, the longer the cast shadow it makes, so a lamp near the table throws a long shadow and a lamp overhead a short one.
facts.hook: Moving a desk lamp around a ball at a summer camp, kids watch the shadow grow and shrink and try to draw both.
facts.activity: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow

facts.fact: Chiaroscuro, an Italian word meaning 'light-dark', is the name for using strong contrast between light and shadow to make shapes look solid.
facts.hook: At an art gallery, a student reads 'chiaroscuro' on a painting's label and realizes it is the same thing as her sphere homework.
facts.activity: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow

facts.fact: Pencils marked H have more clay and make lighter, harder marks, while pencils marked B have more graphite and make softer, darker marks.
facts.hook: A kid can't get her sphere's shadow dark enough with an H pencil and wonders what the letters on the pencils mean.
facts.activity: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow

facts.fact: A blending stump, or tortillon, is a tightly rolled paper stick used to smooth pencil shading into gradual tones without using your finger.
facts.hook: A student smudges her sphere with a finger and leaves greasy marks, so an older artist hands her a paper stick.
facts.activity: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow

facts.fact: A kneaded eraser can be pressed and shaped to lift graphite off the paper, which lets an artist pull a highlight back out of shading.
facts.hook: Having shaded over the highlight on her sphere by accident, a kid learns to dab it back out with a soft, squishy eraser.
facts.activity: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow

facts.fact: Hatching shades an area with rows of parallel lines, and cross-hatching adds another set of lines crossing them to make the area darker.
facts.hook: With only a pen and no pencil at a grandparent's house, a kid has to shade a sphere using nothing but lines.
facts.activity: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow

facts.fact: In one-point perspective, all lines going straight back into the distance meet at a single vanishing point on the horizon line, at the viewer's eye level.
facts.hook: Sketching a street from a summer camp's main road, a student's road edges and sidewalk lines head to three different points.
facts.activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point

facts.fact: In one-point perspective, lines that face you squarely, like window tops and doorframes on a building's front, stay perfectly horizontal or vertical.
facts.hook: A kid slants every line in her street drawing, and the shop fronts facing her now look like they are falling over.
facts.activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point

facts.fact: The lines that run back toward the vanishing point are called orthogonals, and in a street scene they include road edges, curbs and rooflines.
facts.hook: At a community art studio, the teacher says 'draw your orthogonals first' and a student has to figure out which lines those are.
facts.activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point

facts.fact: Parallel lines like railway tracks or the two edges of a road look as if they meet in the distance, even though they never actually meet.
facts.hook: Standing on a quiet footbridge over train tracks, two kids argue about whether the rails really get closer together.
facts.activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point

facts.fact: In one-point perspective, objects of the same real size, like lampposts along a street, are drawn smaller and closer together the farther away they are.
facts.hook: A student draws all the lampposts on a street the same height, and the street looks like a flat wall.
facts.activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point

facts.fact: One-point perspective works when you face straight down a street, so the fronts of objects face you and everything else recedes to one point.
facts.hook: A kid tries to use one vanishing point while standing at a street corner and discovers the view needs something else.
facts.activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point

facts.fact: Masaccio's Holy Trinity fresco in Florence, painted around 1427, is one of the earliest paintings built on a single vanishing point.
facts.hook: Looking at a print of Masaccio's fresco at a gallery, a kid traces the ceiling lines with her finger to find where they meet.
facts.activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point

facts.fact: In Leonardo da Vinci's Last Supper, the single vanishing point is at Christ's head, and a nail hole Leonardo used to stretch his guide strings is still visible there.
facts.hook: A student hears that a tiny nail hole survives in one of the world's most famous paintings and wants to know what it was for.
facts.activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point

facts.fact: Moving the horizon line up or down changes the view: a low horizon makes the street feel seen from a child's height, a high one from a window above.
facts.hook: Two friends draw the same street, one sitting on the curb and one from an upstairs window, and their horizon lines end up in different places.
facts.activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point

facts.fact: Plant cells have a stiff cell wall outside the cell membrane, made mostly of cellulose, which animal cells do not have.
facts.hook: At a community garden, a kid wonders why celery stalks snap crisply while a piece of ham just bends.
facts.activity: to compare a plant cell and an animal cell and name the parts only plants have

facts.fact: Many plant cells have one large central vacuole, a water-filled sac that can take up most of the cell, while animal cells have only small vacuoles, if any.
facts.hook: Looking at a cell model at a science museum, a kid asks what the giant bubble taking up the middle of the plant cell is.
facts.activity: to compare a plant cell and an animal cell and name the parts only plants have

facts.fact: When a plant's central vacuoles are full of water they press outward against the cell walls, and when they lose water the plant wilts.
facts.hook: At a farm, the lettuce seedlings a kid forgot to water have gone floppy, and she wonders what changed inside them.
facts.activity: to compare a plant cell and an animal cell and name the parts only plants have

facts.fact: Both plant and animal cells have mitochondria, which release energy from food, so plants need mitochondria even though they make their own food.
facts.hook: A student labels mitochondria as animal-only on her comparison chart, and a friend points out that plants have them too.
facts.activity: to compare a plant cell and an animal cell and name the parts only plants have

facts.fact: Both plant and animal cells have a cell membrane, cytoplasm and a nucleus; the cell wall in plants lies outside the membrane rather than replacing it.
facts.hook: A kid thinks plant cells swapped their membrane for a wall, until she sees a diagram with both layers drawn.
facts.activity: to compare a plant cell and an animal cell and name the parts only plants have

facts.fact: Plant cells are joined by tiny channels through their walls called plasmodesmata, which let materials pass directly from one cell to the next.
facts.hook: Building a plant cell model at a science museum, a student wonders how cells trapped inside walls can share anything.
facts.activity: to compare a plant cell and an animal cell and name the parts only plants have

facts.fact: Plants store extra food as starch, while animals store it as glycogen.
facts.hook: At a farm stand, a kid learns why potatoes are full of starch and wonders where her own body keeps spare energy.
facts.activity: to compare a plant cell and an animal cell and name the parts only plants have

facts.fact: Most plant cells lack centrioles, small structures animal cells use when they divide.
facts.hook: Checking her cell comparison chart, a student spots a part in the animal cell that her plant cell drawing is missing.
facts.activity: to compare a plant cell and an animal cell and name the parts only plants have

facts.fact: Because of their rigid walls, plant cells usually have fixed, boxy shapes, while animal cells, with only a flexible membrane, are often rounded or irregular.
facts.hook: Under a museum microscope, a kid can tell which slide is leaf and which is cheek cells just from their shapes.
facts.activity: to compare a plant cell and an animal cell and name the parts only plants have

facts.fact: In 1838, the German botanist Matthias Schleiden proposed that all plant tissues are made of cells.
facts.hook: At a science museum timeline, a student notices that plants were declared to be made of cells a year before animals were.
facts.activity: to compare a plant cell and an animal cell and name the parts only plants have

facts.fact: The Galápagos finches have beaks suited to different foods, such as thin beaks for picking insects and deep, heavy beaks for cracking hard seeds.
facts.hook: At a science museum, a kid lines up finch beak models next to seeds and insects and tries to match each beak to its food.
facts.activity: to describe how natural selection changed the beak shapes of finches on different islands

facts.fact: In 1837, ornithologist John Gould told Darwin that his Galápagos birds, some of which Darwin had taken for wrens or blackbirds, were a new group of closely related finches.
facts.hook: A kid misidentifies a bird at a community garden and feels better learning that Darwin did the same thing.
facts.activity: to describe how natural selection changed the beak shapes of finches on different islands

facts.fact: Peter and Rosemary Grant began studying the medium ground finches of the small Galápagos island Daphne Major in 1973, measuring the beaks of individual birds year after year.
facts.hook: Tracking the same pond frogs every week for a project, a student learns that scientists once measured one island's finches for decades.
facts.activity: to describe how natural selection changed the beak shapes of finches on different islands

facts.fact: During a severe drought on Daphne Major in 1977, small seeds ran out, and medium ground finches with larger, deeper beaks survived better because they could crack large, hard seeds.
facts.hook: During a dry summer at a farm, a kid notices only some birds still manage to feed at the tough seed heads.
facts.activity: to describe how natural selection changed the beak shapes of finches on different islands

facts.fact: Beak size is inherited, so after the 1977 drought the survivors' offspring had larger beaks on average than the birds before the drought.
facts.hook: Looking at family photos, a student notices she has her dad's nose and connects it to how finch beaks passed down.
facts.activity: to describe how natural selection changed the beak shapes of finches on different islands

facts.fact: After the very wet El Niño year of 1983 brought many small, soft seeds, selection on Daphne Major's medium ground finches reversed, favouring smaller beaks.
facts.hook: A kid assumes 'bigger beaks are better' until she learns what happened to the finches after a rainy year.
facts.activity: to describe how natural selection changed the beak shapes of finches on different islands

facts.fact: Natural selection requires three things: individuals that vary, traits that are inherited, and some variations helping individuals survive and reproduce more than others.
facts.hook: Explaining the finch story to a younger sibling, a student realizes she has to check all three conditions before calling it natural selection.
facts.activity: to describe how natural selection changed the beak shapes of finches on different islands

facts.fact: Natural selection acts on individuals, but it is populations that evolve; a single finch cannot grow a bigger beak because it needs one.
facts.hook: A classmate says the finches 'grew bigger beaks to survive', and a student has to explain why that isn't how it works.
facts.activity: to describe how natural selection changed the beak shapes of finches on different islands

facts.fact: Charles Darwin published his theory of evolution by natural selection in the book On the Origin of Species in 1859.
facts.hook: Browsing a second-hand bookshop with a grandparent, a kid finds an old copy of On the Origin of Species and checks the original date.
facts.activity: to describe how natural selection changed the beak shapes of finches on different islands

facts.fact: Most food chains start with the sun, because plants and algae, the producers, use sunlight to make their own food by photosynthesis.
facts.hook: At a pond, a kid draws a food chain starting with a frog and a friend asks where the frog's energy really came from.
facts.activity: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears

facts.fact: In a food chain diagram, the arrows point from the thing that is eaten to the thing that eats it, showing the direction the energy flows.
facts.hook: A student's food chain poster has every arrow backward, so it looks like the grass is eating the rabbit.
facts.activity: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears

facts.fact: Animals that eat only producers are called primary consumers, and the animals that eat them are called secondary consumers.
facts.hook: At a farm, a kid sorts the animals she sees into who eats plants and who eats the plant-eaters.
facts.activity: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears

facts.fact: A top, or apex, predator is at the end of its food chain and, as an adult, has no natural predators of its own.
facts.hook: At a science museum, two friends argue whether a hawk or an owl is really at the top of the chain in their local woods.
facts.activity: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears

facts.fact: Decomposers such as fungi and bacteria break down dead plants and animals, returning nutrients to the soil that producers use again.
facts.hook: In a community garden, a kid finds mushrooms growing on an old log and wonders where they fit in her food chain.
facts.activity: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears

facts.fact: Most animals eat more than one kind of food, so real feeding relationships form a food web of many linked chains rather than one single chain.
facts.hook: A student's neat food chain for a pond breaks down when she realises the duck eats both plants and snails.
facts.activity: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears

facts.fact: When ecologist Robert Paine removed a starfish that ate mussels from a stretch of Washington State shore, mussels took over the rocks and crowded out many other species.
facts.hook: At a rocky beach tide pool, a kid learns that taking away one predator changed which animals could live there.
facts.activity: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears

facts.fact: Robert Paine introduced the term 'keystone species' in 1969 for a species whose removal changes its whole community far more than its numbers would suggest.
facts.hook: Building an arch from blocks at a science museum, a kid pulls the middle top stone and the whole arch collapses.
facts.activity: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears

facts.fact: In 1977, scientists in the submersible Alvin found deep-sea vent communities whose food chains start with bacteria using chemicals from the vents, not sunlight.
facts.hook: A kid is sure every food chain begins with the sun until she watches a documentary about creatures living in total darkness.
facts.activity: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears

facts.fact: The thin inner skin of an onion is only one cell thick, so light passes through it and single cells can be seen under a microscope.
facts.hook: A kid tries to look at a thick slice of onion under the microscope and sees only darkness.
facts.activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus

facts.fact: Onion skin cells are nearly colourless, so a drop of iodine stain is often added to make the nucleus and cell wall easier to see.
facts.hook: Under the microscope, an unstained onion slide looks like almost nothing, and a lab partner reaches for the iodine.
facts.activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus

facts.fact: The cell wall is the thick outer border you see around each onion cell, making the cells look like rows of bricks.
facts.hook: A student thinks her slide shows a brick wall until she realizes each 'brick' is a single cell.
facts.activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus

facts.fact: In a healthy onion cell, the cell membrane is pressed tightly against the inside of the cell wall, which makes the membrane very hard to see as a separate line.
facts.hook: Asked to label the cell membrane, a student can't find it anywhere and wonders whether onion cells even have one.
facts.activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus

facts.fact: Placing onion cells in salty water draws water out of them, so the cell membrane shrinks away from the cell wall and can be seen; this is called plasmolysis.
facts.hook: A lab partner adds a drop of salt water to the slide, and suddenly the membrane she couldn't find pulls into view.
facts.activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus

facts.fact: A microscope's total magnification is the eyepiece power multiplied by the objective lens power, so a 10x eyepiece with a 40x objective magnifies 400 times.
facts.hook: Two students argue whether their onion cells are magnified 50 or 400 times, and check the numbers on the lenses.
facts.activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus

facts.fact: When viewing a slide, you start with the lowest-power objective lens to find and focus on the cells before switching to higher power.
facts.hook: A kid starts on the strongest lens, sees only blur, and can't find the onion cells at all.
facts.activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus

facts.fact: Lowering the coverslip onto the slide at an angle, one edge first, helps push out air so fewer bubbles form over the cells.
facts.hook: A student's slide is full of round black-edged circles she mistakes for cells, until someone tells her they are air bubbles.
facts.activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus

facts.fact: The nucleus in an onion cell shows up as a small, round, darker spot, and it holds the cell's genetic material, DNA.
facts.hook: Labelling her drawing, a student is unsure whether the dark dot in each onion cell is dirt or a real part of the cell.
facts.activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus

facts.fact: Robert Hooke named cells in his 1665 book Micrographia after seeing tiny compartments in a thin slice of cork under his microscope.
facts.hook: At a science museum, a kid sees a copy of Hooke's cork drawing and notices it looks like her onion slide.
facts.activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus

facts.fact: The Scottish botanist Robert Brown described the cell nucleus in 1831 while studying orchid cells.
facts.hook: Labelling the nucleus on her onion slide, a student wonders who first noticed that dark spot in plant cells.
facts.activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus

facts.fact: In an atom, protons and neutrons are packed together in a tiny central nucleus, and electrons move in the space around the nucleus.
facts.hook: Building an atom model for a science fair, a kid glues the electrons into the middle with the protons, and a friend spots the mistake.
facts.activity: to build a model of an atom with protons, neutrons and electrons in the right places

facts.fact: Protons have a positive charge, electrons have a negative charge, and neutrons have no charge at all.
facts.hook: Choosing coloured beads for an atom model, a student needs a colour for the particle with no charge.
facts.activity: to build a model of an atom with protons, neutrons and electrons in the right places

facts.fact: An element's atomic number is the number of protons in the nucleus of each of its atoms; every carbon atom, for example, has exactly 6 protons.
facts.hook: Picking an element for her model, a kid reads the number on a periodic table and asks what it is counting.
facts.activity: to build a model of an atom with protons, neutrons and electrons in the right places

facts.fact: A neutral atom has the same number of electrons as protons, so the positive and negative charges cancel out.
facts.hook: A student's carbon model has 6 protons but only 4 electrons, and her grandparent asks whether the charges balance.
facts.activity: to build a model of an atom with protons, neutrons and electrons in the right places

facts.fact: A proton has about 1,836 times the mass of an electron, so almost all of an atom's mass is in its nucleus.
facts.hook: Making a model at home, a kid uses the same size of ball for protons and electrons and learns how wrong that is.
facts.activity: to build a model of an atom with protons, neutrons and electrons in the right places

facts.fact: A neutron has slightly more mass than a proton, so the two are very nearly the same size in a model.
facts.hook: Picking foam balls for her nucleus, a student wonders whether protons and neutrons should be different sizes.
facts.activity: to build a model of an atom with protons, neutrons and electrons in the right places

facts.fact: The most common kind of hydrogen atom has just one proton and one electron and no neutron at all.
facts.hook: A kid building the simplest possible atom at a science museum is surprised it needs no neutron.
facts.activity: to build a model of an atom with protons, neutrons and electrons in the right places

facts.fact: Atoms of the same element can have different numbers of neutrons; these versions are called isotopes, such as carbon-12 with 6 neutrons and carbon-14 with 8.
facts.hook: Two friends build carbon atoms with different numbers of neutrons and argue about which one is really carbon.
facts.activity: to build a model of an atom with protons, neutrons and electrons in the right places

facts.fact: J. J. Thomson discovered the electron in 1897, showing that atoms contain small, negatively charged particles.
facts.hook: Researching a science fair poster, a student finds out which of the three particles was found first.
facts.activity: to build a model of an atom with protons, neutrons and electrons in the right places

facts.fact: In the gold foil experiment, run by Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden under Ernest Rutherford, most alpha particles passed straight through, showing an atom is mostly empty space.
facts.hook: A kid's atom model is packed solid with beads until she learns that atoms are mostly empty space.
facts.activity: to build a model of an atom with protons, neutrons and electrons in the right places

facts.fact: In 1913, Niels Bohr proposed a model in which electrons travel only in certain fixed orbits, or energy levels, around the nucleus.
facts.hook: Deciding whether to use rings of wire for her electrons, a student learns which scientist first drew atoms that way.
facts.activity: to build a model of an atom with protons, neutrons and electrons in the right places

facts.fact: Blue litmus paper turns red when dipped in an acid, and red litmus paper turns blue when dipped in a base.
facts.hook: two strips of litmus paper get mixed up at a science fair booth and a student has to work out which colour means what
facts.activity: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale

facts.fact: Litmus is a dye extracted from lichens, the crusty growths found on rocks and tree bark.
facts.hook: a kid notices lichen on a grandparent's garden wall right after using litmus paper and asks if they are related
facts.activity: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale

facts.fact: Each whole step on the pH scale is a tenfold change, so a solution at pH 3 is ten times more acidic than one at pH 4.
facts.hook: a friend claims pH 3 is only a little more acidic than pH 4, and the other has to show why that is wrong
facts.activity: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale

facts.fact: Litmus paper only shows whether a solution is acidic or basic; it cannot tell how strong the acid or base is.
facts.hook: two very different liquids both turn blue litmus red, and the students realize they need another test to compare them
facts.activity: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale

facts.fact: Universal indicator changes to a range of different colours, and each colour matches a different pH number on a chart.
facts.hook: a science fair team switches from litmus to universal indicator when they need an actual pH number
facts.activity: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale

facts.fact: Lemon juice has a pH of about 2, which makes it strongly acidic compared with most things people drink.
facts.hook: a student guesses lemon juice is neutral because it is food, then the test paper says otherwise
facts.activity: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale

facts.fact: Baking soda dissolved in water makes a mildly basic solution, with a pH of about 8 to 9.
facts.hook: a kid expects baking soda water to test neutral like plain water and is surprised by the result
facts.activity: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale

facts.fact: Most traditional bar soaps are basic, with a pH of around 9 to 10.
facts.hook: a student tests soapy water at a grandparent's sink and finds it on the opposite side of the scale from vinegar
facts.activity: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale

facts.fact: The pH scale was introduced in 1909 by Danish chemist Søren Sørensen, who worked at the Carlsberg Laboratory in Copenhagen.
facts.hook: a museum placard about the pH scale settles an argument about who invented it
facts.activity: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale

facts.fact: In a physical change, a substance changes its shape or state but stays the same substance, the way ice melting into water is still water.
facts.hook: a student watching ice cubes melt at a science museum has to decide if anything new was made
facts.activity: to tell a physical change like melting from a chemical change like rusting or burning

facts.fact: In a chemical change, atoms rearrange to make one or more new substances with different properties from what you started with.
facts.hook: two friends argue whether burnt toast is still bread and look for a way to settle it
facts.activity: to tell a physical change like melting from a chemical change like rusting or burning

facts.fact: Iron rusts when it reacts with oxygen in the presence of water, forming a new substance called iron oxide.
facts.hook: a kid finds a rusty tool left out in a grandparent's garden and wonders why the one in the dry shed is fine
facts.activity: to tell a physical change like melting from a chemical change like rusting or burning

facts.fact: Salt water makes iron rust faster than fresh water, which is one reason cars rust more in places that salt their roads in winter.
facts.hook: a science fair project compares nails soaked in tap water and salt water over two weeks
facts.activity: to tell a physical change like melting from a chemical change like rusting or burning

facts.fact: Burning is a chemical change: wood combines with oxygen and turns into ash, carbon dioxide and water vapour, and it cannot turn back into wood.
facts.hook: at a campfire a student tries to explain why the logs cannot be un-burned like ice can be re-frozen
facts.activity: to tell a physical change like melting from a chemical change like rusting or burning

facts.fact: Gas bubbles that appear when two substances mix, like the fizz when baking soda meets vinegar, are one sign that a chemical change has happened.
facts.hook: a science fair volcano fizzes and a younger sibling asks where the bubbles came from
facts.activity: to tell a physical change like melting from a chemical change like rusting or burning

facts.fact: Toasting bread is a chemical change, because heat creates new brown substances and the toast cannot turn back into soft bread.
facts.hook: a kid burns toast at home and a friend says it is just a physical change, which starts a debate
facts.activity: to tell a physical change like melting from a chemical change like rusting or burning

facts.fact: Dissolving salt in water is a physical change, because evaporating the water leaves the same salt behind.
facts.hook: a student leaves salty water in a sunny window and checks what is left days later
facts.activity: to tell a physical change like melting from a chemical change like rusting or burning

facts.fact: Tearing paper is a physical change even though it cannot be undone, because every torn piece is still paper.
facts.hook: a classmate insists anything you cannot undo must be chemical, and a torn worksheet proves otherwise
facts.activity: to tell a physical change like melting from a chemical change like rusting or burning

facts.fact: In a chemical change the total mass stays the same; burning wood only seems to lose mass because the gases it makes escape into the air.
facts.hook: a student weighs a candle before and after burning and has to explain the missing mass
facts.activity: to tell a physical change like melting from a chemical change like rusting or burning

facts.fact: Frying an egg is a chemical change, because heat permanently changes the proteins in the egg white so it turns solid and white.
facts.hook: a kid cooking breakfast at a friend's house wonders why the egg white will not go clear again when it cools
facts.activity: to tell a physical change like melting from a chemical change like rusting or burning

facts.fact: The bubbles in boiling water are water vapour, the same substance as a gas, so boiling is a physical change even though it makes bubbles.
facts.hook: a student thinks bubbles always mean a chemical change until they watch a pot of water boil
facts.activity: to tell a physical change like melting from a chemical change like rusting or burning

facts.fact: An element's atomic number is the number of protons in the nucleus of every atom of that element.
facts.hook: a student at a science museum's periodic table wall has to find how many protons are in a neon atom
facts.activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number

facts.fact: The periodic table arranges the elements in order of increasing atomic number, so each element has one more proton than the element before it.
facts.hook: two friends notice the numbers on a periodic table poster count up by one and figure out why
facts.activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number

facts.fact: Hydrogen has atomic number 1, so every hydrogen atom has exactly one proton.
facts.hook: a student looks for the simplest element on the table and finds it in the top left corner
facts.activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number

facts.fact: Carbon has atomic number 6, so every carbon atom has six protons in its nucleus.
facts.hook: a kid reading a pencil label about graphite looks up carbon to find its protons
facts.activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number

facts.fact: The number of protons decides which element an atom is: any atom with eight protons is oxygen, and an atom with seven protons is nitrogen.
facts.hook: a quiz question asks what happens if an oxygen atom somehow lost a proton, and the answer surprises the class
facts.activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number

facts.fact: In a neutral atom, the number of electrons equals the number of protons, so the atomic number also tells you how many electrons it has.
facts.hook: a student drawing a model of a sodium atom has to decide how many electrons to add
facts.activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number

facts.fact: Atoms of the same element can have different numbers of neutrons; these versions are called isotopes, but they always have the same number of protons.
facts.hook: a museum guide mentions carbon-14 and a kid wonders whether it is still carbon
facts.activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number

facts.fact: Subtracting an element's atomic number from an atom's mass number gives the number of neutrons, because the mass number counts protons plus neutrons.
facts.hook: a student working a practice sheet at a grandparent's table figures out neutrons without being told them
facts.activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number

facts.fact: Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev published an early version of the periodic table in 1869.
facts.hook: a science museum timeline shows the first periodic table and a kid notices how few elements it had
facts.activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number

facts.fact: Mendeleev left gaps in his table for elements that had not been discovered yet, and later discoveries such as gallium filled them.
facts.hook: a student wonders why an old periodic table has blank spaces in it
facts.activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number

facts.fact: The vertical columns of the periodic table are called groups, and elements in the same group tend to have similar chemical properties.
facts.hook: a kid notices that helium, neon and argon sit in one column and asks what they have in common
facts.activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number

facts.fact: Some element symbols come from Latin names, such as Fe for iron, from the Latin word ferrum.
facts.hook: a student searches the table for an 'I' symbol for iron and cannot find it
