facts.activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number

facts.fact: A bylaw is a rule made by a local government, such as a city or town council, and it applies only within that municipality.
facts.hook: a kid at a community centre learns the skateboard ban at the park is a town bylaw, not a national law
facts.activity: to explain how a citizen can petition a councillor to change a local bylaw

facts.fact: In Canada, municipalities get their power to make bylaws from provincial laws, because the Constitution Act, 1867 gives provinces control over municipal institutions.
facts.hook: a student asks why a city cannot pass any bylaw it likes and a council staff member explains the limits
facts.activity: to explain how a citizen can petition a councillor to change a local bylaw

facts.fact: A petition is a written request, signed by many people, asking a government body to take a specific action.
facts.hook: a group of friends wants a crosswalk near their school and decides to gather signatures
facts.activity: to explain how a citizen can petition a councillor to change a local bylaw

facts.fact: In many cities, each councillor is elected to represent one area of the city, often called a ward.
facts.hook: a student has to find out which ward they live in before knowing which councillor to email
facts.activity: to explain how a citizen can petition a councillor to change a local bylaw

facts.fact: A single councillor cannot change a bylaw alone; a change needs a majority vote of the whole council.
facts.hook: a kid is disappointed when a friendly councillor says they cannot just change the rule themselves
facts.activity: to explain how a citizen can petition a councillor to change a local bylaw

facts.fact: Many Canadian municipalities let residents ask to speak briefly at a council or committee meeting, which is called appearing as a delegation.
facts.hook: a nervous student practises a five-minute delegation speech at a grandparent's house the night before
facts.activity: to explain how a citizen can petition a councillor to change a local bylaw

facts.fact: Municipalities that allow delegations usually require people to register with the city clerk's office before the meeting.
facts.hook: a group shows up to speak at council and learns they needed to sign up with the clerk ahead of time
facts.activity: to explain how a citizen can petition a councillor to change a local bylaw

facts.fact: At a council meeting, a proposal usually needs one member to move it and another to second it before council debates and votes on it.
facts.hook: a student watching council waits anxiously to see if any councillor will second the motion about their park
facts.activity: to explain how a citizen can petition a councillor to change a local bylaw

facts.fact: Councils often send a proposed bylaw change to a committee first, which studies it and recommends whether the full council should approve it.
facts.hook: a group's petition is sent to a committee and they have to decide whether to speak there too
facts.activity: to explain how a citizen can petition a councillor to change a local bylaw

facts.fact: Municipal bylaws commonly cover local matters such as parking, noise, pets and garbage collection.
facts.hook: a kid bothered by late-night noise near home learns there may already be a bylaw about it
facts.activity: to explain how a citizen can petition a councillor to change a local bylaw

facts.fact: In a first-past-the-post election, the candidate with the most votes in a district wins the seat, even if they did not get more than half the votes.
facts.hook: a class election is won by a student with fewer than half the votes, and some classmates object
facts.activity: to compare a first-past-the-post election with proportional representation using a sample vote count

facts.fact: Under first-past-the-post, a candidate with 40 votes beats rivals with 35 and 25 votes, even though 60 of the 100 voters chose someone else.
facts.hook: students tallying a mock vote at a community centre realize the winner was not the choice of most voters
facts.activity: to compare a first-past-the-post election with proportional representation using a sample vote count

facts.fact: Under proportional representation, parties win seats roughly in proportion to their share of the vote, so a party with 30 percent of the vote gets about 30 percent of the seats.
facts.hook: a class recounts the same mock ballots using proportional rules and gets a very different council
facts.activity: to compare a first-past-the-post election with proportional representation using a sample vote count

facts.fact: Under first-past-the-post, votes for losing candidates in a district elect no one, which is why they are sometimes called wasted votes.
facts.hook: a grandparent says their vote never counts in their district, and a student works out why
facts.activity: to compare a first-past-the-post election with proportional representation using a sample vote count

facts.fact: Under first-past-the-post, two similar candidates can split their supporters' votes, letting a third candidate win with fewer votes than their combined total.
facts.hook: two friends with nearly the same platform both run for class rep and a third student wins
facts.activity: to compare a first-past-the-post election with proportional representation using a sample vote count

facts.fact: In Canada's 2015 federal election, the Liberal Party won 184 of 338 seats, a majority, with about 39.5 percent of the popular vote.
facts.hook: a student compares a party's seat share and vote share on an election results page
facts.activity: to compare a first-past-the-post election with proportional representation using a sample vote count

facts.fact: In the 2005 United Kingdom general election, Labour won a majority of seats with 35.2 percent of the vote.
facts.hook: a grandparent who lived in Britain explains how a party won most seats with about a third of the votes
facts.activity: to compare a first-past-the-post election with proportional representation using a sample vote count

facts.fact: New Zealand voted in a 1993 referendum to replace first-past-the-post with a proportional system called MMP, and first used it in the 1996 election.
facts.hook: students debating a switch to proportional voting look for a country that actually made the change
facts.activity: to compare a first-past-the-post election with proportional representation using a sample vote count

facts.fact: Many proportional systems set a minimum vote share for winning seats; in Germany a party usually needs at least 5 percent of the national party vote, with limited exceptions.
facts.hook: a tiny party in a mock election gets 3 percent and the class argues whether it should get any seat
facts.activity: to compare a first-past-the-post election with proportional representation using a sample vote count

facts.fact: Proportional representation more often produces coalition governments, because a single party rarely wins more than half the votes.
facts.hook: a mock parliament has no party with a majority, and students must negotiate to form a government
facts.activity: to compare a first-past-the-post election with proportional representation using a sample vote count

facts.fact: French political scientist Maurice Duverger observed that first-past-the-post elections tend to produce two large parties, an idea now called Duverger's law.
facts.hook: a class wonders why only two parties ever seem to have a chance in their mock elections
facts.activity: to compare a first-past-the-post election with proportional representation using a sample vote count

facts.fact: A proposed law is called a bill until it passes all its stages; once it becomes law it is called an Act.
facts.hook: a student visiting a legislature is confused about why the same law has two different names
facts.activity: to explain how a bill becomes a law by passing through the legislature

facts.fact: In Canada, a federal bill must pass three readings in both the House of Commons and the Senate before it can receive royal assent.
facts.hook: a kid tracking a bill online counts how many stages are still left before it becomes law
facts.activity: to explain how a bill becomes a law by passing through the legislature

facts.fact: In Westminster-style legislatures such as Canada's and the United Kingdom's, first reading introduces a bill and has it printed without debate.
facts.hook: a student watching the legislature on TV is surprised when a bill is introduced in seconds with no speeches
facts.activity: to explain how a bill becomes a law by passing through the legislature

facts.fact: In Canada, the Governor General, or a deputy such as a Supreme Court justice, gives royal assent to federal bills on behalf of the monarch.
facts.hook: a student at a courthouse learns a judge can sometimes stand in to approve a new law
facts.activity: to explain how a bill becomes a law by passing through the legislature

facts.fact: All Canadian provinces have one-chamber legislatures, so a provincial bill passes only one house before the lieutenant governor gives royal assent.
facts.hook: a student compares a federal and a provincial bill and notices the provincial one has fewer steps
facts.activity: to explain how a bill becomes a law by passing through the legislature

facts.fact: In the United States, a bill must pass both the House of Representatives and the Senate in identical form before it goes to the president.
facts.hook: a student notices two versions of a US bill in the news and wonders which one becomes law
facts.activity: to explain how a bill becomes a law by passing through the legislature

facts.fact: In the United States, Congress can override a president's veto if two-thirds of both the House and the Senate vote to pass the bill again.
facts.hook: a class simulation of Congress needs two-thirds of the votes to overturn a veto and falls just short
facts.activity: to explain how a bill becomes a law by passing through the legislature

facts.fact: Under the US Constitution, a bill becomes law without the president's signature if it is not returned within ten days, Sundays excepted, while Congress is still in session.
facts.hook: a student learns a bill can become law even when a president simply does nothing
facts.activity: to explain how a bill becomes a law by passing through the legislature

facts.fact: In the United Kingdom, the Parliament Acts of 1911 and 1949 let the House of Commons pass most bills without the House of Lords' consent after about a year's delay.
facts.hook: a grandparent explains why the unelected British upper house cannot block a bill forever
facts.activity: to explain how a bill becomes a law by passing through the legislature

facts.fact: The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms became part of Canada's Constitution when it was proclaimed on April 17, 1982.
facts.hook: a student reading a Charter poster at a courthouse notices the date and wonders what rights existed before it
facts.activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words

facts.fact: Section 2 of the Canadian Charter protects fundamental freedoms, including freedom of religion, freedom of expression, freedom of peaceful assembly and freedom of association.
facts.hook: students planning a peaceful protest about a park closure look up which section protects them
facts.activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words

facts.fact: Section 1 of the Canadian Charter says its rights are subject to reasonable limits that can be demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society.
facts.hook: a kid claims freedom of expression means anyone can say anything, and a friend reads out section 1
facts.activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words

facts.fact: Section 3 of the Canadian Charter gives every Canadian citizen the right to vote in elections for the House of Commons and provincial legislatures.
facts.hook: at a polling station a student reads the sign about who can vote and connects it to the Charter
facts.activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words

facts.fact: The equality rights in section 15 of the Canadian Charter came into force in 1985, three years after the rest, to give governments time to update their laws.
facts.hook: a student notices one Charter section has a different start date and investigates why
facts.activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words

facts.fact: The Canadian Charter applies to governments and their actions, not directly to private businesses or individuals.
facts.hook: a kid thinks a store broke the Charter by banning backpacks, and learns why that is a different kind of rule
facts.activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words

facts.fact: Section 33 of the Canadian Charter, the notwithstanding clause, lets Parliament or a provincial legislature override certain rights for up to five years, and the override can be renewed.
facts.hook: a news story about the notwithstanding clause prompts a family debate at a grandparent's house
facts.activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words

facts.fact: The first ten amendments to the United States Constitution are called the Bill of Rights, and they were ratified in 1791.
facts.hook: a student with family in the US compares their rights document with the Canadian Charter
facts.activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words

facts.fact: The First Amendment to the US Constitution protects freedom of religion, speech, the press, peaceful assembly and petitioning the government.
facts.hook: a school newspaper editor wonders what protects the press in the United States
facts.activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words

facts.fact: The Fifth Amendment to the US Constitution says no person can be forced, in a criminal case, to be a witness against themselves.
facts.hook: a kid hears 'I plead the Fifth' on a TV show and looks up what it actually means
facts.activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words

facts.fact: Article 1 of Germany's Basic Law, its constitution since 1949, begins with the words 'Human dignity shall be inviolable.'
facts.hook: a student with German cousins compares how their country's constitution opens with Canada's
facts.activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words

facts.fact: A roux is flour cooked in fat, traditionally equal parts by weight, and it is used to thicken sauces.
facts.hook: a kid at a community kitchen weighs butter and flour and wonders why the amounts must match
facts.activity: to make a roux and turn it into a smooth cheese sauce without lumps

facts.fact: Cooking a roux briefly while stirring gets rid of the raw flour taste before any liquid is added.
facts.hook: a friend skips cooking the flour and the sauce tastes pasty, so they try again
facts.activity: to make a roux and turn it into a smooth cheese sauce without lumps

facts.fact: A white roux is cooked only until the raw flour taste is gone and it is still pale, which is the kind used for a white sauce.
facts.hook: two cooks disagree whether the roux should go golden brown for a cheese sauce
facts.activity: to make a roux and turn it into a smooth cheese sauce without lumps

facts.fact: The darker a roux is cooked, the less it thickens, because browning breaks down the flour's starch.
facts.hook: a kid lets the roux brown too long and cannot understand why the sauce stays thin
facts.activity: to make a roux and turn it into a smooth cheese sauce without lumps

facts.fact: A roux thickened with milk makes béchamel, one of the classic mother sauces of French cooking.
facts.hook: a student learns the white sauce they made at a friend's house has a French name
facts.activity: to make a roux and turn it into a smooth cheese sauce without lumps

facts.fact: Béchamel with cheese added to it is called Mornay sauce.
facts.hook: a kid making macaroni and cheese discovers the sauce they made has a proper name
facts.activity: to make a roux and turn it into a smooth cheese sauce without lumps

facts.fact: Adding the milk to a roux a little at a time while whisking lets the flour spread out evenly and helps stop lumps from forming.
facts.hook: a kid dumps all the milk in at once and ends up whisking furiously at lumps
facts.activity: to make a roux and turn it into a smooth cheese sauce without lumps

facts.fact: Flour thickens a sauce because its starch grains soak up liquid and swell when heated, so the sauce thickens as it comes up to a simmer.
facts.hook: a cook worries the sauce is too thin and nearly adds more flour before it has heated through
facts.activity: to make a roux and turn it into a smooth cheese sauce without lumps

facts.fact: Cheese stirred into a sauce that is too hot can turn grainy or greasy, because heat makes its proteins clump and squeeze out fat.
facts.hook: a cheese sauce turns oily at a campsite stove and a friend works out why
facts.activity: to make a roux and turn it into a smooth cheese sauce without lumps

facts.fact: Finely grated cheese melts faster and more evenly into a sauce than chunks of cheese do.
facts.hook: someone drops big cubes of cheddar into the pot and waits too long for them to melt
facts.activity: to make a roux and turn it into a smooth cheese sauce without lumps

facts.fact: A sauce that has turned lumpy can often be rescued by pushing it through a fine sieve or blending it smooth.
facts.hook: a lumpy sauce threatens a community kitchen dinner until someone grabs a sieve
facts.activity: to make a roux and turn it into a smooth cheese sauce without lumps

facts.fact: When cooking several dishes for one meal, start with the one that takes longest and plan backward from the time you want to eat.
facts.hook: a kid cooking dinner for friends writes a schedule working back from seven o'clock
facts.activity: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time

facts.fact: Mise en place is a French cooking term meaning 'putting in place': preparing and measuring every ingredient before you start cooking.
facts.hook: a cook burns the onions while searching for the spices, then learns to set everything out first
facts.activity: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time

facts.fact: Frying whole spices briefly in hot oil or ghee, called tempering or tadka in Indian cooking, releases their flavour into the fat.
facts.hook: a kid wonders why a recipe says to fry the cumin seeds first instead of stirring them in later
facts.activity: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time

facts.fact: Rinsing rice before cooking washes off loose surface starch, which helps the cooked grains stay separate instead of sticky.
facts.hook: a cook's rice comes out gluey and a friend asks whether they rinsed it
facts.activity: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time

facts.fact: In the absorption method, rice cooks in a measured amount of water that it soaks up completely, so no water needs to be drained.
facts.hook: a kid used to boiling pasta starts to drain the rice pot and gets stopped
facts.activity: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time

facts.fact: Lifting the lid while rice simmers lets steam escape, which can leave the grains undercooked.
facts.hook: a nervous cook keeps peeking at the rice and ends up with crunchy grains
facts.activity: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time

facts.fact: Cooked rice can rest off the heat with the lid on for several minutes, which lets the trapped steam finish cooking it and frees the stove for other dishes.
facts.hook: the rice is done too early, and a friend shows it can simply rest while the bread cooks
facts.activity: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time

facts.fact: A chapati cooks on a hot, dry griddle in only a minute or two, which is why flatbreads are usually made last.
facts.hook: a cook makes the flatbreads first and they are cold and stiff by the time the curry is ready
facts.activity: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time

facts.fact: A chapati puffs up on the heat because water in the dough turns into steam.
facts.hook: a friend is amazed when a flat circle of dough suddenly balloons on the pan
facts.activity: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time

facts.fact: Stacking hot flatbreads inside a clean cloth keeps them warm and soft by trapping their steam.
facts.hook: a kid leaves the finished breads on an open plate and they turn stiff before serving
facts.activity: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time

facts.fact: Preheating means waiting until the oven has reached the set temperature before the batter goes in, so baking starts at the right heat.
facts.hook: a kid puts the muffin tray into a cold oven to save time and the results look wrong
facts.activity: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven

facts.fact: Double-acting baking powder releases gas twice: once when it gets wet in the batter and again when it is heated in the oven.
facts.hook: a baker wonders why the recipe says the batter can wait a few minutes before going in the oven
facts.activity: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven

facts.fact: The muffin method mixes the dry ingredients in one bowl and the wet ingredients in another, then combines them only at the end.
facts.hook: a kid dumps everything into one bowl at once and a friend reads the recipe steps aloud
facts.activity: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven

facts.fact: Overmixing muffin batter develops gluten in the flour, which makes muffins tough and can leave long tunnels inside them.
facts.hook: a kid stirs the batter until it is perfectly smooth and the muffins come out chewy
facts.activity: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven

facts.fact: Scooping flour straight from the bag with a measuring cup packs it down and can add noticeably more flour than spooning it in and levelling it off.
facts.hook: two friends' muffins from the same recipe come out different, one dense and dry
facts.activity: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven

facts.fact: A toothpick pushed into the centre of a muffin that comes out clean or with a few dry crumbs shows the muffin is baked through.
facts.hook: the timer goes off but the muffin tops look pale, and the bakers need a way to check inside
facts.activity: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven

facts.fact: Many home ovens run hotter or cooler than the temperature on the dial, which an oven thermometer placed inside can reveal.
facts.hook: muffins keep burning at a grandparent's house even though the recipe was followed exactly
facts.activity: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven

facts.fact: An oven setting of 350 degrees Fahrenheit is about 175 to 180 degrees Celsius.
facts.hook: a recipe from an American website confuses a kid whose oven only shows Celsius
facts.activity: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven

facts.fact: Wet oven mitts can burn your hands, because water in the cloth carries heat quickly and can turn to steam.
facts.hook: a kid grabs the hot muffin tray with a mitt that got splashed at the sink and a friend stops them
facts.activity: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven

facts.fact: Muffin tops turn golden brown in the oven because sugars and proteins react in the heat, a process called the Maillard reaction.
facts.hook: a baker wonders why the muffin tops brown while the insides stay pale
facts.activity: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven

facts.fact: Cutting an onion in half from top to root and laying each half flat side down gives a steady base, so the onion cannot roll while you slice it.
facts.hook: a whole onion keeps rolling off a wobbly camp table until someone halves it first
facts.activity: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch

facts.fact: A damp cloth or damp paper towel under a cutting board stops the board from sliding across the counter while you chop.
facts.hook: the cutting board skids every time a kid presses down at a friend's house
facts.activity: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch

facts.fact: A sharp knife is safer than a dull one because it needs less pressure to cut, so it is less likely to slip off the food.
facts.hook: a kid pushes hard on a blunt knife and it skates off a tomato skin, so an adult swaps in a sharp one
facts.activity: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch

facts.fact: Raw onion tastes sharp, but cooking it slowly over low heat makes it soft and sweet as its natural sugars turn golden brown.
facts.hook: a picky eater who hates raw onion tastes the slow-cooked ones and asks for more
facts.activity: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch

facts.fact: Garlic burns much faster than onion and tastes bitter when burnt, so many cooks add it only after the onions have softened.
facts.hook: the first batch of sauce tastes bitter because the garlic went in with the onions on high heat
facts.activity: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch

facts.fact: Simmering a sauce with the lid off lets water escape as steam, so the sauce slowly gets thicker.
facts.hook: the sauce is too runny at dinnertime and someone realizes the lid has been on the whole time
facts.activity: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch

facts.fact: Pasta releases starch into its cooking water, and a splash of that starchy water helps a sauce thicken and cling to the pasta.
facts.hook: a kid is about to pour all the pasta water down the drain when a friend saves a cupful
facts.activity: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch

facts.fact: If a knife starts to fall, step back and let it drop; trying to catch a falling knife is a common way to get cut.
facts.hook: a knife slides off the counter at a campsite and a kid's first instinct is to grab it
facts.activity: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch

facts.fact: A monologue is a long speech by one character, spoken to other characters on stage or to the audience.
facts.hook: a kid at drama camp thinks a monologue means talking to yourself until the director explains
facts.activity: to perform a monologue from a play using pauses and gestures to show emotion

facts.fact: A soliloquy is a speech a character gives alone on stage, letting the audience hear the character's private thoughts.
facts.hook: at a community theatre a kid wonders who Hamlet is talking to when no one else is on stage
facts.activity: to perform a monologue from a play using pauses and gestures to show emotion

facts.fact: Hamlet's famous speech beginning 'To be, or not to be' is a soliloquy in Act 3, Scene 1 of Shakespeare's play.
facts.hook: a kid picks the most famous speech for an audition and has to find where it sits in the play
facts.activity: to perform a monologue from a play using pauses and gestures to show emotion

facts.fact: When Juliet asks 'Wherefore art thou Romeo?' she means 'Why are you Romeo?', not 'Where are you?', because 'wherefore' means 'why'.
facts.hook: a kid performs Juliet's speech looking around the stage for Romeo, and a friend points out the mistake
facts.activity: to perform a monologue from a play using pauses and gestures to show emotion

facts.fact: Much of Shakespeare's verse is iambic pentameter: lines of ten syllables in five pairs, each an unstressed beat followed by a stressed one.
facts.hook: a kid rushes through a speech until a coach taps out the da-DUM rhythm on the table
facts.activity: to perform a monologue from a play using pauses and gestures to show emotion

facts.fact: In Stanislavski's system, an actor asks what the character wants in the scene, called the objective, and plays every line trying to get it.
facts.hook: a flat monologue comes alive once a kid decides what the character is trying to win
facts.activity: to perform a monologue from a play using pauses and gestures to show emotion

facts.fact: Actors split a script into beats: a new beat starts wherever a character's thought or tactic changes, and a pause often marks that shift.
facts.hook: a kid pencils slashes into a script to mark where to stop and breathe
facts.activity: to perform a monologue from a play using pauses and gestures to show emotion

facts.fact: The playwright Harold Pinter wrote 'Pause' and 'Silence' into his stage directions, treating silences as part of what the characters say.
facts.hook: a kid rehearsing at a grandparent's house finds a script where the pauses are written in like lines
facts.activity: to perform a monologue from a play using pauses and gestures to show emotion

facts.fact: Subtext is what a character means or feels beneath the words they actually say, and actors often show it through pauses, tone and gesture.
facts.hook: a character says 'I'm fine' and the kid has to make the audience know she isn't
facts.activity: to perform a monologue from a play using pauses and gestures to show emotion

facts.fact: In Stephen Toulmin's model of argument, the claim is the point being argued, and the grounds or data are the evidence given to support it.
facts.hook: a debate partner keeps stating opinions until a coach asks for the evidence behind each one
facts.activity: to build a debate case with a claim, evidence and a warrant for each point

facts.fact: The British philosopher Stephen Toulmin described his model of argument, including claim, data and warrant, in his 1958 book 'The Uses of Argument'.
facts.hook: a kid at a debate tournament asks where the word 'warrant' even comes from
facts.activity: to build a debate case with a claim, evidence and a warrant for each point

facts.fact: Toulmin's full model has six parts: claim, data, warrant, backing, qualifier and rebuttal.
facts.hook: a kid builds a case on index cards and realizes there are more boxes to fill than three
facts.activity: to build a debate case with a claim, evidence and a warrant for each point

facts.fact: A qualifier is a word such as 'usually', 'most' or 'probably' that limits how strongly a claim is stated, making it harder to disprove.
facts.hook: an opponent knocks down 'all kids hate homework' with one counterexample
facts.activity: to build a debate case with a claim, evidence and a warrant for each point

facts.fact: In his 'Rhetoric', Aristotle described three ways to persuade: ethos, the speaker's credibility; pathos, the audience's emotions; and logos, reasoning and evidence.
facts.hook: a debater relies only on a sad story and loses to a team with hard numbers
facts.activity: to build a debate case with a claim, evidence and a warrant for each point

facts.fact: An ad hominem argument attacks the person making a claim instead of the claim itself, and it is counted as a fallacy, a flaw in reasoning.
facts.hook: a debater says 'you're just a sixth grader' and the judge marks it down
facts.activity: to build a debate case with a claim, evidence and a warrant for each point

facts.fact: A straw man argument misstates an opponent's position as something weaker or sillier, then attacks that version instead of the real one.
facts.hook: a team twists 'shorter recess' into 'no recess ever' and the other side calls it out
facts.activity: to build a debate case with a claim, evidence and a warrant for each point

facts.fact: Two things happening together, a correlation, does not prove that one causes the other; a third factor may cause both.
facts.hook: a debater claims ice cream causes sunburn because both rise in summer
facts.activity: to build a debate case with a claim, evidence and a warrant for each point

facts.fact: One personal story, called anecdotal evidence, cannot prove a general trend, because a single case may not be typical.
facts.hook: a team's whole case rests on what happened to one cousin
facts.activity: to build a debate case with a claim, evidence and a warrant for each point

facts.fact: The side that proposes a change carries the burden of proof, meaning it must show why the change is needed rather than the other side proving it is not.
facts.hook: a team arguing for a new rule assumes the other side has to prove them wrong
facts.activity: to build a debate case with a claim, evidence and a warrant for each point

facts.fact: Abraham Lincoln's Gettysburg Address, given on November 19, 1863, was about 272 words long and took roughly two minutes to deliver.
facts.hook: a kid complains two minutes is too short to say anything important
facts.activity: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing

facts.fact: People tend to remember the first and last items in a list best, a pattern called the serial position effect, which is why openings and closings matter.
facts.hook: a kid buries the best point in the middle and nobody remembers it
facts.activity: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing

facts.fact: Julius Caesar reported a quick victory at the Battle of Zela in 47 BC with three Latin words, 'Veni, vidi, vici': I came, I saw, I conquered.
facts.hook: a kid struggles to see why three points work better than seven
facts.activity: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing

facts.fact: Repeating the same words at the start of several sentences is called anaphora; Martin Luther King Jr. repeated 'I have a dream' in his 1963 speech.
facts.hook: a kid wants a closing that sticks and borrows a repeated phrase
facts.activity: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing

facts.fact: Glossophobia is the name for fear of public speaking, and it is one of the most commonly reported fears.
facts.hook: a kid's hands shake before the speech and a friend admits hers do too
facts.activity: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing

facts.fact: A hook is the opening line that grabs attention, such as a question, a surprising fact or a very short story.
facts.hook: a kid opens with 'Today I will talk about...' and watches the audience drift off
facts.activity: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing

facts.fact: Signposting words like 'first', 'second' and 'finally' tell listeners where they are in a speech, because they cannot flip back a page the way a reader can.
facts.hook: a grandparent loses track halfway through a practice speech
facts.activity: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing

facts.fact: A short silent pause in place of 'um' or 'uh' makes a speaker sound more confident and gives listeners time to take in the point.
facts.hook: a friend counts every 'um' during a practice run
facts.activity: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing

facts.fact: A callback closing returns to the opening hook at the end, which makes a speech feel complete.
facts.hook: a kid can't think how to end and realizes the answer is in the first line
facts.activity: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing

facts.fact: Practicing a speech out loud with a timer matters because reading silently is faster than speaking, so a speech often runs longer than expected.
facts.hook: a speech that seemed short on paper runs well past the time limit at the first practice
facts.activity: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing

facts.fact: In improv, 'yes, and' means accepting what your partner has established (yes) and then adding something new to it (and).
facts.hook: a kid at drama camp keeps agreeing but never adds anything, and the scene stalls
facts.activity: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and

facts.fact: In improv, an offer is anything a performer says or does that gives information about the scene, such as a place, a name or a problem.
facts.hook: a partner mimes holding a fishing rod and the kid doesn't notice it's an offer
facts.activity: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and

facts.fact: Blocking is rejecting or ignoring a partner's offer, such as saying 'we're not on a boat', and it usually stops the scene from moving forward.
facts.hook: a kid says 'no, that's not my dog' and the audience goes quiet
facts.activity: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and

facts.fact: Endowing means giving your partner a role or trait through what you say, as in 'Doctor, my arm hurts', which makes them the doctor.
facts.hook: a kid freezes on stage until a partner calls her 'Captain'
facts.activity: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and

facts.fact: Specific details, like 'Grandma's red bicycle' instead of 'a bike', give an improv partner more to build on.
facts.hook: a scene about 'some stuff' goes nowhere until one kid names exactly what it is
facts.activity: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and

facts.fact: Viola Spolin's 1963 book 'Improvisation for the Theater' collected theater games and is often called the bible of improv teaching.
facts.hook: a drama camp counselor pulls out a worn book of games
facts.activity: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and

facts.fact: Keith Johnstone's 1979 book 'Impro' taught that characters in a scene play higher or lower status, and shifting status creates drama.
facts.hook: a scene between a king and a servant gets funny when the servant starts giving orders
facts.activity: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and

facts.fact: The Moon makes no light of its own; it shines only because it reflects sunlight.
facts.hook: at a planetarium a kid asks what the Moon burns to glow
facts.activity: to explain the phases of the Moon by modelling it circling Earth with a lamp and a ball

facts.fact: Half of the Moon is always lit by the Sun; the phases show how much of that lit half faces Earth.
facts.hook: in the lamp-and-ball model, a kid sees the ball is always half lit even when it looks like a crescent
facts.activity: to explain the phases of the Moon by modelling it circling Earth with a lamp and a ball

facts.fact: The phases are not caused by Earth's shadow; Earth's shadow falls on the Moon only during a lunar eclipse.
facts.hook: a friend insists the crescent is Earth's shadow until the lamp model shows otherwise
facts.activity: to explain the phases of the Moon by modelling it circling Earth with a lamp and a ball

facts.fact: It takes about 29.5 days for the Moon to go from one new moon to the next.
facts.hook: a kid tracks the Moon on a calendar at a grandparent's house and counts the days
facts.activity: to explain the phases of the Moon by modelling it circling Earth with a lamp and a ball

facts.fact: At new moon, the Moon lies roughly between Earth and the Sun, so its lit side faces away from us and it looks dark.
facts.hook: a kid can't find the Moon at all one night and thinks it has vanished
facts.activity: to explain the phases of the Moon by modelling it circling Earth with a lamp and a ball

facts.fact: At full moon, Earth lies roughly between the Sun and the Moon, so we see the whole lit side.
facts.hook: in the lamp model a kid has to hold the ball behind her own head without blocking the light
facts.activity: to explain the phases of the Moon by modelling it circling Earth with a lamp and a ball

facts.fact: A waxing Moon's lit part is growing night by night, and a waning Moon's lit part is shrinking.
facts.hook: two cousins argue whether the Moon is getting bigger or smaller this week
facts.activity: to explain the phases of the Moon by modelling it circling Earth with a lamp and a ball

facts.fact: The Moon spins once for each trip around Earth, so the same side always faces us.
facts.hook: a kid wonders why the Moon's 'face' pattern never changes
facts.activity: to explain the phases of the Moon by modelling it circling Earth with a lamp and a ball

facts.fact: The Moon rises on average about 50 minutes later each day, because it moves along its orbit while Earth turns.
facts.hook: a kid waiting to see moonrise at the same time as yesterday waits almost an hour
facts.activity: to explain the phases of the Moon by modelling it circling Earth with a lamp and a ball

facts.fact: A waxing crescent is lit on the right side as seen from the Northern Hemisphere, but on the left side as seen from the Southern Hemisphere.
facts.hook: a video call with a cousin in Australia shows the Moon lit on the 'wrong' side
facts.activity: to explain the phases of the Moon by modelling it circling Earth with a lamp and a ball

facts.fact: Erosion is the wearing away and carrying off of rock and soil; deposition is the dropping of that material somewhere else.
facts.hook: at a rock quarry a kid wonders where all the missing rock went
facts.activity: to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years through erosion and deposition

facts.fact: A river cuts downward mainly because the sand, pebbles and boulders it carries grind against its bed, a process called abrasion.
facts.hook: a kid finds a smooth, rounded stone and wonders what polished it
facts.activity: to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years through erosion and deposition

facts.fact: Faster water can carry bigger particles; when a river slows down, it drops its load, with the largest pieces settling first.
facts.hook: a stream table at the science museum leaves pebbles at the top and fine mud at the bottom
facts.activity: to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years through erosion and deposition

facts.fact: Scientists estimate the Colorado River began carving the Grand Canyon about 5 to 6 million years ago.
facts.hook: a kid at a grandparent's house looks at a Grand Canyon postcard and asks how long it took
facts.activity: to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years through erosion and deposition

facts.fact: The Grand Canyon is 277 miles (446 kilometers) long and over a mile deep at its deepest point.
facts.hook: a kid tries to picture a canyon deeper than a mile
facts.activity: to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years through erosion and deposition

facts.fact: In a canyon wall, harder rock layers tend to form steep cliffs and softer layers wear back into gentler slopes, which gives the Grand Canyon its stepped walls.
facts.hook: a kid at a rock quarry notices some layers stick out and others cave in
facts.activity: to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years through erosion and deposition

facts.fact: In layers of rock that have not been flipped or disturbed, the lowest layers are the oldest, an idea called the law of superposition.
facts.hook: a kid guesses the top layer of a canyon wall is the oldest
facts.activity: to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years through erosion and deposition

facts.fact: The Danish scientist Nicolas Steno published the law of superposition, that lower rock layers are older, in 1669.
facts.hook: a museum sign credits one scientist with reading rock layers like pages
facts.activity: to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years through erosion and deposition

facts.fact: The Scottish geologist James Hutton argued in 1785 that slow, everyday processes like erosion, working over immense time, shaped Earth's surface.
facts.hook: a kid can't believe a small river could ever cut a canyon
facts.activity: to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years through erosion and deposition

facts.fact: A delta forms where a river slows as it enters a sea or lake and drops the sediment it was carrying, building up new land.
facts.hook: a kid spots a fan of sand where a stream meets a pond
facts.activity: to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years through erosion and deposition

facts.fact: On a river bend, water flows fastest on the outside, eroding that bank, and slowest on the inside, where it deposits sand and gravel.
facts.hook: a kid notices a sandy beach on one side of a creek bend and a steep cut bank on the other
facts.activity: to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years through erosion and deposition

facts.fact: Igneous rock forms when molten rock cools and hardens.
facts.hook: at a rock quarry a kid holds a speckled rock and asks if it was ever melted
facts.activity: to sort rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic by how they were formed

facts.fact: Molten rock underground is called magma; once it erupts onto the surface it is called lava.
facts.hook: two friends argue whether a volcano spills magma or lava
facts.activity: to sort rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic by how they were formed

facts.fact: Igneous rock that cools slowly underground, like granite, has large crystals, while rock that cools fast at the surface, like basalt, has tiny ones.
facts.hook: a kid compares a sparkly granite countertop with a plain dark basalt pebble
facts.activity: to sort rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic by how they were formed

facts.fact: Obsidian is volcanic glass: lava that cooled so quickly that crystals had no time to form.
facts.hook: a kid at a science museum thinks the shiny black rock is made of glass bottles
facts.activity: to sort rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic by how they were formed

facts.fact: Pumice is an igneous rock full of gas bubbles trapped as lava cooled, and many pieces are light enough to float on water.
facts.hook: a kid drops a rock in a bucket at a grandparent's house and it doesn't sink
facts.activity: to sort rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic by how they were formed

facts.fact: Sedimentary rock forms when layers of sediment such as sand, mud or shells are pressed together and cemented over time.
facts.hook: a kid sees stripes in a cliff at a quarry and asks why rock has layers
facts.activity: to sort rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic by how they were formed

facts.fact: Fossils are found almost only in sedimentary rock, because the heat that forms igneous and metamorphic rock usually destroys remains.
facts.hook: a kid searching for fossils keeps checking the wrong kind of rock
facts.activity: to sort rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic by how they were formed

facts.fact: Limestone is made mostly of calcium carbonate, so a drop of vinegar makes it fizz as carbon dioxide gas is released.
facts.hook: a kid tests quarry rocks with vinegar from a picnic basket
facts.activity: to sort rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic by how they were formed

facts.fact: Metamorphic rock forms when existing rock is changed by heat and pressure deep underground without fully melting.
facts.hook: a kid assumes all rocks that were heated must have melted
facts.activity: to sort rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic by how they were formed

facts.fact: Marble is a metamorphic rock formed when limestone is changed by heat and pressure.
facts.hook: a kid learns the marble statue at the museum started as seabed limestone
facts.activity: to sort rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic by how they were formed

facts.fact: Slate is a metamorphic rock formed from shale, and it splits into thin flat sheets, which is why it has been used for roofs and chalkboards.
facts.hook: an old chalkboard at a grandparent's house turns out to be a rock
facts.activity: to sort rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic by how they were formed

facts.fact: In the rock cycle, any type of rock can become any other type, through melting, weathering, or heat and pressure.
facts.hook: a kid thinks a rock stays the same kind forever
facts.activity: to sort rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic by how they were formed

facts.fact: Earth's axis is tilted about 23.4 degrees from straight up relative to the plane of its orbit around the Sun.
facts.hook: at a planetarium a kid notices the globe on display is leaning
facts.activity: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons

facts.fact: Earth's axis points in the same direction in space all year, so for part of the orbit the Northern Hemisphere leans toward the Sun and later leans away.
facts.hook: a kid walking a tilted globe around a lamp keeps turning it by mistake
facts.activity: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons

facts.fact: In summer, sunlight strikes the ground more directly, so the same light is concentrated on a smaller area and heats it more.
facts.hook: a flashlight pointed straight down makes a bright small circle, tilted it makes a dim wide one
facts.activity: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons

facts.fact: The hemisphere tilted toward the Sun also gets longer days, giving sunlight more hours to warm the ground.
facts.hook: a kid notices summer camp bedtime comes before dark
facts.activity: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons

facts.fact: The noon Sun climbs higher in the sky in summer than in winter, so shadows at noon are shorter in summer.
facts.hook: a kid measures a fence post's noon shadow in June and December
facts.activity: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons

facts.fact: Around June 21, the noon Sun is directly overhead at the Tropic of Cancer; around December 21, it is directly overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn.
facts.hook: a kid finds the two dotted lines on a globe and asks what they mark
facts.activity: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons

facts.fact: At the equinoxes, around March 20 and September 22, day and night are roughly equal in length all over Earth.
facts.hook: a kid on a video call with a cousin across the world finds their sunsets match
facts.activity: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons

facts.fact: North of the Arctic Circle, the Sun stays up for at least one full day around the June solstice, which is called the midnight sun.
facts.hook: a traveler's photo shows the Sun low in the sky at midnight
facts.activity: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons

facts.fact: Near the equator, sunlight stays fairly direct all year, so temperatures change little and many places have wet and dry seasons instead of warm and cold ones.
facts.hook: a friend from near the equator laughs at the idea of four seasons
facts.activity: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons

facts.fact: The hottest weeks usually come several weeks after the summer solstice, because land and oceans take time to warm up.
facts.hook: a kid expects the longest day to be the hottest and it isn't
facts.activity: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons

facts.fact: Earth's tilt slowly varies between about 22.1 and 24.5 degrees over a cycle of about 41,000 years.
facts.hook: a planetarium show asks what would happen if Earth leaned more
facts.activity: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons

facts.fact: If Earth's axis had no tilt, sunlight would hit each place at the same angle all year, so there would be almost no seasons.
facts.hook: a kid holds the globe perfectly upright in the model and the seasons disappear
facts.activity: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons

facts.fact: Interest is the price of borrowing money, usually charged as a percentage of the amount borrowed.
facts.hook: a kid at a bank asks why you pay back more than you borrowed
facts.activity: to compare the cost of borrowing money on a credit card with saving up first

facts.fact: APR stands for annual percentage rate, the yearly interest rate a lender charges on money you borrow.
facts.hook: a kid reads 'APR' on a credit card ad at a grandparent's house
facts.activity: to compare the cost of borrowing money on a credit card with saving up first

facts.fact: When unpaid interest is added to a debt, the next month's interest is charged on that interest too, so the debt grows faster over time.
facts.hook: a cousin's small balance keeps getting bigger even though she stopped using the card
facts.activity: to compare the cost of borrowing money on a credit card with saving up first

facts.fact: Borrowing 100 dollars at 20 percent yearly interest and repaying it after one year costs about 20 dollars in interest, or more if interest compounds.
facts.hook: a kid wants a bike now instead of saving from lemonade stand earnings
facts.activity: to compare the cost of borrowing money on a credit card with saving up first

facts.fact: Paying only the minimum on a credit card means much of each payment goes to interest, so paying off the balance can take years.
facts.hook: a relative explains why the card bill never seems to shrink
facts.activity: to compare the cost of borrowing money on a credit card with saving up first

facts.fact: Many credit cards charge no interest on new purchases if the full statement balance is paid by the due date; this is called a grace period.
facts.hook: a kid learns her parent uses a card every week but never pays interest
facts.activity: to compare the cost of borrowing money on a credit card with saving up first

facts.fact: Credit card interest rates are usually much higher than the interest a savings account pays you.
facts.hook: a kid at a bank compares the two rates on a brochure
facts.activity: to compare the cost of borrowing money on a credit card with saving up first

facts.fact: The rule of 72 estimates how many years money takes to double: divide 72 by the yearly interest rate, so at 24 percent, about three years.
facts.hook: a kid calculates how fast an unpaid card debt could double
facts.activity: to compare the cost of borrowing money on a credit card with saving up first

facts.fact: Cash advances from a credit card usually carry a higher interest rate than purchases, plus a fee, and interest often starts right away.
facts.hook: someone at a farmers' market pulls cash from a credit card and a friend warns her
facts.activity: to compare the cost of borrowing money on a credit card with saving up first

facts.fact: A share of stock is a small piece of ownership in a company, so a stockholder owns part of the business and shares in its gains or losses.
facts.hook: a grandparent gives a teen one share of a sneaker company, and the teen wonders whether that means free shoes
facts.activity: to compare a stock and a bond and explain which is riskier and why

facts.fact: A bond is a loan from an investor to a government or company, which promises to pay interest and to repay the original amount on a set date.
facts.hook: at a bank, a kid is confused that the savings bond they were given counts as a loan they made
facts.activity: to compare a stock and a bond and explain which is riskier and why

facts.fact: If a company goes bankrupt, its bondholders must be paid back before its stockholders, who are last in line and often receive nothing.
facts.hook: two cousins argue over whether the stock or the bond of a failed toy company is worth keeping
facts.activity: to compare a stock and a bond and explain which is riskier and why

facts.fact: A company can cut or skip the dividends it pays stockholders, but missing a promised interest payment on its bonds counts as a default.
facts.hook: a teen's stock stops paying its small dividend, while her brother's bond from the same company keeps paying
facts.activity: to compare a stock and a bond and explain which is riskier and why

facts.fact: If a company fails completely, its stock price can fall to zero, so a stockholder can lose every dollar they put in.
facts.hook: a friend who bet all his birthday money on one hyped company learns what 'zero' looks like
facts.activity: to compare a stock and a bond and explain which is riskier and why

facts.fact: Over the past century, U.S. stocks have earned higher average yearly returns than U.S. government bonds, but with much bigger drops along the way; the extra return rewards the extra risk.
facts.hook: a class investing game splits into a stock team and a bond team, and the lead keeps changing hands
facts.activity: to compare a stock and a bond and explain which is riskier and why

facts.fact: When interest rates rise, the prices of existing bonds fall, because buyers can get new bonds that pay more interest.
facts.hook: a teen tries to sell an old low-interest bond and finds nobody will pay full price for it
facts.activity: to compare a stock and a bond and explain which is riskier and why

facts.fact: U.S. Treasury bonds are backed by the full faith and credit of the U.S. government and are considered among the safest investments in the world.
facts.hook: a grandparent explains why she keeps her emergency savings in Treasury bonds instead of stocks
facts.activity: to compare a stock and a bond and explain which is riskier and why

facts.fact: Bonds from borrowers more likely to fail to pay are called high-yield or 'junk' bonds, and they must pay higher interest to attract lenders.
facts.hook: a student spots a bond paying twice the usual interest and has to figure out what the catch is
facts.activity: to compare a stock and a bond and explain which is riskier and why

facts.fact: Buying a fund that holds many different stocks, called diversifying, means one company's collapse hurts much less than if all the money were in that one stock.
facts.hook: two friends compare what happened when one company crashed: one owned only that stock, the other owned a fund
facts.activity: to compare a stock and a bond and explain which is riskier and why

facts.fact: After the 1929 crash, the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell about 89 percent from its September 1929 peak to its low in July 1932.
facts.hook: a history project on a great-grandparent's lost savings makes stock risk suddenly feel real
facts.activity: to compare a stock and a bond and explain which is riskier and why

facts.fact: A bond held until its maturity date pays back its full face value, as long as the issuer does not default, no matter how its price moved in between.
facts.hook: a teen panics when her bond's price dips, until she checks when it matures
facts.activity: to compare a stock and a bond and explain which is riskier and why

facts.fact: The law of demand says that when the price of something rises, people buy less of it, as long as nothing else changes.
facts.hook: at a farmers' market, a stand doubles its strawberry price and the line suddenly disappears
facts.activity: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter

facts.fact: The law of supply says that when the price of something rises, sellers offer more of it, because producing it becomes more profitable.
facts.hook: after strawberry prices jump, a kid notices three new berry stands at the market the next week
facts.activity: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter

facts.fact: The equilibrium price is the price at which the amount buyers want to buy equals the amount sellers want to sell.
facts.hook: two kids running a fruit stand keep adjusting their sign until they sell out right at closing time
facts.activity: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter

facts.fact: Where strawberries ripen outdoors in early summer, a flood of local berries raises the supply all at once, which usually pushes their price down.
facts.hook: a kid is amazed that summer strawberries at the market cost half what they did in March
facts.activity: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter

facts.fact: In winter, strawberries sold in cold regions are usually trucked or flown in from warmer places, and the cost of that transport helps make them pricier.
facts.hook: a grocery trip for a winter birthday cake turns into a question about why berries cost so much
facts.activity: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter

facts.fact: If a price is held below the equilibrium price, buyers want more than sellers will offer, and the result is a shortage.
facts.hook: a class sale prices strawberry cups too low and runs out in five minutes, leaving a long angry line
facts.activity: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter

facts.fact: If a price is held above the equilibrium price, sellers offer more than buyers want, and unsold goods pile up as a surplus.
facts.hook: a lemonade stand's pricey strawberry lemonade leaves them with jugs of it at the end of the day
facts.activity: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter

facts.fact: Fresh strawberries spoil within days of picking, so a grower with too many cannot store them for later and often has to cut the price to sell them.
facts.hook: at closing time a farmer slashes her strawberry price, and a kid figures out why
facts.activity: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter

facts.fact: A frost, hailstorm or drought that ruins part of a strawberry crop reduces the supply, which pushes the price of the remaining berries up.
facts.hook: after a late frost, a kid's favorite berry stand posts a much higher price
facts.activity: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter

facts.fact: British economist Alfred Marshall popularized the supply-and-demand diagram, with its two crossing curves, in his 1890 book Principles of Economics.
facts.hook: a student drawing the crossing curves for homework wonders who first made them famous
facts.activity: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter

facts.fact: Simple interest is paid only on the original amount deposited, called the principal, so it adds the same dollar amount every year.
facts.hook: a kid checks a savings statement and notices the interest is exactly the same every year
facts.activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years

facts.fact: Compound interest is paid on the principal plus all the interest already earned, so the interest itself starts earning interest.
facts.hook: at the bank, a teen learns her interest payment grew a little even though she added nothing
facts.activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years

facts.fact: At 5 percent simple interest, $1,000 earns $50 a year, so after five years the account holds $1,250.
facts.hook: a grandparent offers to hold a teen's $1,000 for five years at 5 percent simple interest
facts.activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years

facts.fact: At 5 percent interest compounded once a year, $1,000 grows to $1,276.28 after five years.
facts.hook: a teen compares the grandparent's offer with a bank paying 5 percent compounded yearly
facts.activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years

facts.fact: The simple interest formula is I = P x r x t: interest equals the principal times the yearly rate times the number of years.
facts.hook: a student checks a bank's advertised interest with a pencil and the formula
facts.activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years

facts.fact: With interest compounded once a year, the balance after n years equals P x (1 + r) to the power n, where r is the yearly rate as a decimal.
facts.hook: a kid uses a calculator's power key to see what their savings will be at graduation
facts.activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years

facts.fact: At the same yearly rate, interest compounded monthly grows a little faster than interest compounded yearly, because each month's interest starts earning sooner.
facts.hook: two bank ads offer the same rate, and a teen has to spot why one pays slightly more
facts.activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years

facts.fact: The rule of 72 estimates how long money takes to double with compound interest: divide 72 by the yearly percentage rate, so about 12 years at 6 percent.
facts.hook: a teen wonders how old they will be when their savings doubles
facts.activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years

facts.fact: In the United States, the Truth in Savings Act of 1991 requires banks to state savings rates as an annual percentage yield, or APY, which includes the effect of compounding.
facts.hook: a kid notices a bank poster lists both an interest rate and a slightly higher APY
facts.activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years

facts.fact: On a graph, a simple-interest balance rises in a straight line, while a compound-interest balance curves upward, gaining more each year than the year before.
facts.hook: a math class plots two savings accounts and sees the lines slowly pull apart
facts.activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years

facts.fact: The saying that compound interest is 'the eighth wonder of the world' is often credited to Albert Einstein, but there is no reliable evidence he ever said it.
facts.hook: a student about to quote Einstein in a presentation checks the source first
facts.activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years

facts.fact: If prices rise faster than a savings account's interest rate, the money in the account buys less each year even though the balance grows.
facts.hook: a teen's savings grew for five years, yet it no longer covers the bike it once would have
facts.activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years

facts.fact: A contour line on a topographic map joins points that are all at the same height above sea level.
facts.hook: at home, a kid planning a hike with a grandparent traces one wiggly brown line all the way around a hill
facts.activity: to read contour lines on a topographic map to find the steepest slope of a hill

facts.fact: Where contour lines are packed close together the ground is steep; where they are spread far apart the slope is gentle.
facts.hook: two friends choose a trail up a hill and one insists the route with crowded lines will be brutal
facts.activity: to read contour lines on a topographic map to find the steepest slope of a hill

facts.fact: The contour interval is the difference in height between one contour line and the next, and it is printed in the map's legend.
facts.hook: a kid miscalculates a hill's height until they read the tiny note in the map's legend
facts.activity: to read contour lines on a topographic map to find the steepest slope of a hill

facts.fact: Where contour lines cross a stream, they bend into a V shape that points uphill, toward the stream's source.
facts.hook: a kid figuring out which way a creek flows notices the Vs in the contour lines
facts.activity: to read contour lines on a topographic map to find the steepest slope of a hill

facts.fact: A closed contour loop with short tick marks pointing inward, called hachures, shows a hollow or depression rather than a hilltop.
facts.hook: a hiker expecting a lookout point on the map finds a sunken pond instead
facts.activity: to read contour lines on a topographic map to find the steepest slope of a hill

facts.fact: Slope steepness can be found by dividing the rise in height by the horizontal distance; rising 100 meters over 500 meters is a 20 percent grade.
facts.hook: a cyclist uses a map to work out whether a road hill will be too steep to ride
facts.activity: to read contour lines on a topographic map to find the steepest slope of a hill

facts.fact: Contour lines spaced evenly apart show a slope that has the same steepness all the way along it.
facts.hook: a sledding crew hunts on a map for a slope that won't suddenly get steeper
facts.activity: to read contour lines on a topographic map to find the steepest slope of a hill

facts.fact: The U.S. Geological Survey's standard 7.5-minute topographic maps use a scale of 1:24,000, so one inch on the map equals 2,000 feet on the ground.
facts.hook: a kid measuring a trail on a grandparent's old map with a ruler needs to convert inches to distance
facts.activity: to read contour lines on a topographic map to find the steepest slope of a hill

facts.fact: On U.S. Geological Survey topographic maps, contour lines are printed in brown.
facts.hook: a kid unfolding a map at home wonders what all the thin brown squiggles mean
facts.activity: to read contour lines on a topographic map to find the steepest slope of a hill

facts.fact: The word monsoon comes from the Arabic word mawsim, meaning 'season', because a monsoon is a wind that reverses direction with the seasons.
facts.hook: at a travel agency, a family wonders why the brochure warns about 'monsoon season'
facts.activity: to explain how a monsoon forms and why it matters for rice farming in South Asia

facts.fact: In summer, land heats up faster than the ocean, so warm air rises over the land and moist air from the ocean flows in to replace it.
facts.hook: a kid visiting relatives in India asks why the rain arrives right when the heat is worst
facts.activity: to explain how a monsoon forms and why it matters for rice farming in South Asia

facts.fact: India's summer monsoon is called the southwest monsoon because its moist winds blow in mostly from the southwest, across the Arabian Sea.
facts.hook: at an airport, a kid watches a weather map arrow and asks why it points from the sea
facts.activity: to explain how a monsoon forms and why it matters for rice farming in South Asia

facts.fact: The India Meteorological Department gives June 1 as the normal date for the southwest monsoon to reach Kerala, on India's southwestern coast.
facts.hook: a grandparent in Kerala marks early June on the calendar every year and explains why
facts.activity: to explain how a monsoon forms and why it matters for rice farming in South Asia

facts.fact: Mawsynram, in India's Meghalaya state, is often called the wettest place on Earth, averaging nearly 12 meters of rain a year.
facts.hook: at a travel agency, a teen spots a trip to the 'wettest place on Earth' and has questions
facts.activity: to explain how a monsoon forms and why it matters for rice farming in South Asia

facts.fact: Rice is usually grown in flooded fields called paddies, and the standing water helps keep many weeds from growing.
facts.hook: a kid sees photos of rice fields that look like shallow lakes and wonders why
facts.activity: to explain how a monsoon forms and why it matters for rice farming in South Asia

facts.fact: In South Asia, crops sown at the start of the summer monsoon and harvested in autumn are called kharif crops, and rice is the main one.
facts.hook: a grandparent who farmed in Punjab explains why planting waited for the first big rains
facts.activity: to explain how a monsoon forms and why it matters for rice farming in South Asia

facts.fact: Rice seedlings are often grown first in a small nursery bed and then transplanted, often by hand, into flooded paddy fields.
facts.hook: a kid visiting a farm is surprised that rice gets planted twice
facts.activity: to explain how a monsoon forms and why it matters for rice farming in South Asia

facts.fact: When the monsoon arrives late or brings too little rain, rice planting is delayed and harvests can shrink, which can push food prices up.
facts.hook: a family notices rice costing more at their grocery after news of a weak monsoon
facts.activity: to explain how a monsoon forms and why it matters for rice farming in South Asia

facts.fact: In northern summer, the rainy band of rising air near the equator, called the Intertropical Convergence Zone, shifts north over South Asia and helps bring monsoon rains.
facts.hook: a student comparing satellite images from January and July sees the cloud band move north
facts.activity: to explain how a monsoon forms and why it matters for rice farming in South Asia

facts.fact: Latitude measures how far north or south a place is from the equator, from 0 degrees at the equator to 90 degrees at each pole.
facts.hook: at a travel agency, a kid tries to guess which city on a list is closest to the equator
facts.activity: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city

facts.fact: Longitude measures how far east or west a place is from the prime meridian, from 0 degrees up to 180 degrees east or west.
facts.hook: a kid at an airport reads coordinates on a flight screen and can't tell which number is which
facts.activity: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city

facts.fact: The prime meridian, at 0 degrees longitude, was set through the Royal Observatory in Greenwich, London, by an international conference held in Washington, D.C., in 1884.
facts.hook: a kid on a London trip stands on a line at Greenwich and asks why the world's zero is there
facts.activity: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city

facts.fact: By convention, a location's latitude is written first and its longitude second, as in about 40 degrees north, 74 degrees west for New York City.
facts.hook: two friends swap the numbers in a map app and end up looking at the wrong place
facts.activity: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city

facts.fact: Each degree of latitude or longitude is divided into 60 minutes, and each minute into 60 seconds, to pinpoint an exact spot.
facts.hook: a kid sees 'minutes' on a map coordinate and assumes it has to do with time
facts.activity: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city

facts.fact: One degree of latitude covers about 111 kilometers, or about 69 miles, of north-south distance.
facts.hook: a kid estimates how far a grandparent's hometown is by counting degrees on a map
facts.activity: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city

facts.fact: Lines of longitude meet at the poles, so a degree of longitude spans about 111 kilometers at the equator but shrinks to zero at the poles.
facts.hook: a student on a globe notices the longitude lines squeezing together near the top
facts.activity: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city

facts.fact: Lines of latitude are also called parallels because they never meet, and lines of longitude are called meridians.
facts.hook: a kid reading an old atlas at a grandparent's house hits the words 'parallel' and 'meridian'
facts.activity: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city

facts.fact: Quito, the capital of Ecuador, lies less than a quarter of a degree south of the equator, so its latitude is almost zero.
facts.hook: at a travel agency, a teen finds a capital city with a latitude that starts with zero
facts.activity: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city

facts.fact: In the decimal coordinates used by GPS and online maps, latitudes south of the equator and longitudes west of the prime meridian are written as negative numbers.
facts.hook: a kid drops a minus sign typing coordinates and the map lands on the other side of the world
facts.activity: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city

facts.fact: Earth turns 15 degrees of longitude every hour, which is why time zones are roughly 15 degrees wide.
facts.hook: at an airport, a kid works out the time back home from how far east they flew
facts.activity: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city

facts.fact: In 1714 the British Parliament offered a prize of up to 20,000 pounds for a practical way to find a ship's longitude at sea.
facts.hook: a student wonders why sailors could find latitude easily but needed a prize to solve longitude
facts.activity: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city

facts.fact: A climate graph usually shows each month's average temperature as a line and each month's average rainfall as bars on the same chart.
facts.hook: at home, a kid tries to read a climate graph and first mistakes the bars for temperature
facts.activity: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs

facts.fact: A desert is often defined as a place that gets less than about 250 millimeters, or 10 inches, of rain a year.
facts.hook: a kid is surprised to learn a cold, snowy place can count as a desert by its rainfall
facts.activity: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs

facts.fact: In the Koppen climate system, a tropical rainforest climate has every month averaging at least 18 degrees Celsius and at least 60 millimeters of rain.
facts.hook: a student checks each month on a climate graph to decide if a city counts as rainforest
facts.activity: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs

facts.fact: A rainforest climate graph shows a nearly flat temperature line, because temperatures there stay warm and change little from month to month.
facts.hook: at a travel agency, a teen asks which month is best for a rainforest trip and finds they all look alike
facts.activity: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs

facts.fact: In tropical rainforests, the difference between day and night temperatures can be larger than the difference between the warmest and coolest months.
facts.hook: a kid packing for a rainforest trip is told to bring a sweater for nights despite the steady yearly heat
facts.activity: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs

facts.fact: Parts of Chile's Atacama Desert are so dry that some weather stations there have never recorded rain.
facts.hook: a student makes a desert climate graph where some bars are simply missing
facts.activity: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs

facts.fact: Many of the world's hot deserts lie near 30 degrees north or south of the equator, where sinking air warms up and dries out.
facts.hook: a kid on a globe notices the big deserts line up in two belts
