facts.fact: Before fitting a new tube, the inside of the tyre should be checked for the thorn or glass that caused the flat, or it will puncture again.
facts.hook: a new tube goes flat on the first ride
facts.activity: to change a flat bicycle tyre using tyre levers and a pump

facts.fact: Putting a little air in a new tube before fitting it gives it shape, so it is less likely to twist or get pinched under the tyre.
facts.hook: a floppy tube keeps getting caught as the tyre goes back on
facts.activity: to change a flat bicycle tyre using tyre levers and a pump

facts.fact: A pinch flat, often called a snakebite, is two small parallel slits made when an under-inflated tyre hits a sharp edge like a kerb.
facts.hook: a kid finds two neat holes side by side after hitting a kerb
facts.activity: to change a flat bicycle tyre using tyre levers and a pump

facts.fact: When patching a tube with glue-on patches, the glue must be left to dry until it is no longer wet before the patch is pressed on.
facts.hook: an impatient patch job peels off within a mile
facts.activity: to change a flat bicycle tyre using tyre levers and a pump

facts.fact: Counting up is a quick way to check change: start at the price and add each coin and note handed back until you reach the amount you paid.
facts.hook: a kid at the corner store is unsure the change is right and counts up
facts.activity: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change

facts.fact: If milk costs 2.65 and you pay with 5.00, the correct change is 2.35, whatever the currency.
facts.hook: a cashier hands back too little and the kid notices
facts.activity: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change

facts.fact: In the United States and Canada, shelf prices usually leave out sales tax, which is added at the till; in the UK and EU, shown prices already include VAT.
facts.hook: a kid brings the exact shelf price and is still a few cents short
facts.activity: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change

facts.fact: Since Canada stopped distributing pennies in 2013, cash totals there are rounded to the nearest five cents, while card payments are still charged to the exact cent.
facts.hook: a total of 3.02 becomes 3.00 when a kid pays in cash
facts.activity: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change

facts.fact: Many stores stock shelves 'first in, first out', putting older products at the front, so the carton with the latest date is often at the back.
facts.hook: a kid checks the dates and reaches behind the front row of milk
facts.activity: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change

facts.fact: Many shelf labels show a unit price, such as the price per litre, so different sizes can be compared; the bigger carton is often, but not always, cheaper per litre.
facts.hook: a kid has to decide between one big carton and two small ones
facts.activity: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change

facts.fact: A receipt lists every item and the amount paid, so reading it before leaving the till catches a scanning mistake while it is easy to fix.
facts.hook: milk scanned twice is noticed on the receipt
facts.activity: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change

facts.fact: US food safety guidance says perishable food such as milk should not sit out for more than two hours, or one hour above 32 degrees Celsius.
facts.hook: a kid stops at a friend's house on a hot day with the milk in the bag
facts.activity: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change

facts.fact: US food safety agencies advise keeping a refrigerator at 4 degrees Celsius, or 40 degrees Fahrenheit, or colder.
facts.hook: milk goes sour early and a kid checks the fridge dial
facts.activity: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change

facts.fact: On a care label, an empty triangle means any bleach may be used, while a triangle with a cross through it means the garment must not be bleached.
facts.hook: a kid reaches for the bleach to whiten a striped shirt and spots the crossed-out triangle just in time
facts.activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding

facts.fact: Dots on the iron symbol set the highest safe iron setting: one dot is low, about 110 degrees Celsius, two is medium, about 150, and three is high, about 200.
facts.hook: a nylon costume shirt goes shiny under an iron left on the cotton setting
facts.activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding

facts.fact: Laundry is sorted by colour because new dark or bright clothes can release dye into the wash water, and that dye can tint white and pale clothes.
facts.hook: a white school shirt comes out pink after sharing a load with one new red sock
facts.activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding

facts.fact: Wool shrinks in hot, sloshing water because tiny scales on each wool fibre open up and lock onto neighbouring fibres, pulling the knit tighter. This is called felting.
facts.hook: a grandparent's hand-knitted sweater comes out of a hot wash small enough for a doll
facts.activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding

facts.fact: Detergent molecules have one end that is attracted to water and another end that is attracted to oil and grease, so they lift greasy dirt off fabric into the wash water.
facts.hook: a pizza-grease stain that water alone would not shift finally lifts out with detergent
facts.activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding

facts.fact: Chlorine bleach must never be mixed with cleaners containing ammonia, because together they release chloramine, a toxic gas.
facts.hook: a kid helping with a big clean reads both bottle labels and stops before pouring one into the other
facts.activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding

facts.fact: According to the U.S. Fire Administration, failing to clean the dryer is the leading factor in home clothes dryer fires, because built-up lint blocks the airflow and lets heat collect.
facts.hook: a thick grey mat of lint in the dryer filter turns out to be a job nobody has been doing
facts.activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding

facts.fact: A paper tissue left in a pocket breaks apart in the wash and scatters white shreds over every item in the load, which is why pockets are checked before washing.
facts.hook: a whole load of dark clothes comes out speckled white from one forgotten tissue
facts.activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding

facts.fact: Clothes left crumpled in a dryer or basket after the cycle ends tend to wrinkle as they cool, so taking them out promptly and folding them helps keep them smooth.
facts.hook: a shirt left in the dryer overnight comes out creased on the morning of a job interview for a sibling
facts.activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding

facts.fact: In F. Scott Fitzgerald's novel The Great Gatsby, published in 1925, a green light glows at the end of Daisy Buchanan's dock, across the water from Gatsby's house.
facts.hook: a book club member notices Gatsby reaching toward a light on the very first night of the story
facts.activity: to track how a symbol changes meaning across the chapters of a novel

facts.fact: Readers usually take The Great Gatsby's green light to stand for Gatsby's hope of winning Daisy, and by the novel's end for a dream that cannot be reached, however rich he becomes.
facts.hook: two friends argue over whether the green light means the same thing in chapter one and the last chapter
facts.activity: to track how a symbol changes meaning across the chapters of a novel

facts.fact: In William Golding's Lord of the Flies, published in 1954, Ralph blows a conch shell like a horn to gather the stranded boys, and the shell becomes a sign of order and fair meetings.
facts.hook: a student marks every page where someone holds the conch and sees who gets to speak
facts.activity: to track how a symbol changes meaning across the chapters of a novel

facts.fact: In Lord of the Flies, the conch is smashed at the same moment Piggy is killed, which readers take as the final collapse of order among the boys.
facts.hook: a reader realizes the conch and Piggy disappear from the story together
facts.activity: to track how a symbol changes meaning across the chapters of a novel

facts.fact: In Lord of the Flies, Piggy's glasses are first used to light the boys' signal fire for rescue, and later Jack's tribe steals them in the night.
facts.hook: a student's chart shows the glasses changing hands from rescue to raid
facts.activity: to track how a symbol changes meaning across the chapters of a novel

facts.fact: In Lord of the Flies, the beast the boys fear on the mountain turns out to be the body of a dead airman under a parachute, which they mistake for a monster.
facts.hook: a reader rereads the mountain scene after learning what the shape really was
facts.activity: to track how a symbol changes meaning across the chapters of a novel

facts.fact: In Lord of the Flies, Simon comes to understand that the beast is not a creature on the island but something inside the boys themselves.
facts.hook: a book club discussion turns when someone asks whether the beast was ever real
facts.activity: to track how a symbol changes meaning across the chapters of a novel

facts.fact: In Nathaniel Hawthorne's The Scarlet Letter, published in 1850, Hester Prynne's scarlet A begins as a mark of shame, but years later many townspeople say it stands for Able.
facts.hook: a student tracks what the letter A means to the town at the start and near the end
facts.activity: to track how a symbol changes meaning across the chapters of a novel

facts.fact: In Harper Lee's To Kill a Mockingbird, published in 1960, Miss Maudie explains that it is a sin to kill a mockingbird because mockingbirds do nothing but sing their hearts out for us.
facts.hook: a reader starts listing which characters in the book are like mockingbirds
facts.activity: to track how a symbol changes meaning across the chapters of a novel

facts.fact: In Suzanne Collins's The Hunger Games, published in 2008, Madge Undersee gives Katniss a mockingjay pin before Katniss goes into the arena.
facts.hook: a reader wonders why a small gift in chapter one matters so much by the end of the series
facts.activity: to track how a symbol changes meaning across the chapters of a novel

facts.fact: In The Hunger Games, mockingjays were never planned by the Capitol: they came from its engineered jabberjay birds breeding with wild female mockingbirds.
facts.hook: a book club member argues that the bird already means something before Katniss ever wears it
facts.activity: to track how a symbol changes meaning across the chapters of a novel

facts.fact: A motif is an image, object or idea that keeps recurring through a literary work, and tracking where it reappears helps a reader see what it comes to mean.
facts.hook: a student keeps sticky notes on every page where a certain object shows up
facts.activity: to track how a symbol changes meaning across the chapters of a novel

facts.fact: In Shakespeare's English, wherefore means why, so Juliet's line "Wherefore art thou Romeo?" asks why he has to be Romeo, not where he is.
facts.hook: a student's paraphrase says Juliet is looking for Romeo, and a classmate checks the word
facts.activity: to read a Shakespeare scene and paraphrase the speeches into modern English

facts.fact: In Shakespeare's time, thou was used for close friends, family or people of lower rank, and sometimes as an insult, while you was the polite form for superiors and strangers.
facts.hook: a reader notices a character suddenly switching from you to thou in the middle of an argument
facts.activity: to read a Shakespeare scene and paraphrase the speeches into modern English

facts.fact: In Shakespeare's English, thee is the object form of thou, the way me is the object form of I, so "I love thee" means "I love you".
facts.hook: a student paraphrasing a speech gets stuck on why the word keeps changing between thou and thee
facts.activity: to read a Shakespeare scene and paraphrase the speeches into modern English

facts.fact: In Shakespeare's English, verbs used with thou usually end in -est, so "thou knowest" means "you know".
facts.hook: a reader stumbles over a line full of -est words until the pattern clicks
facts.activity: to read a Shakespeare scene and paraphrase the speeches into modern English

facts.fact: In Shakespeare's English, he or she verbs often end in -eth or -th, so doth means does and hath means has.
facts.hook: a paraphrase group turns "she hath" into plain modern English
facts.activity: to read a Shakespeare scene and paraphrase the speeches into modern English

facts.fact: In Shakespeare's English, anon means at once or soon, so a servant calling "Anon!" is saying "Coming right away!"
facts.hook: a class reads a scene where a servant keeps shouting the same odd word at the door
facts.activity: to read a Shakespeare scene and paraphrase the speeches into modern English

facts.fact: Prithee is a squeezed-together form of "I pray thee" and means please.
facts.hook: a student realizes a character who says prithee is being polite, not strange
facts.activity: to read a Shakespeare scene and paraphrase the speeches into modern English

facts.fact: In Shakespeare's English, a line beginning "Would that" expresses a wish, so "Would that it were so" means "I wish it were so".
facts.hook: a reader misreads a wish as a question until someone explains the old use of would
facts.activity: to read a Shakespeare scene and paraphrase the speeches into modern English

facts.fact: Shakespeare wrote much of his verse in iambic pentameter: lines of about ten syllables in five pairs, each an unstressed syllable followed by a stressed one.
facts.hook: a class taps out the beat of a speech on their desks, da-DUM five times
facts.activity: to read a Shakespeare scene and paraphrase the speeches into modern English

facts.fact: A soliloquy is a speech in which a character, usually alone on stage, speaks their private thoughts aloud so the audience can hear them.
facts.hook: a student paraphrasing a soliloquy realizes the character is telling the audience a secret
facts.activity: to read a Shakespeare scene and paraphrase the speeches into modern English

facts.fact: The stage direction exit is Latin for "he or she goes out," and exeunt is Latin for "they go out," used when two or more characters leave.
facts.hook: a reader wonders why the script says exeunt at the end of a crowded scene
facts.activity: to read a Shakespeare scene and paraphrase the speeches into modern English

facts.fact: A topic is a subject a novel is about, such as friendship, while a theme is a full statement of what the novel says about that subject.
facts.hook: a student writes "the theme is friendship" and a book club friend asks what the book says about it
facts.activity: to find the theme of a novel and back it up with a quotation from the text

facts.fact: A novel's theme is usually implied rather than stated outright, so readers infer it from what the characters do and what happens to them.
facts.hook: a reader searches the book for a sentence that says the moral and cannot find one
facts.activity: to find the theme of a novel and back it up with a quotation from the text

facts.fact: Novels commonly have more than one theme, so two readers can name different themes for the same book and both support them with evidence.
facts.hook: two friends at a book club each defend a different theme for the same novel
facts.activity: to find the theme of a novel and back it up with a quotation from the text

facts.fact: A theme is usually written about people in general rather than one character, so it could apply to readers' lives outside the book.
facts.hook: a student rewrites "Auggie learns to be brave" into something anyone could learn
facts.activity: to find the theme of a novel and back it up with a quotation from the text

facts.fact: A quotation used as evidence must be copied word for word, with the same spelling and punctuation, inside quotation marks.
facts.hook: a student quotes a line from memory, then checks the page and finds two words were wrong
facts.activity: to find the theme of a novel and back it up with a quotation from the text

facts.fact: In MLA style, three spaced periods, called an ellipsis, show where words have been left out of the middle of a quotation.
facts.hook: a quotation is too long for a paragraph, so a student trims the middle and has to show it
facts.activity: to find the theme of a novel and back it up with a quotation from the text

facts.fact: In MLA style, square brackets go around any word a writer adds to a quotation, to show it was not in the original text.
facts.hook: a quote says "he" and a student needs to make clear which character that means
facts.activity: to find the theme of a novel and back it up with a quotation from the text

facts.fact: In MLA style, an in-text citation for a novel gives the author's last name and the page number in parentheses, with no comma between them.
facts.hook: a teacher's note says the essay's quotes need page numbers the reader can check
facts.activity: to find the theme of a novel and back it up with a quotation from the text

facts.fact: In MLA style, a prose quotation longer than four lines is set as an indented block, half an inch from the margin, without quotation marks.
facts.hook: a student's favourite passage is too long to fit inside a sentence
facts.activity: to find the theme of a novel and back it up with a quotation from the text

facts.fact: A character's words are not always the author's view, because a novel may show a character's opinion only to argue against it.
facts.hook: a student quotes a bully's line as the book's message and a friend points out who said it
facts.activity: to find the theme of a novel and back it up with a quotation from the text

facts.fact: In R. J. Palacio's novel Wonder, published in 2012, the teacher Mr. Browne gives the precept "When given the choice between being right or being kind, choose kind."
facts.hook: a reader picks the one quotation that best backs up the book's theme about kindness
facts.activity: to find the theme of a novel and back it up with a quotation from the text

facts.fact: In S. E. Hinton's The Outsiders, published in 1967, Johnny's dying message to Ponyboy is to "stay gold," meaning to hold on to his goodness and innocence.
facts.hook: a book club uses two short words from a letter to prove what the whole novel is about
facts.activity: to find the theme of a novel and back it up with a quotation from the text

facts.fact: Foreshadowing is a hint early in a story about something that will happen later, often noticed only on a second reading.
facts.hook: a reader finishing a short story flips back and finds the clue was there on page one
facts.activity: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest

facts.fact: A red herring is a false clue placed on purpose to lead readers toward the wrong conclusion, so not every hint in a story is real foreshadowing.
facts.hook: a book club is sure they know the ending, and the clue they trusted was a trap
facts.activity: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest

facts.fact: Shirley Jackson's story The Lottery, published in The New Yorker in 1948, opens with children piling up stones, a detail that hints at how the lottery ends.
facts.hook: a class rereads the calm first paragraph after finishing the story and sees the stones differently
facts.activity: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest

facts.fact: In W. W. Jacobs's 1902 story The Monkey's Paw, Sergeant-Major Morris warns that the paw's wishes bring terrible results and throws it into the fire before the family rescues it.
facts.hook: a reader argues that the story warned everyone before the first wish was made
facts.activity: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest

facts.fact: In Richard Connell's 1924 story The Most Dangerous Game, the island's name, Ship-Trap Island, and sailors' fear of it hint at the danger waiting there.
facts.hook: a student notices that a place name gives away more than the characters realize
facts.activity: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest

facts.fact: In James Hurst's 1960 story The Scarlet Ibis, a storm-blown red bird dies in the family garden, foreshadowing the fate of the fragile boy Doodle.
facts.hook: a reader connects a bird's death to what happens to a character a few pages later
facts.activity: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest

facts.fact: A symbol is an object, person or event that stands for an idea beyond itself, and a reader must support any meaning they give it with details from the story.
facts.hook: a book club member claims a red door means danger and is asked to prove it from the text
facts.activity: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest

facts.fact: The haka Ka Mate was composed around 1820 by the Ngāti Toa chief Te Rauparaha to celebrate surviving after hiding from enemies who were chasing him.
facts.hook: a student learning the haka for a school welcome asks what the words are celebrating
facts.activity: to learn a traditional dance or song well enough to perform it at a community gathering

facts.fact: Hula kahiko, the older style of Hawaiian hula, is danced to chanting and traditional instruments such as gourd drums rather than to sung melodies.
facts.hook: a young dancer practising for a festival learns to keep time to a chant instead of a song
facts.activity: to learn a traditional dance or song well enough to perform it at a community gathering

facts.fact: Hula ʻauana, the modern style of Hawaiian hula that grew up under Western influence, is danced to sung melodies with instruments such as guitar and ukulele.
facts.hook: a cousin shows the difference between two hula styles by switching the music
facts.activity: to learn a traditional dance or song well enough to perform it at a community gathering

facts.fact: In the Philippine dance tinikling, two people tap bamboo poles on the ground twice and then clap them together on the third beat while dancers step in and out.
facts.hook: a nervous dancer keeps count out loud so their ankles stay clear of the closing poles
facts.activity: to learn a traditional dance or song well enough to perform it at a community gathering

facts.fact: A Chinese lion dance is normally performed by two dancers inside one costume, one working the head and the other the tail, to drums, gongs and cymbals.
facts.hook: two friends practising the lion dance keep tripping until they learn to move as one
facts.activity: to learn a traditional dance or song well enough to perform it at a community gathering

facts.fact: Bharatanatyam, a classical dance from Tamil Nadu in India, uses symbolic hand gestures called mudras that work like words to tell a story.
facts.hook: a student practising for a festival forgets one hand gesture and changes the meaning
facts.activity: to learn a traditional dance or song well enough to perform it at a community gathering

facts.fact: A Bharatanatyam dancer's first full solo performance is called an arangetram, meaning ascending the stage, and marks the end of their first formal training.
facts.hook: an older cousin's arangetram inspires a younger dancer to keep practising
facts.activity: to learn a traditional dance or song well enough to perform it at a community gathering

facts.fact: In traditional and competition Irish step dancing, dancers keep the upper body and arms held still while the feet do fast, intricate footwork.
facts.hook: a beginner's arms keep flapping until a teacher has them practise with hands pressed to their sides
facts.activity: to learn a traditional dance or song well enough to perform it at a community gathering

facts.fact: In call-and-response singing, a leader sings a line and the group answers; the pattern is deeply rooted in African musical traditions and in gospel and work songs.
facts.hook: a shy singer volunteers to lead the call at a community event
facts.activity: to learn a traditional dance or song well enough to perform it at a community gathering

facts.fact: In Hinduism, the soul passes through samsara, a cycle of birth, death and rebirth, and a person's karma, the results of their actions, shapes their next life.
facts.hook: a student compares notes with a Hindu friend at a family gathering after a grandparent's death
facts.activity: to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death

facts.fact: In Hinduism, moksha is liberation from the cycle of rebirth, and it is considered the highest goal of human life.
facts.hook: a kid asks a grandparent whether being reborn is something to hope for or to escape
facts.activity: to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death

facts.fact: Hindus usually cremate the dead, returning the body to the five elements, though young children and some holy people are traditionally buried instead.
facts.hook: a student notices two families at different ceremonies handle funerals very differently
facts.activity: to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death

facts.fact: Buddhism teaches rebirth but denies a permanent soul, called anatta or no-self, so what continues from life to life is a chain of karma, not an unchanging self.
facts.hook: two friends comparing Hindu and Buddhist beliefs discover a difference they had missed
facts.activity: to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death

facts.fact: In Buddhism, reaching nirvana ends the cycle of rebirth by ending the craving and ignorance that keep it going.
facts.hook: a student writes a comparison chart and has to explain how the cycle stops in each faith
facts.activity: to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death

facts.fact: Sikhism accepts rebirth and karma, but Guru Nanak taught that the body takes birth because of karma while salvation is attained through God's grace.
facts.hook: a Sikh classmate explains why good deeds alone are not the whole answer in her faith
facts.activity: to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death

facts.fact: In Islam, barzakh, an Arabic word for barrier, is the stage the soul passes through between a person's death and the resurrection.
facts.hook: a Muslim friend at a cemetery visit explains where her grandfather is now, according to her faith
facts.activity: to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death

facts.fact: Islam teaches that on the Day of Judgment, called Yawm al-Qiyamah, all people will be raised and judged, and sent to paradise or hell.
facts.hook: a comparison project puts one faith's single life and judgment beside another's many lives
facts.activity: to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death

facts.fact: The Catholic Church teaches purgatory, a state of purification after death before entering heaven, but most Protestant churches reject the idea.
facts.hook: two Christian friends are surprised to find their churches teach different things
facts.activity: to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death

facts.fact: The Nicene Creed, recited in many Christian churches, ends by looking forward to the resurrection of the dead and the life of the world to come.
facts.hook: a student hears the creed at a funeral and asks what those final words mean
facts.activity: to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death

facts.fact: The Jewish afterlife is often called olam ha-ba, meaning the world to come, though the phrase itself does not appear in the Hebrew Bible.
facts.hook: a Jewish friend explains a Hebrew phrase heard at a shiva house
facts.activity: to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death

facts.fact: Jewish views of the afterlife vary widely: Orthodox Judaism holds to a future resurrection of the dead, while Reform Judaism puts more weight on how people live now.
facts.hook: two Jewish cousins from different synagogues give different answers to the same question
facts.activity: to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death

facts.fact: Shabbat, the Jewish day of rest, begins at sunset on Friday and ends after nightfall on Saturday.
facts.hook: a kid spending a Friday at a friend's house is surprised when the phones are put away at sunset
facts.activity: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why

facts.fact: Havdalah, a Hebrew word meaning separation, is the ceremony that ends Shabbat on Saturday night once three stars can be seen in the sky.
facts.hook: a family's children race to the window to count the first three stars
facts.activity: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why

facts.fact: The Havdalah ceremony uses a cup of wine or grape juice, fragrant spices to smell, and a braided candle with several wicks.
facts.hook: a younger sibling is allowed to hold the braided candle for the first time
facts.activity: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why

facts.fact: Islam excuses people who are sick or travelling from the Ramadan fast, and they make up the missed days later.
facts.hook: a kid with a fever worries about missing the fast until a parent explains the rule
facts.activity: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why

facts.fact: During Ramadan, Muslims eat a meal called suhur before the dawn prayer, then go without food and drink until sunset.
facts.hook: an alarm goes off before dawn and the whole family gathers sleepily in the kitchen
facts.activity: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why

facts.fact: The Yom Kippur fast lasts about 25 hours, from sunset one day until after nightfall the next.
facts.hook: a kid who wants to try the fast asks how long it really lasts
facts.activity: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why

facts.fact: Jewish law waives the Yom Kippur fast when health is in danger, and in that case a person is actually required to eat or drink.
facts.hook: a diabetic cousin is told by the rabbi that eating is the religious thing to do
facts.activity: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why

facts.fact: On Buddhist observance days called uposatha, devout lay Buddhists may take eight precepts, including not eating after midday.
facts.hook: a kid visits a temple with family and learns why no one is eating an afternoon snack
facts.activity: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why

facts.fact: Ekadashi, the eleventh day of each half of the Hindu lunar month, is a fasting day dedicated to Vishnu on which many Hindus avoid grains and beans.
facts.hook: a kid wonders why a grandparent skips rice twice a month
facts.activity: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why

facts.fact: Muslims perform the ritual prayer, salah, five times a day, facing the Kaaba in Mecca.
facts.hook: a Muslim student at a community hall uses a phone compass to find the right direction to pray
facts.activity: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why

facts.fact: A Torah scroll is written without vowels or musical marks, so a bar or bat mitzvah student learns the chanted melody of their reading in advance from a printed book.
facts.hook: a student opens the real scroll at rehearsal and sees none of the marks from their practice book
facts.activity: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart

facts.fact: A Torah reader follows the words with a yad, a pointer whose name means hand, so that the parchment itself is not touched.
facts.hook: a nervous student's finger drifts toward the scroll and a teacher hands over the pointer
facts.activity: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart

facts.fact: At a bar or bat mitzvah, the young person often also chants the haftarah, a reading from the books of the Prophets.
facts.hook: a student realizes they have two readings to learn, not one
facts.activity: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart

facts.fact: Japji Sahib is also recited at the Sikh Khalsa initiation ceremony, called Amrit Sanchar.
facts.hook: a young Sikh preparing for initiation learns why the morning prayer matters so much
facts.activity: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart

facts.fact: A person who has memorized the entire Quran, all 114 chapters, is called a hafiz, and keeping it perfectly remembered takes constant practice.
facts.hook: a kid meets an older cousin who recites from memory what the kid is still learning
facts.activity: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart

facts.fact: In Mexican tradition, a quinceañera, the celebration of a girl's fifteenth birthday, usually begins with a Mass of thanksgiving.
facts.hook: a girl preparing for her quinceañera has to learn a reading for the Mass
facts.activity: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart

facts.fact: The method of loci is a memory trick of linking each part of a text to a place along a familiar route, then walking that route in your mind to recall it.
facts.hook: a kid memorizes each line of a reading by placing it in a different room of a grandparent's house
facts.activity: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart

facts.fact: In Spanish, a la derecha means to the right, but derecho, as in sigue derecho, means keep going straight, and learners often confuse the two.
facts.hook: a traveller turns right after being told to go straight on
facts.activity: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer

facts.fact: In French, à droite means to the right, while tout droit means straight ahead, a pair that often trips up learners asking for directions.
facts.hook: a student on a school trip turns right when the passer-by meant straight ahead
facts.activity: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer

facts.fact: In German, links means left, rechts means right, and geradeaus means straight ahead.
facts.hook: a kid at a language class practises by guiding a blindfolded friend around the room
facts.activity: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer

facts.fact: In Spanish, the question "¿Dónde está...?" means "Where is...?", and adding "por favor" makes it polite.
facts.hook: a student at a cultural festival needs to find the bathroom and has only one phrase ready
facts.activity: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer

facts.fact: In Spanish, a la izquierda means to the left, so la primera calle a la izquierda means the first street on the left.
facts.hook: a learner repeats the directions back to check which street to take
facts.activity: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer

facts.fact: In much of Latin America, a cuadra is a city block, so directions like dos cuadras mean two blocks.
facts.hook: a traveller counts streets instead of blocks and walks past the place
facts.activity: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer

facts.fact: When asking a stranger for directions, Spanish speakers usually use the polite usted, French speakers vous, and German speakers Sie, rather than the familiar form.
facts.hook: a student asks an older woman for directions and catches their too-casual pronoun
facts.activity: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer

facts.fact: In Spanish, "Más despacio, por favor" means "More slowly, please," a phrase that helps learners follow a fast answer.
facts.hook: a passer-by's directions come too fast until the student asks them to slow down
facts.activity: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer

facts.fact: In French, "Excusez-moi" is used to get a stranger's attention politely before asking a question, and "s'il vous plaît" means please.
facts.hook: a learner practising at home rehearses how to stop someone on the street politely
facts.activity: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer

facts.fact: In Mandarin Chinese, zuǒ means left and yòu means right, each said with its own tone.
facts.hook: a grandparent teaches a kid the two direction words while walking to the market
facts.activity: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer

facts.fact: Street names are rarely used in Japanese addresses outside a few cities such as Kyoto, so people giving directions usually point to landmarks and train stations.
facts.hook: a student asks for a street name in Japanese and gets directions by landmarks instead
facts.activity: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer

facts.fact: Language learners can usually understand more words than they can say, so a learner may follow spoken directions they could not yet give themselves.
facts.hook: a kid who could barely ask the question understands most of the answer
facts.activity: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer

facts.fact: In Spanish, the simple future adds an ending to the whole infinitive, so "hablar" (to speak) becomes "hablaré," meaning "I will speak."
facts.hook: a student writing to a pen pal keeps chopping "hablar" down to "habl-" and a friend spots the mistake
facts.activity: to write a paragraph in a new language about plans for next year using the future tense

facts.fact: Regular Spanish verbs share the same future endings whether they end in -ar, -er or -ir, so "I will eat" is "comeré" and "I will live" is "viviré."
facts.hook: a kid memorizing three separate ending charts discovers they only needed one
facts.activity: to write a paragraph in a new language about plans for next year using the future tense

facts.fact: Some Spanish verbs change their stem in the future tense: "tener" (to have) becomes "tendré," meaning "I will have," not "teneré."
facts.hook: a paragraph about next year's plans comes back with one verb circled in red
facts.activity: to write a paragraph in a new language about plans for next year using the future tense

facts.fact: Spanish speakers often talk about plans with "ir a" plus an infinitive, as in "Voy a estudiar," meaning "I am going to study."
facts.hook: a grandparent answers a question about next year using a form the textbook chapter never mentioned
facts.activity: to write a paragraph in a new language about plans for next year using the future tense

facts.fact: In French, the simple future is also built on the infinitive: "parler" (to speak) becomes "je parlerai," meaning "I will speak."
facts.hook: a student who learned Spanish first notices the French future works almost the same way
facts.activity: to write a paragraph in a new language about plans for next year using the future tense

facts.fact: The French verb "être" (to be) has an irregular future stem, "ser-," so "I will be" is "je serai."
facts.hook: a sentence about being in grade eight next year needs a verb that looks nothing like its infinitive
facts.activity: to write a paragraph in a new language about plans for next year using the future tense

facts.fact: French has a "near future" made with the verb "aller" plus an infinitive: "Je vais voyager" means "I am going to travel."
facts.hook: two friends argue over which future form sounds more natural in their summer-plans paragraph
facts.activity: to write a paragraph in a new language about plans for next year using the future tense

facts.fact: English verbs have no future ending; English shows the future with helper words such as "will" or "going to" placed before the verb.
facts.hook: a language partner asks what the English future ending is, and the answer surprises everyone
facts.activity: to write a paragraph in a new language about plans for next year using the future tense

facts.fact: German can form the future with "werden" plus an infinitive at the end of the sentence, as in "Ich werde Deutsch lernen," meaning "I will learn German."
facts.hook: a student keeps putting the main verb in the middle of the sentence and the German sounds wrong
facts.activity: to write a paragraph in a new language about plans for next year using the future tense

facts.fact: German speakers often use the present tense with a time word for future plans: "Nächstes Jahr fahre ich nach Berlin" means "Next year I am going to Berlin."
facts.hook: a kid thinks a German friend made a mistake by using the present tense for next year
facts.activity: to write a paragraph in a new language about plans for next year using the future tense

facts.fact: Mandarin Chinese verbs do not change form for tense; a future plan is shown with time words like "míngnián" (next year) or helper words like "huì" (will).
facts.hook: a learner searches a Mandarin grammar book for future endings that do not exist
facts.activity: to write a paragraph in a new language about plans for next year using the future tense

facts.fact: Japanese has no separate future tense: one verb form, called the non-past, covers both present and future, and a time word like "rainen" (next year) shows when.
facts.hook: a student's sentence about next year seems to be in the present until the time word is added
facts.activity: to write a paragraph in a new language about plans for next year using the future tense

facts.fact: Spanish nouns have grammatical gender, so a male dog is "el perro" and a female dog is "la perra."
facts.hook: a kid describing their female dog accidentally calls her by the male word
facts.activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences

facts.fact: In Spanish, the masculine plural "hermanos" can mean brothers, or brothers and sisters together, so "Tengo dos hermanos" might describe one brother and one sister.
facts.hook: a classmate is confused when a girl with a sister and a brother says she has two "hermanos"
facts.activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences

facts.fact: Spanish adjectives usually come after the noun they describe, so "a black cat" is "un gato negro."
facts.hook: a description of a pet sounds backwards until the word order is swapped
facts.activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences

facts.fact: Spanish generally uses "ser" for lasting traits and "estar" for temporary states: "Mi hermano es alto" means he is tall, while "Mi hermano está cansado" means he is tired.
facts.hook: a sentence about a brother accidentally says he is permanently tired
facts.activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences

facts.fact: French uses the verb "avoir" (to have) to give age: "J'ai douze ans" means "I am twelve," but word for word says "I have twelve years."
facts.hook: a student translates their age into French word for word from English and gets it wrong
facts.activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences

facts.fact: French possessive words agree with the thing owned, not the owner, so "sa mère" can mean either "his mother" or "her mother."
facts.hook: a listener cannot tell whose mother is being described until they ask
facts.activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences

facts.fact: In German, every noun begins with a capital letter, so "I have a dog and a cat" is written "Ich habe einen Hund und eine Katze."
facts.hook: a spell-checker flags every lowercase noun in a German description of a family
facts.activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences

facts.fact: German has one word, "Geschwister," for brothers and sisters together, the way English uses "siblings."
facts.hook: a kid with three brothers and a sister looks for a shorter way to say it
facts.activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences

facts.fact: Mandarin Chinese puts a measure word between a number and a noun: "one cat" is "yì zhī māo," where "zhī" is the measure word used for many animals.
facts.hook: a grandparent gently adds a missing little word to a grandchild's sentence about the cat
facts.activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences

facts.fact: Mandarin has separate words for older and younger siblings: "gēge" means older brother and "dìdi" means younger brother.
facts.hook: a kid has to decide which word fits a twin brother born ten minutes later
facts.activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences

facts.fact: Japanese uses different family words for your own family and someone else's: you call your own mother "haha" when talking to others, but a friend's mother is "okaasan."
facts.hook: a student politely describes their own mother with the word meant for someone else's
facts.activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences

facts.fact: In Spanish, "¿Cuánto cuesta?" means "How much does it cost?" and is the usual way to ask the price of one item.
facts.hook: a kid at a festival food stall points at a dish and needs the price before ordering
facts.activity: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs

facts.fact: To ask for the bill in a Spanish-speaking restaurant, a customer can say "La cuenta, por favor," meaning "The bill, please."
facts.hook: a family waits a long time for a bill that nobody asked for
facts.activity: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs

facts.fact: Spanish speakers ordering politely often say "Quisiera...", a softer form of "querer" (to want) that means "I would like..."
facts.hook: a student notices the server smiling more when they switch from "quiero" to "quisiera"
facts.activity: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs

facts.fact: In French, "Je voudrais..." means "I would like..." and sounds more polite than "Je veux...", which means "I want..."
facts.hook: a practice role-play where "I want" sounds rude and gets redone
facts.activity: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs

facts.fact: French speakers ask a price with "C'est combien ?" or "Combien ça coûte ?", both meaning "How much is it?"
facts.hook: a kid at a crêpe stand needs to check if their money is enough
facts.activity: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs

facts.fact: To ask for the bill in French, you say "L'addition, s'il vous plaît," meaning "The bill, please."
facts.hook: a student asks for "la note" or "la facture" and has to find the restaurant word instead
facts.activity: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs

facts.fact: French speakers normally address a server with the formal "vous," not the familiar "tu," which is kept for friends, family and children.
facts.hook: a student realizes they just spoke to a waiter the way they speak to their little cousin
facts.activity: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs

facts.fact: In German, a customer can ask for the bill by saying "Die Rechnung, bitte," meaning "The bill, please."
facts.hook: a class trip lunch runs late until someone remembers how to ask for the bill
facts.activity: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs

facts.fact: In Mandarin Chinese, "Duōshǎo qián?" means "How much money?" and is the everyday way to ask a price.
facts.hook: a kid at a dumpling stall practices the question before reaching the front of the line
facts.activity: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs

facts.fact: In Spanish, "para llevar" means "to take away," so a customer who wants food to go asks for it "para llevar."
facts.hook: an order meant to be eaten on the bus gets served on plates instead
facts.activity: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs

facts.fact: In France and many other European countries, prices use a comma where English uses a decimal point, so twelve euros fifty is written "12,50 €."
facts.hook: a kid reading a menu thinks a sandwich costs over a thousand euros

facts.fact: In Japan, tipping in restaurants is generally not expected, and leaving extra money on the table can confuse the staff.
facts.hook: a server runs after a family to return the change they left behind
facts.activity: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs

facts.fact: A mediator is a neutral third person who helps two sides reach their own agreement; unlike a judge, a mediator does not decide who is right.
facts.hook: two friends each expect the kid in the middle to announce a winner
facts.activity: to mediate an argument between two friends without taking a side

facts.fact: The word "mediate" comes from the Latin "medius," meaning "middle," because a mediator stands between the two sides.
facts.hook: a kid literally sits between two arguing friends at a party table
facts.activity: to mediate an argument between two friends without taking a side

facts.fact: Mediators usually start by setting ground rules, such as one person speaks at a time and no name-calling, which both sides agree to before talking.
facts.hook: an argument restarts twice until someone suggests rules for the conversation itself
facts.activity: to mediate an argument between two friends without taking a side

facts.fact: In mediation, each person usually gets to tell their side without being interrupted while the other person listens.
facts.hook: a friend keeps cutting in until the mediator asks them to wait their turn
facts.activity: to mediate an argument between two friends without taking a side

facts.fact: Paraphrasing, or restating what someone said in your own words, shows them they were heard and lets them correct any misunderstanding.
facts.hook: a friend realizes the fight started over something that was never actually said
facts.activity: to mediate an argument between two friends without taking a side

facts.fact: A "position" is what someone demands, while an "interest" is the reason they want it; people with clashing positions often have interests that could both be met.
facts.hook: two friends both demand the same seat, but for completely different reasons
facts.activity: to mediate an argument between two friends without taking a side

facts.fact: An "I-statement," such as "I feel left out when plans change," describes the speaker's own feelings instead of blaming, which makes the listener less likely to get defensive.
facts.hook: "You always ditch me" starts a fight, and a different sentence ends it
facts.activity: to mediate an argument between two friends without taking a side

facts.fact: Reframing means restating an insult in neutral words, turning "She's so selfish" into "You want a fairer share," so the conversation can keep moving.
facts.hook: a mediator catches an insult before it gets repeated to the other friend
facts.activity: to mediate an argument between two friends without taking a side

facts.fact: Mediators sometimes meet with each side privately, and this separate meeting is called a caucus.
facts.hook: a kid takes each friend aside one at a time at a family dinner
facts.activity: to mediate an argument between two friends without taking a side

facts.fact: Many schools run peer mediation programs, in which trained students help classmates settle conflicts, usually with an adult supervisor available.
facts.hook: a student who trained as a peer mediator uses the steps outside school for the first time
facts.activity: to mediate an argument between two friends without taking a side

facts.fact: Mediation usually ends with both sides agreeing on specific actions they will each take, so each person knows exactly what they promised.
facts.hook: a vague "let's just be friends again" falls apart the next day
facts.activity: to mediate an argument between two friends without taking a side

facts.fact: Robert's Rules of Order, a guide to running meetings fairly, was first published in 1876 by U.S. Army officer Henry Martyn Robert.
facts.hook: a club president finds a very old book on the shelf when meetings keep turning into shouting
facts.activity: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak

facts.fact: "Agenda" is a Latin word meaning "things to be done," and a meeting agenda lists the topics in the order they will be discussed.
facts.hook: a club meeting spends forty minutes on snacks because nobody wrote down what else to discuss
facts.activity: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak

facts.fact: In meeting procedure, a quorum is the minimum number of members who must be present for the group's decisions to count.
facts.hook: three members vote on the club budget before the rest arrive, and others object
facts.activity: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak

facts.fact: A motion is a formal proposal for a group to do something; under Robert's Rules, most motions need another member to second them before discussion begins.
facts.hook: one member's idea gets debated for ages even though nobody else supported it
facts.activity: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak

facts.fact: Minutes are the written record of a meeting, noting what was decided rather than every word said, and a secretary usually takes them.
facts.hook: two members remember last week's decision differently and nobody wrote it down
facts.activity: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak

facts.fact: Under Robert's Rules, a majority vote means more than half of the votes cast.
facts.hook: a club vote comes out five to four with two members not voting, and someone asks if it passed
facts.activity: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak

facts.fact: Under Robert's Rules, a tie vote means a motion fails, because it has not won more than half of the votes cast.
facts.hook: a club splits evenly on a field trip and has to work out what happens next
facts.activity: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak

facts.fact: A round-robin, in which each person speaks in turn around the circle, gives quieter members a guaranteed chance to share their ideas.
facts.hook: the shyest club member finally gets heard and has the best idea of the meeting
facts.activity: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak

facts.fact: A timekeeper watches how long each agenda item takes, so one topic does not use up the time planned for the others.
facts.hook: the club never reaches the last agenda item three meetings in a row
facts.activity: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak

facts.fact: A "parking lot" is a list where a meeting leader writes down off-topic ideas so they can be discussed later instead of derailing the current item.
facts.hook: a member's great but unrelated idea keeps pulling the meeting off track
facts.activity: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak

facts.fact: A meeting chair decides who speaks next and usually calls on someone who has not spoken yet before letting someone speak again.
facts.hook: the same two friends keep talking while others' hands stay raised
facts.activity: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak

facts.fact: Stating the problem as a shared question, like "We disagree about whether the ball was out," keeps the talk on the rule instead of on who is to blame.
facts.hook: a backyard game stops over one call, and "you cheated" is making it worse
facts.activity: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule

facts.fact: In "divide and choose," one person splits something into two parts and the other picks first, so the divider has a reason to make the parts equal.
facts.hook: two cousins fight over the last piece of cake at a birthday party
facts.activity: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule

facts.fact: In rock-paper-scissors, each choice beats exactly one other choice and loses to exactly one, so no choice is better than the others.
facts.hook: a kid insists rock always wins, and a friend proves it cannot
facts.activity: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule

facts.fact: A fair coin toss gives each side an equal chance, which is why sports such as American football and cricket use a coin toss to decide how a game starts.
facts.hook: two teams argue over who goes first until someone pulls out a coin
facts.activity: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule

facts.fact: The official Monopoly rules say that if a player lands on an unowned property and chooses not to buy it, the bank auctions it to the players.
facts.hook: a family game stalls when one player refuses to buy, and someone checks the rule sheet
facts.activity: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule

facts.fact: Collecting money on Free Parking in Monopoly is a common house rule, not one of the official rules, which is why players from different homes argue about it.
facts.hook: a friend lands on Free Parking and expects a pile of cash the host family never uses
facts.activity: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule

facts.fact: In formal chess, the touch-move rule says a player who deliberately touches one of their own pieces must move it, if that piece has a legal move.
facts.hook: a grandparent insists a grandchild move the knight they just picked up and put back
facts.activity: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule

facts.fact: The phrase "according to Hoyle" means following the rules exactly; it comes from Edmond Hoyle, whose 1742 book set down the rules of the card game whist.
facts.hook: a grandparent says a card game must be played "according to Hoyle" and a grandchild asks who Hoyle was
facts.activity: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule

facts.fact: Agreeing on a rule before a game starts is fairer than deciding it mid-game, because nobody yet knows whether the rule will help or hurt them.
facts.hook: a player suggests a new rule right when it would win them the game
facts.activity: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule

facts.fact: Scrabble players often settle arguments about whether a word is allowed by agreeing, before the game, on one dictionary to check.
facts.hook: a word game at a grandparent's house stops over whether "qi" is a real word
facts.activity: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule

facts.fact: A 2001 study that observed children on school playgrounds found that other children were present during 88 percent of bullying episodes.
facts.hook: a kid realizes they are almost never the only one who sees the teasing
facts.activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse

facts.fact: A 2001 study of school playgrounds found that when a classmate stepped in to stop bullying, the bullying stopped in more than half of the cases.
facts.hook: a kid hesitates, unsure whether saying anything could actually help
facts.activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse

facts.fact: Researchers usually define bullying as hurtful behavior that is repeated and involves an imbalance of power, unlike a one-time argument between equals.
facts.hook: a kid tries to decide whether what keeps happening to a classmate is just joking
facts.activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse

facts.fact: The bystander effect is the finding that people are less likely to help when many others are watching, because each person assumes someone else will act.
facts.hook: a whole group watches a classmate being teased and nobody moves
facts.activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse

facts.fact: Teasing often depends on an audience, so walking away with the targeted classmate, saying something like "Come on, let's go," can end it without a confrontation.
facts.hook: a kid at a party pulls a teased friend into another room to help with the snacks
facts.activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse

facts.fact: Distracting, such as changing the subject or starting a new game, can interrupt teasing without challenging the teaser directly.
facts.hook: a kid suddenly announces that the cake is being cut just as the teasing starts
facts.activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse

facts.fact: Answering an insult with another insult tends to escalate a situation, while a short, calm statement like "That's not funny, stop" gives nothing new to fight about.
facts.hook: a kid's clever comeback makes the teasing much worse, so they try again differently
facts.activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse

facts.fact: Checking in privately afterward with a classmate who was teased, and telling them it was not okay, can help them feel less alone even if nobody stepped in at the time.
facts.hook: a kid who froze during the teasing finds the classmate later to talk
facts.activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse

facts.fact: Telling a trusted adult is not tattling when the goal is to protect someone from harm rather than to get someone in trouble.
facts.hook: a kid worries about being called a snitch for reporting teasing that keeps happening
facts.activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse

facts.fact: An "upstander" is someone who speaks up or acts to support a person being mistreated, instead of only watching as a bystander.
facts.hook: a class discussion leaves a kid wondering which word describes what they did at lunch
facts.activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse

facts.fact: Laughing along with teasing, even just to fit in, signals approval to the person teasing and tends to encourage them to keep going.
facts.hook: a kid notices the teaser glancing at the laughing group after every joke
facts.activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse

facts.fact: Saving screenshots of hurtful online messages gives a trusted adult a record to act on, since messages can be deleted later.
facts.hook: mean comments in a group chat disappear before a kid can show anyone
facts.activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse

facts.fact: With three strides between hurdles, a hurdler takes off from the same foot every time, because an odd number of steps keeps the same leg leading.
facts.hook: a runner keeps arriving at each hurdle on the wrong foot and counts their steps
facts.activity: to hurdle a row of low hurdles with a three-step rhythm between them

facts.fact: The lead leg is the leg that goes over the hurdle first, and the trail leg is the one that follows, folding out to the side to clear the bar.
facts.hook: a runner keeps clipping hurdles with a trailing knee and a coach names the problem
facts.activity: to hurdle a row of low hurdles with a three-step rhythm between them

facts.fact: Hurdlers try to run over hurdles rather than jump them, staying low so they spend as little time in the air as possible.
facts.hook: a runner leaps high over each hurdle and falls far behind
facts.activity: to hurdle a row of low hurdles with a three-step rhythm between them

facts.fact: A sprint hurdler leans the chest forward over the lead leg while clearing a hurdle, so the body keeps moving forward instead of rising up.
facts.hook: a runner sitting upright over each hurdle lands slowly and loses rhythm
facts.activity: to hurdle a row of low hurdles with a three-step rhythm between them

facts.fact: Hurdlers take off farther from a hurdle than they land after it; taking off too close forces the lead knee up steeply and slows them down.
facts.hook: a runner crowding each hurdle keeps hitting it with their knee
facts.activity: to hurdle a row of low hurdles with a three-step rhythm between them

facts.fact: The lead leg should drive over the hurdle knee first and then straighten, rather than swinging up stiff and straight, which lifts the body too high.
facts.hook: a runner's stiff-legged kick makes them float over the hurdle
facts.activity: to hurdle a row of low hurdles with a three-step rhythm between them

facts.fact: While clearing a hurdle, the arm opposite the lead leg reaches forward to balance the twist of the body.
facts.hook: a runner's arms flail over each hurdle and their body twists off line
facts.activity: to hurdle a row of low hurdles with a three-step rhythm between them

facts.fact: Runners learning a three-step rhythm often practice with hurdles set lower and closer together than race spacing, then move them apart as they get faster.
facts.hook: a runner who cannot reach the next hurdle in three steps asks to move the hurdles
facts.activity: to hurdle a row of low hurdles with a three-step rhythm between them

facts.fact: Both sprint hurdle races, the men's 110 metres and the women's 100 metres, have ten hurdles.

facts.fact: The point guard is usually the team's main ball handler and is called the "1" in basketball's numbered positions.
facts.hook: a new player is told to "play the one" and does not know what it means
facts.activity: to call plays as a point guard and run a pick and roll

facts.fact: A pick, also called a screen, is when an offensive player stands still in a defender's path so a teammate can get free.
facts.hook: a guard cannot shake a tight defender until a teammate steps into the way
facts.activity: to call plays as a point guard and run a pick and roll

facts.fact: A screener must be standing still when contact is made; moving into the defender is an offensive foul called a moving screen.
facts.hook: a teammate's screen gets whistled because they stepped into the defender
facts.activity: to call plays as a point guard and run a pick and roll

facts.fact: In a pick and roll, after setting the screen, the screener turns and moves toward the basket, ready for a pass from the ball handler.
facts.hook: a screener stands still after the pick and nobody is open for the pass
facts.activity: to call plays as a point guard and run a pick and roll

facts.fact: In a "pick and pop," the screener steps away from the basket to an open spot for a jump shot instead of rolling toward the hoop.
facts.hook: the defense keeps stopping the roll, so the point guard calls a different option
facts.activity: to call plays as a point guard and run a pick and roll

facts.fact: Defenders can answer a pick by switching, meaning the two defenders trade the players they are guarding.
facts.hook: a guard comes off the screen and finds a new defender waiting
facts.activity: to call plays as a point guard and run a pick and roll

facts.fact: When defenders switch on a pick and roll, it can create a mismatch, such as a tall player guarding a quick guard or a short player guarding a tall one.
facts.hook: a point guard spots the smallest defender now guarding the team's tallest player
facts.activity: to call plays as a point guard and run a pick and roll

facts.fact: If both defenders go after the ball handler on a pick and roll, the rolling screener is often left open for a pass.
facts.hook: a point guard trapped by two defenders finally looks for the teammate cutting to the basket
facts.activity: to call plays as a point guard and run a pick and roll

facts.fact: Point guards often call plays with a hand signal, a number or a code word, so teammates know the play while the defense does not.
facts.hook: the other team keeps guessing plays because the calls are shouted in plain words
facts.activity: to call plays as a point guard and run a pick and roll

facts.fact: An assist is credited to a player whose pass leads directly to a teammate's basket.
facts.hook: a point guard who scored no points learns they helped score the most
facts.activity: to call plays as a point guard and run a pick and roll

facts.fact: The NBA adopted a 24-second shot clock for its 1954-55 season, requiring a team to attempt a shot within 24 seconds of getting the ball.

facts.fact: In front crawl, swimmers breathe out underwater through the mouth and nose, so they only need a quick breath in when the face turns to the side.
facts.hook: a swimmer tries to breathe out and in during one short turn and swallows water
facts.activity: to swim twenty-five metres front crawl with side breathing

facts.fact: Breathing every three strokes makes a swimmer breathe on alternate sides, because an odd number of arm strokes switches which arm is recovering.
facts.hook: a swimmer who only ever breathes on one side starts swimming crooked
facts.activity: to swim twenty-five metres front crawl with side breathing

facts.fact: Lifting the head forward to breathe makes the hips and legs sink, adding drag; turning the head to the side keeps the body flat.
facts.hook: a swimmer's legs drag lower every time they look up for air
facts.activity: to swim twenty-five metres front crawl with side breathing

facts.fact: During a side breath in front crawl, skilled swimmers keep one goggle lens in the water and turn only far enough for the mouth to clear the surface.
facts.hook: a swimmer turning their whole face to the sky loses speed at every breath
facts.activity: to swim twenty-five metres front crawl with side breathing

facts.fact: In front crawl, the body rolls from side to side with each stroke, and the breath is taken as part of that roll rather than by twisting the neck alone.
facts.hook: a swimmer's neck gets sore from craning to breathe while lying flat
facts.activity: to swim twenty-five metres front crawl with side breathing

facts.fact: A swimmer's head pushes a bow wave that leaves a dip in the water beside the face, letting the mouth reach air below the level of the flat surface.
facts.hook: a swimmer notices a small pocket of air right beside their face
facts.activity: to swim twenty-five metres front crawl with side breathing

facts.fact: The urge to breathe is triggered mainly by rising carbon dioxide in the blood, not by falling oxygen.
facts.hook: a swimmer who holds air in feels desperate for a breath halfway down the pool
facts.activity: to swim twenty-five metres front crawl with side breathing

facts.fact: The flutter kick in front crawl should come from the hips with fairly straight legs, since kicking mostly from the knees creates drag.
facts.hook: a swimmer kicks hard with bent knees and barely moves forward
facts.activity: to swim twenty-five metres front crawl with side breathing

facts.fact: For most swimmers, most of the forward push in front crawl comes from the arms, while the kick mainly keeps the legs high and the body balanced.
facts.hook: a swimmer tries to kick their way across the pool and tires quickly
facts.activity: to swim twenty-five metres front crawl with side breathing

facts.fact: Almost all swimmers choose front crawl in freestyle races because it is the fastest of the competitive swimming strokes.
facts.hook: a swimmer asks why every lane in the freestyle race uses the same stroke
facts.activity: to swim twenty-five metres front crawl with side breathing
